Your Berserker Fury lasts for 1 minute or until you end it (no action required), or if you have the {@condition Incapacitated} condition. Once you use this feature, you can't use it again until you finish a {@variantrule Long Rest|XPHB}.

feat.name: Bloodied Resilience
entries: You gain the following benefits.

entries.name: Bloodied Reaction
entries: While you're {@status Bloodied|XPHB} and take any damage, you can spend one of your {@variantrule Hit Point Dice|XPHB|Hit Dice} as a {@variantrule Reaction|XPHB} and reduce the damage you take by the amount rolled. You can only spend one {@variantrule Hit Point Dice|XPHB|Hit Die} at a time in this way, each time you are damaged.

entries.name: Bloodied Saves
entries: If you succeed on a Strength or Constitution saving throw that would normally cause you to take half damage, you take no damage instead.

feat.name: Bloody Resolve
entries: You gain the following benefits.

entries.name: Inner Fire
entries: Pain bolsters your resolve. When you take damage, you gain a +1 bonus to saving throws until the end of your next turn. While you are {@status Bloodied|XPHB}, the bonus to saves increases to +2, and you also gain a +1 bonus to attack and damage rolls until the end of your next turn.

feat.name: Boisterous Roar
entries: You gain the following benefits.

entries.name: Mighty Yell
entries: When you score a {@variantrule Critical Hit|XPHB} against a target, you let out a boisterous roar. You and allies within 5 feet of you have {@variantrule Resistance|XPHB} to all damage until the end of your next turn, and enemies within 5 feet of you have {@variantrule Vulnerability|XPHB} to all damage until the end of your next turn.

feat.name: Brazen Courage
entries: You gain the following benefits.

entries.name: Staunch Will
entries: You have {@variantrule Advantage|XPHB} on saving throws against the {@condition Frightened} condition. Also, you can use a {@variantrule Bonus Action|XPHB} to end the {@condition Frightened} condition on yourself a number of times per day equal to your {@variantrule Proficiency|XPHB|Proficiency Bonus}. You regain all expended uses when you finish a {@variantrule Long Rest|XPHB}.

feat.name: Chosen by Fate
entries: The Norns have chosen you for greater things. As a result, you gain the following benefits.

entries.name: Heroic Resurgence
entries: If you use {@variantrule Heroic Inspiration|XPHB} and the die roll fails, your use of {@variantrule Heroic Inspiration|XPHB} isn't expended (though you can't use it again for the same {@variantrule d20 Test|XPHB}).

entries.name: Heroic Windfall
entries: Whenever you use {@variantrule Heroic Inspiration|XPHB}, you regain a number of {@variantrule Hit Points|XPHB} equal to the die roll. If you are already at your {@variantrule Hit Points|XPHB|Hit Point maximum} when you use {@variantrule Heroic Inspiration|XPHB}, you instead gain {@variantrule Temporary Hit Points|XPHB} equal to the die roll. If you use {@variantrule Heroic Inspiration|XPHB}, and you roll higher on the die than is necessary to restore you to your {@variantrule Hit Points|XPHB|Hit Point maximum}, you gain any excess as {@variantrule Temporary Hit Points|XPHB}.

feat.name: Clout
entries: You gain the following benefits.

entries.name: Strong Influence
entries: You have {@variantrule Advantage|XPHB} on Charisma ({@skill Deception}, {@skill Intimidation}, and {@skill Persuasion}) checks when interacting with Vikings, professional warriors, and other martial folk. When using the {@feat Inspiring Leader|XPHB} feat, you also add your Strength modifier to the {@variantrule Temporary Hit Points|XPHB} you grant.

feat.name: Cold Water Warrior
entries: You have become accustomed to spending time in cold, treacherous waters. You gain the following benefits.

entries.name: Against the Current
entries: You automatically succeed on Strength checks to move through rough water.

entries.name: Cold Water Resistance
entries: You have {@variantrule Immunity|XPHB} to the effects of immersion in frigid water for a number of hours equal to your {@variantrule Proficiency|XPHB|Proficiency Bonus}.

entries.name: Swimming Leap
entries: You can make {@variantrule Long Jump|XPHB} and {@variantrule High Jump|XPHB} while swimming. If you swim at least 10 feet before a jump, you are considered to have a running start.

entries.name: Water Combatant
entries: You have {@variantrule Advantage|XPHB} on {@variantrule Initiative|XPHB} if you begin combat at least partially submerged in a body of water.

feat.name: Combat Flyting
entries: You gain the following benefits.

entries.name: Taunt
entries: As a {@variantrule Bonus Action|XPHB} on your turn, you can demean and bait an opponent within 30 feet of you that can hear and understand you. The target must succeed on a Charisma Saving Throw (DC 8 plus your Charisma modifier plus your {@variantrule Proficiency|XPHB|Proficiency Bonus}). On a failed save, the target takes a -1 penalty to attack rolls against you. You can use another {@variantrule Bonus Action|XPHB} on each of your subsequent turns to impart another -1 penalty; these effects stack to a maximum equal to your Charisma modifier. The target is allowed a save against each of these uses.

This effect ends if you drop to 0 {@variantrule Hit Points|XPHB}, have the {@condition Incapacitated} condition, you fail to use a {@variantrule Bonus Action|XPHB} each round to maintain it, or if the target moves more than 30 feet away from you. Otherwise, it continues for a maximum number of rounds equal to your {@variantrule Proficiency|XPHB|Proficiency Bonus}.
A creature that succeeds on the saving throw has {@variantrule Immunity|XPHB} to your Taunts for 24 hours.

feat.name: Cut Down the Nithingr
entries: You gain the following benefits.

entries.name: Coward's Bane
entries: You have a +2 bonus to damage rolls you make against creatures with the {@condition Frightened} condition.

entries.name: Frightful Visage
entries: When you use a spell or effect that causes the {@condition Frightened} condition, the duration is doubled.

feat.name: Endurance Conditioning
entries: You gain the following benefits.

entries.name: Quick Recovery
entries: Once per day, you can recover from 1 level of {@condition Exhaustion} after completing a {@variantrule Short Rest|XPHB}. In addition, a {@variantrule Long Rest|XPHB} removes 2 levels of {@condition Exhaustion} (instead of 1).

feat.name: Faster Crafting
entries: You gain the following benefits.

entries.name: Increased Artisan Proficiency
entries: You may either gain proficiency with an {@item Artisan's Tools|XPHB|Artisan's Tool} of your choice or {@variantrule Advantage|XPHB} on ability checks with a single {@item Artisan's Tools|XPHB|Artisan's Tool} with which you are already proficient.

entries.name: Combat Quickcraft
entries: While in combat, you can use a {@variantrule Bonus Action|XPHB} to craft one piece of gear from the Fast Crafting table, provided you have the {@item Artisan's Tools|XPHB} associated with that item, have proficiency with those tools, and do not have the {@condition Incapacitated} condition. The item lasts until the end of your next turn, or until you craft an additional item, at which point it falls apart.

entries.name: Short Rest Crafting
entries: You can craft an item from the Fast Crafting table during a {@variantrule Short Rest|XPHB}. It lasts until the end of the day, you use this aspect of the feat again, or your next {@variantrule Long Rest|XPHB}, whichever comes first, at which point it falls apart.

feat.name: Fjord Jumper
entries: You gain the following benefits.

entries.name: Cliff Leaping
entries: Your jumping distance (whether {@variantrule High Jump|XPHB|High} or {@variantrule Long Jump|XPHB|Long}) increases by 10 feet. You also have {@variantrule Advantage|XPHB} on any attack roll, Dexterity ({@skill Acrobatics}) check, or Strength ({@skill Athletics}) check you make after jumping at least 10 feet high or 20 feet long.

entries.name: Safe Diving
entries: If you fall into a liquid, such as water, and you spend your {@variantrule Reaction|XPHB} and succeed on a {@dc 15} Strength ({@skill Athletics}) or Dexterity ({@skill Acrobatics}) check, you take no damage from the fall. You also have {@variantrule Advantage|XPHB} on that check.

feat.name: Frost Eyed
entries: You gain the following benefits.

entries.name: Bright Eyed
entries: You have {@variantrule Advantage|XPHB} on Wisdom ({@skill Perception}) checks in {@variantrule Bright Light|XPHB}, and you do not have {@variantrule Disadvantage|XPHB} on Wisdom ({@skill Perception}) checks in {@variantrule Dim Light|XPHB}.

entries.name: Ice Tracker
entries: You are proficient in the {@skill Survival} skill. You treat both snow and icy terrain as normal terrain. You have {@variantrule Advantage|XPHB} on {@skill Survival} checks made in snow or ice.

feat.name: Frost-Touched
entries: Your connection to the ancient frozen power of the Northlands grants you the following benefits.

entries.name: Frost Magic
entries: You know your choice of the {@spell Frostbite|XPHB} or {@spell Ray of Frost|XPHB} cantrip. Choose one level 1 spell that deals Cold damage from the Druid, Sorcerer, or Wizard spell lists. You always have that spell and the {@spell Gust of Wind|XPHB} spell prepared. You can cast each of these spells without expending a spell slot. Once you cast either spell in this manner, you can't cast that spell again until you complete a {@variantrule Long Rest|XPHB}. You can also cast these spells using spell slots you have of the appropriate level. The spells' spellcasting ability is the ability increased by this feat.

feat.name: Giant Slayer
entries: You gain the following benefits.

entries.name: Duck and Weave
entries: If you are within 5 feet of a Large or larger creature, you can take the {@action Dodge} action as a {@variantrule Bonus Action|XPHB}.

entries.name: The Bigger They Are
entries: You're adept at knocking Large or larger creatures off their feet. When you use the {@itemMastery Topple} Weapon Mastery feature against a creature of Large or larger size, it has {@variantrule Disadvantage|XPHB} on its save.

feat.name: Greater Blessing of Baldur
entries: You gain the following benefits.

entries.name: Divine Resilience
entries: When you finish a {@variantrule Long Rest|XPHB}, you have {@variantrule Resistance|XPHB} to one damage type of your choice. This {@variantrule Resistance|XPHB} lasts until you finish a {@variantrule Long Rest|XPHB}.

feat.name: Greater Blessing of Boreas
entries: You gain the following benefits.

entries.name: Cold-Forged
entries: You have {@variantrule Resistance|XPHB} to Cold damage. Additionally, you can summon a shield of cold to block fire-based effects. As a {@variantrule Reaction|XPHB}, when you would take Fire damage, you can gain {@variantrule Resistance|XPHB} to Fire damage until the beginning of your next turn.

feat.name: Greater Blessing of Freyr and Freyja
entries: You gain the following benefits.

entries.name: Healing Magic
entries: You always have the {@spell Cure Wounds|XPHB} spell prepared. You can cast it without using a spell slot a number of times per day equal to your {@variantrule Proficiency|XPHB|Proficiency Bonus}, and you regain all uses when you finish a {@variantrule Long Rest|XPHB}. You can also cast it using spell slots you have of the appropriate level. The spell's spellcasting ability is the ability you chose when you took the Blessing of Freyr and Freyja feat. When you cast the spell on a Beast or Plant creature, the amount healed is doubled.

feat.name: Greater Blessing of Jormungandr
entries: You gain the following benefits.

entries.name: Serpent's Aspect
entries: You can channel the fear inspired by serpents and dragons. You can use an {@variantrule Action|XPHB} to force a number of creatures of your choice equal to your {@variantrule Proficiency|XPHB|Proficiency Bonus} within 30 feet of you that can see you to make a Wisdom saving throw (DC 8 plus your Charisma modifier and your {@variantrule Proficiency|XPHB|Proficiency Bonus}). On a failed save, a target has the {@condition Frightened} condition for 1 minute. Such a creature can repeat the saving throw at the end of each of its turns, ending the effect on itself on a success. You can use this feature a number of times equal to your {@variantrule Proficiency|XPHB|Proficiency Bonus}, and you regain all expended uses when you finish a {@variantrule Long Rest|XPHB}.

feat.name: Greater Blessing of Loki
entries: You gain the following benefits.

entries.name: Lord of Lies
entries: You have {@variantrule Advantage|XPHB} on Charisma ({@skill Deception}) checks.

entries.name: Mask Magic
entries: You always have the {@spell Alter Self|XPHB} spell prepared. You can cast it without expending a spell slot. Once you cast the spell in this way, you can't cast it in this way again until you finish a {@variantrule Long Rest|XPHB}. You can also cast it using spell slots you have of the appropriate level. The spell's spellcasting ability is the one you chose when you took the Blessing of Loki feat.

feat.name: Greater Blessing of Sif
entries: You gain the following benefits.

entries.name: Sif's Arrow
entries: As a {@variantrule Bonus Action|XPHB}, you can channel the power of the god Sif for 1 minute. During that time, when you hit with a ranged weapon attack, you deal extra damage of the weapon's type equal to your {@variantrule Proficiency|XPHB|Proficiency Bonus}. You can deal this extra damage no more than once on each of your turns. You can channel Sif's power in this way a number of times equal to your {@variantrule Proficiency|XPHB|Proficiency Bonus}, and you regain all expended uses when you finish a {@variantrule Long Rest|XPHB}.

feat.name: Greater Blessing of Thor
entries: You gain the following benefits.

entries.name: Storm Strike
entries: As a {@variantrule Bonus Action|XPHB}, you can channel the power of the god Thor for 1 minute. During that time, when you hit with a melee weapon attack, you deal extra damage of the weapon's type equal to your {@variantrule Proficiency|XPHB|Proficiency Bonus}. You can deal this extra damage no more than once on each of your turns. You can channel Thor's power in this way a number of times equal to your {@variantrule Proficiency|XPHB|Proficiency Bonus}, and you regain all expended uses when you finish a {@variantrule Long Rest|XPHB}.

feat.name: Greater Blessing of Wotan
entries: You gain the following benefits.

entries.name: Lore Master
entries: You have {@variantrule Advantage|XPHB} when rolling checks for the skill you selected for your Lore Bound trait from the Blessing of Wotan feat.

entries.name: Magical Foresight
entries: You always have the {@spell Augury|XPHB} spell prepared. You can cast it without expending a spell slot. Once you cast the spell in this way, you can't cast it in this way again until you finish a {@variantrule Long Rest|XPHB}. You can also cast this spell using spell slots you have of the appropriate level. The spell's spellcasting ability is the ability you chose when you took the Blessing of Wotan feat.

feat.name: Heroic Rush
entries: You gain the following benefits.

entries.name: Triumphant Boost
entries: When you score a {@variantrule Critical Hit|XPHB}, your {@variantrule Speed|XPHB} increases by 10 feet and you have {@variantrule Advantage|XPHB} on attack rolls. These benefits last until the end of your next turn.

entries.name: Victorious Inspiration
entries: When you reduce a creature to 0 {@variantrule Hit Points|XPHB} with an attack, you can choose one ally within 30 feet of you to receive {@variantrule Heroic Inspiration|XPHB}. The ally must use this {@variantrule Heroic Inspiration|XPHB} before the end of their next turn or it is wasted. You can use this feature twice, regaining all expended uses when you finish a {@variantrule Short Rest|XPHB|Short} or {@variantrule Long Rest|XPHB}.

feat.name: Holmganga Master
entries: Your experience in dueling gives you the following benefits.

entries.name: Battle Primed
entries: You have {@variantrule Advantage|XPHB} on {@variantrule Initiative|XPHB} at the start of a Holmganga or other duel.

entries.name: Duel Intimidation
entries: As a {@variantrule Bonus Action|XPHB}, you can make a Charisma ({@skill Intimidation}) check against your holmganga opponent. If the check succeeds (GM's discretion), you have {@variantrule Advantage|XPHB} on your next attack against the target, and the target has {@variantrule Disadvantage|XPHB} on its next attack against you.

feat.name: Hunter
entries: You gain the following benefits.

entries.name: Improved Tracking
entries: You have {@variantrule Advantage|XPHB} on Wisdom ({@skill Perception}) and Wisdom ({@skill Survival}) checks to follow or identify tracks.

entries.name: Greater Stealth
entries: You have {@variantrule Advantage|XPHB} when on Dexterity ({@skill Stealth}) checks while outdoors.

feat.name: Ice Mastery
entries: You gain the following benefits.

entries.name: Fimbulwinter's Grasp
entries: Your cold spells carry the strength of Fimbulwinter. Whenever you deal Cold damage to a creature with a spell of at least 1st level, you can choose one of the following additional effects.

items: The creature has {@variantrule Disadvantage|XPHB} on Dexterity checks for 1 minute as a terrible cold numbs its body.

The creature is coated in ice. It has the {@condition Restrained} condition until it succeeds on a Dexterity saving throw to free itself (equal to your spell saving throw DC) or takes at least 10 points of Bludgeoning or Fire damage. It can make the save to end this effect at the end of each of its turns.

The creature has {@variantrule Vulnerability|XPHB} to Cold damage for 1 minute. It can make a Constitution saving throw (equal to your spell saving throw DC) to end this effect at the end of each of its turns.

entries: You can use Fimbulwinter's Grasp a number of times equal to your {@variantrule Proficiency|XPHB|Proficiency Bonus}, and you regain all uses when you finish a {@variantrule Long Rest|XPHB}.

feat.name: Lightning Mastery
entries: You gain the following benefits.

entries.name: Thor's Fury
entries: Your lightning spells are laced with extra power. Whenever you deal Lightning damage to a creature with a spell of at least 1st level, you can choose one of the following additional effects.

items: The creature has the {@condition Stunned} condition until the end of your next turn, if it failed its save against the spell.

The creature takes half of the Lightning damage it initially took again at the beginning of its next turn. It can make a saving throw against your spell saving throw DC to negate this additional damage.

The creature gains {@variantrule Vulnerability|XPHB} to Lightning damage for 1 minute. It can make a Constitution saving throw (equal to your spell saving throw DC) to end this effect at the end of each of its turns.

entries: You can use Thor's Fury a number of times equal to your {@variantrule Proficiency|XPHB|Proficiency Bonus}, and you regain all uses when you finish a {@variantrule Long Rest|XPHB}.

feat.name: Living off the Land
entries: You gain the following benefits.

entries.name: Herbalist
entries: When you take a {@variantrule Long Rest|XPHB} in a natural area (natural caves, forest, tundra, etc.), you can locate materials to create a {@item Healer's Kit|XPHB}, and enough mushrooms, berries, or root vegetables to feed one Medium creature for one day.

entries.name: Survival Shelter
entries: You can spend 30 minutes to create a lean-to, bivouac, tree well, igloo, or other temporary shelter out of snow, tree boughs, rocks, and sticks, suitable for 4-5 Medium humanoids. While inside your survival shelter, creatures automatically succeed on Constitution saving throws against {@hazard Extreme Cold|XDMG} and {@hazard Extreme Heat|XDMG}.

feat.name: Long Haft Strike
entries: You gain the following benefits.

entries.name: Bypass Shield
entries: When you make an attack with a weapon with the Reach property against a creature wielding a {@item Shield|XPHB}, that creature doesn't benefit from the {@item Shield|XPHB}'s {@variantrule Armor Class|XPHB} bonus.

entries.name: Reaching Defense
entries: While wielding a weapon with reach, you have a +1 bonus to your {@variantrule Armor Class|XPHB}.

feat.name: Moon-Touched
entries: Your connection to the moon and its otherworldly radiance grants you the following benefits.

entries.name: Moon Magic
entries: You know your choice of the {@spell Dancing Lights|XPHB} or {@spell Light|XPHB} cantrip. Choose one level 1 spell that creates or emits light, such as {@spell Color Spray|XPHB} or {@spell Faerie Fire|XPHB}, from the Druid, Sorcerer, or Wizard spell lists. You always have that spell and the {@spell Moonbeam} spell prepared. You can cast each of these spells without expending a spell slot. Once you cast either spell in this way, you can't cast that spell in this way again until you finish a {@variantrule Long Rest|XPHB}. You can also cast these spells using spell slots you have of the appropriate level. The spells' spellcasting ability is the ability increased by this feat.

feat.name: Mounted Leap
entries: You gain the following benefits.

entries.name: Equestrian Prowess
entries: While you're riding a mount, that mount's jump distance is doubled.

entries.name: Leaping Charge Attack
entries: While jumping from a moving mount, your jump distance is calculated using the mount's {@variantrule Speed|XPHB} in place of yours (if its {@variantrule Speed|XPHB} is better than yours). If you make a successful melee attack roll against a creature after jumping, choose one of the following effects: gain a {@dice 1d8} bonus to the attack's damage roll, or make the target have the {@condition Prone} condition if the target is one size category larger than you or smaller. You can use this benefit only once on each of your turns.

feat.name: Northlands Hardiness
entries: You gain the following benefits.

entries.name: Cold Weather Resilience
entries: You have {@variantrule Advantage|XPHB} on saving throws against {@hazard Extreme Cold|XDMG}. If you already have {@variantrule Resistance|XPHB} to Cold damage, you also gain {@variantrule Advantage|XPHB} on saving throws against Cold damage.

entries.name: Inexhaustible
entries: The first time in a day that you receive a level of {@condition Exhaustion}, your {@variantrule Speed|XPHB} is not reduced. In addition, you may ignore the effects of {@condition Exhaustion} on a {@variantrule D20 Test|XPHB}.

feat.name: Primal
entries: You gain the following benefits.

entries.name: Primal Magic
entries: Choose two of the following spells: {@spell Animal Friendship|XPHB}, {@spell Entangle|XPHB}, {@spell Goodberry|XPHB}, or {@spell Speak with Animals|XPHB}. You always have those two spells and the {@spell Barkskin|XPHB} spell prepared. You can cast each of these spells without expending a spell slot. Once you cast a spell in this way, you can't cast that spell in this way again until you finish a {@variantrule Long Rest|XPHB}. You can also cast these spells using spell slots you have of the appropriate level. The spells' spellcasting ability is the ability increased by this feat.

feat.name: Ravens' Friend
entries: You gain the following benefits.

entries.name: Quick Study
entries: You gain proficiency in your choice of one of the following skills: {@skill Arcana}, {@skill History}, {@skill Investigation}, {@skill Nature}, or {@skill Religion}.

entries.name: Raven's Whispers
entries: Ravens sometimes tell you secrets. When you take the {@action Study} action, you can give yourself {@variantrule Advantage|XPHB} on the roll. You can do this a number of times equal to your {@variantrule Proficiency|XPHB|Proficiency Bonus}, and you regain all expended uses when you finish a {@variantrule Long Rest|XPHB}.

feat.name: Spear Expert
entries: You gain the following benefits.

entries.name: Deflecting Haft
entries: You can use a {@item Spear|XPHB} to deflect incoming attacks. While holding a {@item Spear|XPHB}, you gain a +1 bonus to your AC.

entries.name: Expert Thrower
entries: The range of any {@item Spear|XPHB} you throw is 30/90.

entries.name: Spear Ready
entries: If you take the {@action Ready} action to attack with the {@item Spear|XPHB}, you have {@variantrule Advantage|XPHB} on the triggered attack.

feat.name: Surtr's Touch
entries: You gain the following benefits.

entries.name: Touch of Flame
entries: As a {@variantrule Bonus Action|XPHB}, you can imbue your touch with the power of fire for 1 minute. During that time, when you hit with a melee weapon attack, you deal extra Fire damage equal to your {@variantrule Proficiency|XPHB|Proficiency Bonus}. You can use this feat a number of times equal to your {@variantrule Proficiency|XPHB|Proficiency Bonus}, and you regain all expended uses when you finish a {@variantrule Long Rest|XPHB}.

feat.name: Trickster's Toolbox
entries: You gain the following benefits.

entries.name: Tricksy Magic
entries: Choose two level 1 spells from the Enchantment or Illusion school of magic. You always have those spells and the {@spell Tasha's hideous laughter|XPHB|Hideous Laughter} spell prepared. You can cast each of these spells without expending a spell slot. Once you cast one of these spells in this way, you can't cast that spell in this way again until you finish a {@variantrule Long Rest|XPHB}. You can also cast these spells using spell slots you have of the appropriate level. The spells' spellcasting ability is the ability increased by this feat.

feat.name: Wild Lore
entries: You gain the following benefits.

entries.name: Knowledge of the Land
entries: You have {@variantrule Advantage|XPHB} on all Intelligence ({@skill Nature}) checks.

entries.name: Provider
entries: You can use your knowledge of the land to find food and fresh water for yourself and up to 3 other people each day.

feat.name: Glima
entries: Glima is the name for a style of unarmed fighting in the North similar to wrestling. When you hit with an unarmed attack against a creature within 5 feet of you, if that creature is one size larger than you or smaller, you can choose to force that creature to make a Strength saving throw (DC equals 8 + your {@variantrule Proficiency|XPHB|Proficiency Bonus} + your Strength modifier). On a failed save, the target creature has the {@condition Prone} condition.

feat.name: Raider's Rush
entries: You have {@variantrule Advantage|XPHB} on attack rolls against any creature within 5 feet of one of your allies if you move at least 15 feet and stop within 5 feet of that ally.

feat.name: Savagery
entries: When you make your first melee weapon attack roll on your turn, you can decide to attack savagely. Doing so allows you to add your {@variantrule Proficiency|XPHB|Proficiency Bonus} to your melee weapon damage rolls but lowers your AC by 2 until the start of your next turn.

feat.name: Shield Wall
entries: You gain the following benefits.

entries.name: Shield Ally
entries: When a creature you can see hits an ally adjacent to you with an attack, you can take a {@variantrule Reaction|XPHB} to grant your ally your {@item Shield|XPHB}'s {@variantrule Armor Class|XPHB} bonus against the triggering attack.

entries.name: Shoulder to Shoulder
entries: When you and an ally are both wielding a {@item Shield|XPHB} and are adjacent to each other, you both gain a +1 bonus to {@variantrule Armor Class|XPHB}.

feat.name: Skirmisher
entries: You gain the following benefits.

entries.name: Mobility
entries: Your {@variantrule Speed|XPHB} increases by 10 feet.

entries.name: Strike and Fade
entries: Once on each of your turns, you can deal extra damage equal to your {@variantrule Proficiency|XPHB|Proficiency Bonus} to a creature you hit with an attack that deals Bludgeoning, Piercing, or Slashing damage, as long as you have moved 15 feet prior to making the attack.

feat.name: Underfoot
entries: You can end your movement in a space occupied by a creature two sizes larger than you. If you attack that creature while you share its space, you have {@variantrule Advantage|XPHB} on your attack roll. If that creature attacks you while it shares your space, it has {@variantrule Disadvantage|XPHB} on its attack roll.

deity.name: Angrboda
deity.title: Mother of Monsters
altNames: Mother of Fenris, Hel, and Jormungandr
deity.symbol: Black Tree and a Coiled Serpent
deity.worshipers: Giantkin, giants, monsters, seers, werekin, witches
entries: Firstborn child of Aurgelmir, the wild and sorrowful Angrboda is a shapechanging jotun goddess. She is the untamed face of nature, the uncontained force of change destroying the old to make way for the new. Angrboda believes the gods perverted the path of nature when they constructed this world from the body of her father, and only its destruction can restore things to their true state. Her influence is felt in the darkened sky, the howling winds, and the roars of the monsters in the dark.

When she chooses, Angrboda appears as a fierce giant with wild, red-streaked black hair; a beautiful raven-haired maiden; or a gnarled hag with ebony-clawed hands. She typically spares no thought to her garb, appearance, or behavior, preferring to act in the moment. The few icons or statues of her show her wearing ragged robes of fur and animal hides and carrying a skull-tipped staff.

entries.name: Worshipers
entries: Angrboda's followers include giants, trolls, ogres, and giantkin. Many werekin venerate her as the mother of Fenris and the World Serpent. Across the Northlands, prayers and sacrifices to Angrboda are often offered during dangerous weather or when monsters attack, if only to persuade the goddess to vent her wrath elsewhere.

Some druid circles and witch covens in the North revere Angrboda not as an evil destroyer but as a force of change. In Vargrike, a cult of werekin and lycanthrope druids called the Ironhowl Circle conducts rites around ancient standing stones and trains monstrous beasts to protect wild places from encroaching civilization.

entries.name: Symbols and Books
entries: Angrboda's symbols include a black tree and a coiled serpent. Before they were stolen by Wotan, she was associated most closely with the Eiwaz and Thurisaz runes. Outside of Jotunheim, cults found displaying any of the symbols of Angrboda are rooted out and their members either exiled or killed.

Most of Angrboda's lore is passed from believer to believer as sung or spoken liturgy. However, she does have a sacred text called Blotmodr, the Sacrificial Womb, an account of her love affair with Loki and the birth of their monstrous children. Between the various salacious or horrible entries are fell curses, ancient magics, and world-changing prophecies.

entries.name: Shrines and Priests
entries: In the lands south of Jotunheim, Angrboda is only worshiped in carefully hidden shrines or wild places touched by storm and grief. Most giant settlements have a public shrine to Angrboda, and she is openly worshiped.

Angrboda's priests never stay in one place for long, preferring to wander in the wilds communing with their goddess and her children. They are a two-edged blade, offering healing and aid, especially to those in childbirth or injured by monstrous creatures. Yet they also rail against despoiling the wilderness and are never reticent about bringing down the wrath of their goddess.

deity.name: Baldur
deity.title: Bringer of Light
deity.symbol: A golden sunburst shining off the blade of a silver sword
entries: Baldur, the son of Wotan and Frigg, is the god of radiance, purity, forgiveness, and peace. He appears as a tall, black-haired Northlander with a trim black beard and bluebells woven into his tidy plaited hair. His eyes are the bright blue of the sky reflected off a winter-frozen lake. Baldur travels the worlds with a perpetual smile and can often be found singing quietly to himself. The clothing he wears is of purest white fabric, except for his polished leather boots. All his attire seems to gleam like steel in the sunlight.

The Fair is renowned as one of the kindliest of the Aesir, and he takes great pains to aid anyone in need. Tales abound of lost travelers finding both food and their bearings on a sun-dappled patch of ground, and of warriors in desperate straits who, while fighting to protect their companions, have a losing battle turn in their favor due to a piercing ray of sunlight blinding their foes. To aid one of his devout who are fighting undead abominations, Baldur might send a lance of light to destroy the hated creature outright.

The Bleeding God is prophesied to be slain at the hands of his blind brother Hodr, which will herald the beginning of Fimbulwinter and the coming of Ragnarok. After the destruction of the world, Baldur will be resurrected to rule over the gods of the new world that will form.

entries.name: Worshipers
entries: Baldur's followers include valorous warriors, poets, lovers, and travelers. In the Northlands, more paladins swear oaths to him than to any of the other Aesir, including the war gods, such as Tyr. His faith is commonplace and well known, and even those who have never prayed at one of the Bleeding God's shrines know some of his songs and aphorisms.

Though Baldur is not a god of battle, his followers know that to fail to fight the evil represented by giants and other monsters of the North is to invite a world devoid of light and beauty. Against such opponents, warriors who fight in the name of Baldur are as implacable as any war-weary veteran. When confronting more human opponents, however, followers of Baldur are more likely to give quarter and try to determine the root of the conflict.

entries.name: Symbols And Books
entries: Baldur's symbol is a golden sunburst shining off the blade of a silver sword.

The primary holy text of Baldur is The Mirror of Pure Joy, copies of which are written by hand on sheets of birch bark that have been sun-bleached until they are almost white. Each book has been copied by hand from another copy, so there are large variances in the text due to changes in interpretations, as well as due to simple errors made by the hand that produced the copy.

Though they are not recognized as official texts of the faith, many children's tales recounting Baldur's deeds and beliefs have been transcribed to parchment and subsequently reproduced so that they are easily found by children and families. Some of the most popular titles are The Healer of Song, Word of the Fairest-Spoken, and Rebirth of the Sun.

entries.name: Shrines and Priests
entries: Every sizable settlement in the Northlands has a temple to Baldur. His holy houses take the form of multilevel longhouses with a central steel spire that, by the laws of the faith, must be taller than the surrounding structures. During sunrise and again at sunset, the bright Northern sun shines off the spire, creating an aurora-like effect around it.

Shrines to The Bleeding God can be found along every well-traveled road and path, and even on the peaks of some mountains, though these are often pillaged by giants or other monsters hateful of the worship of the Aesir. If possible, even his shrines have some sort of reflective component built into them, such as a silver coin or a shard of steel.

Priests of Baldur, sometimes called lightbringers, dress in meticulously kept robes of gold and white, and wear copper or bronze helmets on their heads. Some more whimsical members of the clergy affix golden wings or sunbursts to the sides of the caps, resting just above the wearer's ears. Most priests are robust and physically attractive, though this is not a requirement. Priests of Baldur are welcome everywhere goodly people gather in the Northlands.

deity.name: Bergelmir
deity.title: Voice of the Titans
altNames: God of Glory, Revenge, and Domination
deity.symbol: A spiral of ice and a screaming face
entries: Bergelmir is the last son of Aurgelmir and the only child of the First Giant to survive the death of his father other than Angrboda. He is the embodiment of all of the rage and fury the giants continue to nurse over Aurgelmir's murder. As First Warlord, it is Bergelmir who will lead the jotun and giants against the hated gods when the time comes for them to seek their revenge. All giants call upon Bergelmir when they charge into battle, hoping the Voice of the Titans will bless them with victory.

Bergelmir appears as a towering, deathly pale giant cloaked in the hides of monstrous beasts. It is said that a nimbus of killing frost surrounds him, his voice can shatter mountains, and his long beard and hair are formed of jagged spikes of ice. In statues and icons, he is shown wearing rune-carved armor and holding a two-handed maul.

entries.name: Worshipers
entries: Bergelmir is worshiped by all giants, ogres, and trolls. He is the patron of the jotun and clearly favors them over other giants, yet all the descendants of Aurgelmir fear slighting the God of Glory lest he withhold his blessings on them in times of need. He is also venerated by some berserkers, reavers, and warlords, who swear oaths to him in times of desperation, begging for the strength to dominate or destroy. Ceremonies and rites dedicated to Bergelmir often involve roaring chants, blood rituals, and oaths of vengeance.
The Bellowing Storm demands that his followers always prove their strength over weaker creatures, conquer in his name, punish cowardice and timidity, and glorify combat.

entries.name: Symbols and Books
entries: Bergelmir's symbols include a spiral of ice and a screaming face. Before they were stolen by Wotan, he was represented by the Berkanan, Sowilo, and Tiwaz runes. His followers inscribe his symbol onto weapons, bones, and shields, believing his sigil will strengthen them in battle.

The Voice of the Titans has many sacred texts, despite his appearance as a revenge-obsessed god of war. Among the most important are The Bellowing, a hymnal of jotun chant-cycles passed down from the First Age, and the Oathbound Litany, a chronicle of leadership studied by giant warlords and would-be cult leaders.

entries.name: Shrines and Priests
entries: Temples to Bergelmir are built from blackened ice, colossal bones, or the ribcages of titanic beasts, and can be found deep in mountain caverns or atop howling cliffs, where the wind amplifies his name. One well-known temple is the Hall of Resounding Glory in Agnalan, where Bergelmir's priests train giantkin warriors to fill Jotunheim's armies.

Bergelmir's priests are war leaders, raiders, tyrants, and warlords, always at the forefront of the charge with howling prayers on their lips. Though the god's clergy has no formal structure, all clerics regularly challenge each other in ritual duels to establish their status in relation to each other and to maintain their authority. Bergelmir's most feared priest is Kolrjot Icehowl, a jotun skald who once froze an avalanche with a single bellow. He wields a great axe named Rifkljufr, or "Rib-Splitter," and leads the Bloodhail raiders out of a hidden redoubt north of the Alvavann Forest in Wolfheim.

deity.name: Bengta
deity.title: The Bear Maiden
deity.symbol: A golden bee gathering pollen from a honeysuckle plant set in front of a radiant violet eye
entries: The Bear Maiden is beloved in the Northlands. She is the preeminent goddess of the bearfolk and patron of Bjornrike, but her worship as a protector and champion spans the breadth of the North. Bengta presents a contrasting aspect, both the peaceful provider of nature's bounty, and, at the same time, the fierce guardian, like a mother bear protecting her cubs.

The Beekeeper teaches that community is all-important and must be protected, even at great cost. She leads by example, showing that every member of a community must pitch in and contribute to the success of the whole. She is a proponent of law and order who encourages agents of dissent in a settlement to rethink their methods, but she is unafraid to destroy them if they can't work within the structure of society.

Bengta is a warrior, and her tales are rife with battles against the monsters and giants that threaten settlements. She has a love-hate relationship with the fey of the Northlands, as she often treats with the animal lords to good effect while battling the mischievous pucks that collapse the peace of a community into disarray.

entries.name: Worshipers
entries: Bengta is most worshiped by bearfolk, but she boasts almost as many human and dwarf adherents. She receives prayers from healers and berserkers, who ask for skill and guidance in battle and its aftermath, but community leaders look to her for guidance when their settlements are beset by challenges. As travel increases throughout the Northlands and opportunities for profit grow, more and more merchants turn to The Golden Radiance to pray for safety from bandits, monsters, and other threats that haunt road and trail.

The Bear Maiden demands that her worshipers place those they care for above all else. She requires selfless action and constant vigilance against evils that would affect close-knit groups. She encourages her chosen to create joy and prosperity for all within their reach. And whenever this prosperity is threatened, she demands swift action to destroy the cause of the disturbance. A follower who spends their time industriously is likely to receive the god's full favor.

entries.name: Symbols And Books
entries: Bengta's symbol is a golden bee gathering pollen from a honeysuckle plant set in front of a radiant violet eye. Many of her priests weave honeysuckle vines through their braided hair, or they wear wreaths of blossoming vines either as crowns or around their necks.

The Bear Maiden's sacred books include the Promise of Light (a book of prophecies, parables, and stories of kindness, forgiveness, and healing) and the Summer Book (a book of prayers, hymns, and blessings). Another, much beloved book is titled after one of her nicknames: Keeper of Community. The work is a collection of parables promoting the virtues of community, battle and marching songs, and recipes. Most copies of the book have numerous notations and loose pages containing the music and lyrics of new songs as well as favorite recipes.

entries.name: Shrines and Priests
entries: The bearfolk settlement of Bjornrike is the heart of Bengta's worship, and one can barely take more than a few steps before finding a small shrine or statue, or even a bench or beehive marked with a favorite aphorism or line of scripture. Likewise, the trade roads leading to and from the city are littered with shrines and offerings. Shrines can be found throughout the Northlands, in the wide plains of southern lands, and even on some distant planes.

Temples to The Beekeeper are surrounded by meadows of clover and lavender, and honeysuckle climbs the exteriors unhindered, even sometimes completely obscuring the walls and roofs with vines and blossoms. Every temple also serves as an apiary, providing honey and wax to nearby communities while keeping enough to appease the Goddess.

Priests of Bengta are gregarious and friendly, rarely eschewing an opportunity to share a meal and story with neighbor or stranger alike. Despite their open and warm natures, Bengta's priests are on the front line of battle against any threat to community.

deity.name: Boreas
deity.title: The Devouring Wind
altNames: Bringer of Storms and Killing Cold
deity.symbol: A circling and knotted line of wind
deity.worshipers: Frost giants, ice elves, ogres, trolls
entries: Boreas, God of the North Wind, seeks to blanket the entirety of the world in an endless winter. He feels that the prophesied Fimbulwinter that will precede the death of the gods at Ragnarok is confirmation that his desire will come to pass, though he would like that time to be sooner than later. Regardless of when that day will come, the Devouring Wind is tireless in his efforts to visit evil and strife upon the world, knowing that his favored giants are sturdy enough to withstand the icy death he brews.

Once, Boreas was the primordial spirit of the North Wind, birthed at the dawn of creation. He was exiled by his sibling wind spirits over a disagreement about mortals, and he fled into the Northlands. Here, he shed his spiritual form to be reborn as a god.

His typical guise is an eagle-winged frost giant dressed in furs and sporting a wild, wind-swept beard. Like most of the gods, though, he can appear however he wishes, though all of his aspects are shaggy and unkempt.

entries.name: Worshipers
entries: Boreas's primary followers are the giants and goblinoids of the Northlands, which include ogres, trolls, true giants, goblins, hobgoblins, and bugbears. Clans of Northern dwarves that have turned away from community and embraced bitterness and greed also claim the patronage of the Devouring Wind. Some of Boreas's most powerful and prominent adherents are even more monstrous in nature, with many winter wolves taking up his call and delivering frigid deaths to the unworthy and unbelieving. Worshipers sacrifice captive creatures by exposing them naked to the winter night. They sabotage hearth fires and storehouses and assist yeti, ice maidens, and other creatures to do Boreas's will. Theft is no crime for Boreas's followers, and burning the homes, hearths, and altars of his enemies is a sacred duty.

Boreas demands that those who serve him work to destroy the power of the other gods and cover the North with ice and snow. The faithful believe their veneration of the North Wind will spare them when he achieves his inevitable victory.

entries.name: Symbols And Books
entries: The holy symbol of Boreas is a circling and knotted line of wind.

No sacred texts are claimed by Boreas. Some of his adherents use the blood and bone of their victims to paint crude scenes of his power and dominance beneath rocky outcroppings and on cavern walls. These depictions always show humans and other smaller folk beneath the giant boots and talons of Boreas's monstrous followers. The similarity in style and substance of these painted devotions has led some explorers to conclude that a single hand has created these grisly works of art. A few of them dare suppose that the artist is the Devouring Wind himself, seeking to build his own prominence in the absence of having others to do it for him.

entries.name: Shrines and Priests
entries: Shrines to Boreas are few and far between, and temples are virtually unheard of. The Devouring Wind does not need holy sites or places of power; he feeds directly from the blood spilled by his followers and uses that to empower his giants and other monstrous worshipers to commit more violence against the humanoids that try to tame and settle the wild North.

Boreas has no organized priesthood. He grants power to the depraved and vicious clerics, druids, and rangers who spill blood in his name. Some warlocks hear the whispers of the Devouring Wind and do their bloody bidding in exchange for power and protection from the cold.

deity.name: Freyr and Freyja
deity.title: Twins of Passion
altNames: Lord and Lady of the Vanir
God of Nature and the Living World
Goddess of Beauty, Fertility, and Magic
deity.symbol: Antlers tied with sheafs of wheat, a glass of wine or mead, and golden boars (Freyr). A golden falcon feather, falcons and cats (Freyja)
entries: Twin deities of the Vanir, Freyr and Freyja were once hostages but now dwell among the Aesir as equals. They taught the gods witchcraft and druidic lore, and together sponsored Njord, the sea god, for divinity. Freyr brings peace and the harvest, protects farmers, and opposes fire giants. Freyja is a skilled witch associated with beauty, fertility, gold, magic, and war. Both adventurous deities have seen their share of battles. As the patron of shield-maidens, Freyja is gathering fallen warriors to her hall of Sessrumnir, where they are forming an army the Vanir will lead alongside the Aesir at Ragnarok.

Freyr is depicted as a golden-haired, beautiful man crowned with antlers or wheat, often shown riding the shining metal boar known as Gullinbursti. Freyja is depicted as a radiant, golden-haired woman wearing a falcon-feather cloak and the fabled Necklace of the Brisings. She is often shown riding in a chariot pulled by huge magical cats.

entries.name: Worshipers
entries: Freyr's followers include rustic people of the land, such as farmers, hunters, shepherds, druids, and witches. To follow Freyr is to cherish the bounty of the land and not despoil nature. It is common practice to spill a drop of mead for the god before a meal as thanks.

Freyja's worshipers are bards, lovers, seers, wizards, and shield-maidens. Freyja teaches that beauty can be found in all things: the wild, magic, and even the battlefield. Martial training is practiced daily by those who venerate Freyja, and many of her worshipers wear a small gold pin or bead on their clothes.
Kosslock or "Final Kiss," a particularly dark sect of Freyja's faithful, believes that finishing off wounded foes on the battlefield with a poisoned blade honors the goddess.

entries.name: Symbols and Books
entries: Common symbols of Freyr are antlers tied with sheafs of wheat, a glass of wine or mead, and golden boars. Freyja's symbols are a golden falcon feather, as well as falcons and cats. The Jera rune is also associated with the twins.

Freyr's sacred text is Coming of the Green Gods, a farmer's gospel of planting techniques, animal husbandry, soil-blessing chants, and crop rotation wisdom. The holy writing of Freyja is Wisdom of the Vanir, a grimoire of charms, curses, natural omens, and divination rituals.

entries.name: Shrines and Priests
entries: The largest stone temple dedicated to the twins is the Temple of the Hive and Flower, in the city of Bjeornheim. This sweet-smelling temple's priests include a few bearfolk as well as humans. A particularly well-known temple to Freyja, Feather Rise Hall, is a cliff-top shrine in Thrumagard where falcons sacred to Freyja roost. The legends say the goddess can bless the particularly faithful with the power to fly.

Priests of Freyr typically travel from village to village or put down roots in one community. Freyja's clerics, on the other hand, tend to be itinerant, making their way as seers, healers, and shield-maidens.

deity.name: Loki
deity.title: Shapeshifting God of Cunning
altNames: Father of Fenris, Hel, and Jormungandr
deity.symbol: The blade, the intertwined serpents, and the golden net
entries: A god of tricksters, Loki is the son of a jotun and an Aesir goddess. He swore a blood-oath with Wotan to become a member of the Aesir, but he has never been wholly trusted by the other gods, and for good reasons. An unwise dalliance with Angrboda resulted in Fenris, Jormungandr, and Hel, the goddess of death. Wotan and other gods believe he is fated to usher in the end of all things, but they plan on locking the Trickster God away before he can begin Ragnarok. Loki plots to avoid any destiny he doesn't choose for himself. Indeed, his greatest trick may be turning the Age of the Void into a time of rebirth. Loki's cunning is legendary, and despite his reputation, he helps mortals far more often than he gets credit for.

When he chooses, vainglorious Loki appears as a slightly androgynous man with unkempt red hair and a sly smile. He wears fine clothing, often embroidered with runes or patterns. On statues or symbols, he is often displayed as holding daggers or a golden net, or a serpent.

entries.name: Worshipers
entries: Those who follow Loki are inevitably thieves, cultists, gamblers, reavers, and others who chafe against the confines of "normal" society. Despite his presence among the Aesir, many giants give offerings to him. Some void cultists worship him as the Herald of the End Time, the Bringer of Woe. The worshipers of Loki embrace change and relish the opportunity to see the world in a different way. They take any chance to tweak the noses of the powerful with a good trick. A popular ritual is to commit small acts of theft during a full moon on a winter's night.

The Fading Legion, a secret cult of Loki operating out of Stannisgard, specializes in theft, arson, defacement, and even kidnappings and murder, for the right price. They use illusions and face-altering magics to disguise their operatives.

entries.name: Symbols and Books
entries: Loki's symbols include the blade, the intertwined serpents, and the golden net. He is also associated with the Perto rune. If the god of deception has a sacred text, it is the Lokasenna, a humorous narrative poem regaling some of Loki's greatest pranks, quips, and deeds both for and against the gods. Some older versions of this tome contain charms, cantrips, and hexes, as well as suggestions on how to use them to maximize the chaos of a situation.
A popular expletive in the Northlands is to say, "Loki's luck be upon you!" which Loki finds quite unfair.

entries.name: Shrines and Priests
entries: There are no formal temples to Loki, though many make prayers and offerings to him, hoping to gain a bit of luck for their endeavors. A few localized cults that venerate him keep small shrines decorated with preserved serpents hanging in golden nets. The Mirthmasks, a well-know "secret" order among the Skaldholm bardic schools, playfully conducts rituals to Loki, especially on the night of the Askrhlattr festival.
Perhaps Loki's most renowned priest is Brynja Firegrin, a flame giantkin, who uses pranks and laughter to heal and spread hope among the downtrodden.

deity.name: Njord
deity.title: God of the Seas
deity.symbol: A blue longship, the golden trident, and a gold coin marked with a pattern of waves
entries: Njord rules the sea not with chaos but with wisdom. He commands the winds, blesses the sails of the worthy, and watches over coastal peoples and fisherfolk. Though calm and generous, he is not a god to be taken lightly. Storms gather at his call, and wizards whisper that he hoards all the ancient knowledge lost beneath the sea.

Njord appears as a man in his late fifties, stout and sunburned, with streaks of silver through his brown hair and beard. His garments ripple as though submerged, and his piercing blue eyes reflect the stillness of deep water. He is usually depicted in robes of blue and sea-green, wearing gold coin jewelry, holding a trident, standing atop waves, or casting a net over a storm.

entries.name: Worshipers
entries: Njord is honored by sailors, shipwrights, fishers, traders, sea-wizards, and any who ply the sea. Coastal towns host feasts in his name before longships depart on raids or to celebrate the return of the fishing fleet. His clerics bless sails and use spells to calm storms or call forth the wind. Merchants and reavers alike spill a bit of wine or mead overboard for Njord at the start of a journey to ensure fine winds and a profitable voyage.
The Oarbound, an order of Njord sea-priests, sails between ports, offering healing, divination, and weather magic. Half of what they are given as payment is thrown to the sea in thanks to their god.

entries.name: Symbols and Books
entries: The symbols of the sea god include a blue longship, the golden trident, and a gold coin marked with a pattern of waves. He is commonly associated with the Laukaz rune. Njord's priests have many sacred texts and tomes, collectively called the Tide-Songs, which are full of sea-lore, tidal observations, and navigational charts.

The oldest known text of Njord are the fragments of the Scrolls of Foam and Wave. Many believe these scattered parchments are pieces of Njord's spellbook from before he ascended to divinity. The scrolls are said to contain forgotten storm-binding spells and even the ritual he used to hold back the Swive, but not enough fragments have yet been found to reconstruct that ceremony.

entries.name: Shrines and Priests
entries: Shrines to Njord exist in harbor towns, cliffside grottos, and aboard seafaring vessels. His altars are often built from driftwood, coral, or stone, and decorated with shells, fish-bone charms, and pieces of shipwrecks. Priests of Njord wear robes of sea-blue, often adorned with silver fish-hooks. They preside over sea burials, bless voyages, and call or calm winds with ritual chants.

The greatest temple to Njord is the Tideward Hall in Noatun. The altar there contains a barnacle-encrusted staff left by Njord as a symbol of his patronage. The high priest of the temple is Vetra Saltvoice (trollkin priest) famed across the Northlands for singing storms to sleep and calling whales to her aid.

deity.name: Sif
deity.title: The Sword Maiden
altNames: Patron of Women Warriors and Archers
deity.symbol: A bundled sheaf of arrows and a silver sword
entries: Golden-haired Sif is the goddess of battle and mistress of Valkyries, the battle-maiden of the frozen worlds, the enemy of giants and trolls. She excels at archery and brewing ale. She calls Freyja her "ale-sister" and Freyr her "hunting brother." Sif is the Mistress of the Valkyries, leading them on behalf of Wotan to collect the honored dead. As a goddess of war, she encourages the development of fighting prowess, in contrast to the followers of her husband Thor, who value strength over skill. Above all, she despises cowardice and treachery. Sif's presence is strong wherever courage and loyalty dwell.

Sif appears as a sharp-featured human woman, beautiful and strong. She wears silver clothing or armor and has long hair made of actual gold, usually braided. On statues and symbols, she wears armor and holds a sword raised high.

entries.name: Worshipers
entries: Sif's faithful, known as sifjar, include archers, female warriors, and farmers. Anyone who fights for honor or to protect can earn her favor. The sifjar gather at her temples for three great musters every year: Remembrance (Spring), Fortitude (Autumn), and Repentance (Winter). Sif teaches might alone is not enough; it is skill and the honor that matter. She demands her followers be fierce and fight for what they believe in. Those who pray to Sif before a battle may receive her blessing. On rare occasions, she attends a battle personally and leaves a magical gift to those truly exceptional warriors.

Two of her most notable worshipers are Rhiam Skyddaboggon, a human shield-maiden raising a warband in Huldramose, and Olympia Ferrymantle, a dwarven dragon-hunting scout from Trollheim, who is said to move with Sif's own grace.

entries.name: Symbols and Books
entries: Sif's symbols include a bundled sheaf of arrows and a silver sword. She is associated with the protective nature of the rune Gebo. Rather than sacred texts, sifjar memorize tales of worthy warriors and champions. One of the most revered is Regina of the Bow, who is held as a paragon of archers. Many followers honor Sif by braiding yellow ribbons into their hair or dyeing a lock of hair gold. Every morning, the faithful practice their fighting skills, engaging in non-lethal duels. Sacrifices to Sif include ritually burning arrows or broken weapons in sacred fires, especially during one of the great musters.

entries.name: Shrines and Priests
entries: Temples to Sif are fortified halls doubling as training grounds. All her clergy must prove their prowess by dueling the head of the local order at least three times a year. Visitors to the temples are similarly encouraged to train. The temple walls ring with the clash of steel, and many adventurers seek them out for training or pilgrimage.

Priests of Sif are skilled warriors, chosen for their quick wit, physical aptitude, and strength of personality. Many believe Valkyries watch over them, not to protect them but to ensure they are worthy to be among Sif's priesthood.

deity.name: Thor
deity.title: The Thunderer
altNames: Slayer of Monsters and Protector of Mortals
Patron of the North, Dwarves, and Reavers
deity.symbol: The hammer, a representation of Mjolnir
entries: Thor, the red-maned God of Thunder, is the boldest of Wotan's sons and the mightiest warrior in the heavens. Riding his chariot pulled by celestial goats and wielding the rune-etched hammer Mjolnir, he is the eternal foe of giants, trolls, and monsters. Thunder is his war cry, and lightning the swing of his arm. Though not known for wisdom, he possesses unmatched courage, good humor, and a roaring love of battle. When not battling foes, he dwells in his hall, Bilskirnir, with his wife Sif.

Thor appears as a burly, broad-shouldered man clad in sleeveless armor, with wild red hair and a beard like a blazing storm cloud. His eyes shine with fierce joy when battle calls. Around his waist is Megingjord, a magical belt of might inscribed with ancient runes, and Mjolnir always hangs at his side, short-hafted and thick-headed and radiating power.

entries.name: Worshipers
entries: Thor's followers are warriors, reavers, raiders, guards, and any who live by the strength of their arm. Dwarves are both wary and reverent of Thor. They honor him both as creator and protector, but some also believe he smote their empire during the Reaving for favoring Volund over him.
Everyone from raiders to farmers make offerings to Thor. Warriors look to him for strength and bravery, while peaceful folk display his hammer to ward off trolls and keep danger from their doors.

Thor teaches his faithful to believe strength is both virtue and weapon, and to meet every challenge head-on. To them, death in battle is the highest honor; Thor despises a "straw death" from age or illness. A popular battle cry to the storm god is "Thor's thunder in your ears!"

entries.name: Symbols and Books
entries: Thor's most sacred symbol is the hammer, a representation of Mjolnir, worn as a charm or painted on shields. He is associated with the rune Thurisaz. Many mortals, not just his worshipers, see storms as a symbol of Thor's will or wrath. Lightning is said to strike places of great valor or danger. Thunderstorms during births or duels are seen as blessings. In rural households, hammer-shaped charms are used to bless weddings, protect newborns, or keep trolls away from the hearth.

Those who follow Thor hold no faith in sacred books or tomes, preferring to tell stories and songs of his adventures around crackling fires with mugs of mead in hand. Some of the most popular are the Lay of Hymir, in which Thor catches Jormungandr on a fishing line, and Haustlong, where Thor battles a mighty jotun.

entries.name: Shrines and Priests
entries: Most shrines to Thor are open to the sky and often built atop windswept cliffs or along storm-wracked coastlines. Offerings of bear's blood, oxen, and shattered weapons are left upon the altar, preferably during thunderstorms. His greatest temple is the Hall of Golden Hammers in Thrumagard, led by Ulfrich Thorson, a famed dwarven priest of the Order of the Thunderer. Thor's clergy wear armor at all times and are taught to never refuse a challenge. They preach strength, honesty, and defiance in the face of evil. Sparring contests between Thor's priests and those of his wife Sif are common, testing whether brute strength or refined technique wins the gods' favor.

deity.name: Tyr
deity.title: The God of Justice
entries: The God of Justice is worshiped widely by the humans and dwarves of the Northlands, and his priests can be found among all of the so-called civilized peoples. Though he and his clergy are feared and loathed by the giants and their servitors, even they respect his right to prosecute his responsibilities on the battlefield. Wherever oaths are upheld or blood is spilled in conflict, Tyr is said to walk.

Unlike other gods of war, Tyr does not embrace chaos. His name is often invoked when oaths are sworn or contracts are signed. The duality of war and justice runs through the worship of Tyr. He directs that battle should be used as a means to protect communities from the dangers posed by giants and other agents that work in opposition to orderly society. In times of peace, leaders look to the priesthood of Tyr to guide them to deliver justice for their people and work toward what is best for the greatest number of people.

The sagas tell that Tyr lost his right hand and gained the title the Odd Handed while endeavoring with the Aesir to bind and fetter Fenris, the Twilight Wolf. The truth, however, is somewhat different. To avoid being bound, Fenris played at being tame enough to live in peace with the Aesir. To prove his claim, he urged Tyr to place his hand in the wolf's mouth. Despite his words and true to his monstrous nature, Fenris bit Tyr's hand off and swallowed it in a single gulp. Sometimes the other gods snicker to one another about Tyr's gullibility, though the fierce God of Justice's glares quell the whispers with remarkable speed.

entries.name: Worshipers
entries: Warriors, magistrates, guards, judges, and community leaders pay homage to the Odd Handed. Those who feel they have been treated unfairly call to Tyr for justice and aid, as do duelists and those who seek to redress the wrongs done to them in battle.

Tyr calls on his followers to obey the laws and commands of their jarls, as it is order that separates the hero from the lowly cur. Bring battle to the forces that oppose righteous order. Treat others with hospitality and honor.

entries.name: Symbols And Books
entries: Tyr's symbol is a longsword held upright.

The Law of Sword and Axe holds the tenets of Tyr's faith and serves as a guide to living a good and just life. It is written in a straightforward, if somewhat dry, style that is intended to require little interpretation, though scholars still argue over it as they do everything else. Oaths in the Northlands are often sworn while holding one's left hand to Tyr's holy text.

entries.name: Shrines and Priests
entries: Temples to Tyr are sturdy and workmanlike, more like fortified keeps and armories than the wonders of art and majesty favored by less martial faiths. Though most structures and habitations in the Northlands are built of wood, mud, and moss, Tyr's temples are constructed of stone, if possible. In a siege, they serve as command centers and, if the siege goes poorly, as a final bastion to fall back to. In times of peace, they serve as courthouses and even sometimes as feasthalls.

Priests of Tyr do not shy away from battle, nor do they lust for it. They see that war is just one method by which disputes can be determined and peace can be assured. In larger cities, some priests take on roles as judges and magistrates, ensuring that contracts are fulfilled as promised and that laws are followed to the letter.

deity.name: Volund
deity.title: Master of Fire and Anvil
altNames: God of Horses, Smiths, and Marriage
deity.symbol: Anvil, emblazoned with a horse's head, and weapons (hammer or battleaxe)
entries: Volund is the god of earth and fire, of the hammer's ring as it lands upon the anvil and the hiss of steam as a new-forged sword is quenched. He is one of the divine patrons of the reaver dwarves, but many others revere him as a paragon artisan and lord of all the jewels and precious metals in the earth. Though primarily a god of fire, creation, and smith work, Volund is also the god of family and hospitality, especially among humans. As a hammer has two heads, the Master of Fire and Anvil has inspired the crafting of potent magical items, but he has also inspired ancient, cursed relics that still linger in the world into the present day.

The Smith God appears as a bald, powerfully built dwarf with a long red beard divided into braids set with metal clasps and rings. In statues and iconography, he is always shown wearing practical clothes that match the rare reports of visions of the god. His wide belt is festooned with all manner of smithing and crafting tools.

entries.name: Worshipers
entries: The followers of Volund are typically smiths, craftspeople, artists, and reavers, but anyone who feels the fierce joy of creation and crafting can find a place among Volund's faithful. Those who venerate the Smith God often wear an anvil-shaped pin or amulet.

Volund demands his followers craft great works in his name and harness stone, metal, and fire to their will. He encourages forming bonds within a community (such as blood-oaths and marriages). Some humans add expertise in riding to his divine edicts. His faithful makes pilgrimages to shrines and temples far and wide, especially to the major forge-shrines, adding something, no matter how small, that they have personally wrought to every shrine they visit.

entries.name: Symbols and Books
entries: The symbols of Volund are his anvil, emblazoned with a horse's head, and his weapons, the hammer among humans and the battleaxe among dwarves. He is associated with the Kaunen rune. His holy writings are the Book of the Anvil and the Saga of Volund's Wanderings, both concerned with tempering steel and souls.

Clerics at his temples turn each liturgy into crafting sessions where circles of priest-smiths sing hymns from Volund's Wanderings as they hammer. The anvils of the major forge-shrines are tuned to ring out different notes and chords, creating a ritual effect that transforms items into Volund's songsteel.

entries.name: Shrines and Priests
entries: Volund is one of the most widely worshiped gods, with major temples across the Northlands and more in southern lands. The greatest of his forge-shrines is Stannasgard's Shrine of a Thousand Anvils, which is a popular pilgrimage destination. Those seeking Volund's blessing bring ingots of metal for the creation of new anvils.

On days holy to Volund, his priests work at an ever-burning forge, their hammers striking in unison like a monk's plainchant. The greatest of Volund's clerics include the aggressive Opir Skapti (human warpriest), priest-captain of the young dwarven company of the Hall of Spears in Stannasgard.

deity.name: Wotan
deity.title: All Father
altNames: God of the Tree and Raven
King of Asgard and Lord of Valhalla
deity.symbol: The world tree Yggdrasil, the single eye, and the runes
entries: The most powerful of the Aesir, Wotan led the gods to defeat Aurgelmir at the dawn of time, carving up the body of the first giant to make the world, and so he earned the enmity of all giantkind. He rewards the heroic dead with a place at his table and is the patron of proud and ruthless kings. Ravens fly across the world to bring him news and rumors, and from his enchanted throne he can spy upon all creation. He plucked out his own eye in return for wisdom, and when that wasn't enough, he hung himself from the Tree of Worlds, stealing secrets from the Void beyond existence. He is the god of strife, chieftains, and kings, master of runes and stealer of wisdom. Wotan's superior cunning and wisdom ensures he triumphs time and time again, until Ragnarok swallows the world.

Wotan appears as a dour, powerfully built, older man with long, grey hair and a flowing beard. He wears patched and somewhat ragged clothing in shades of blue, grey, and brown. Often, he has a raven on each shoulder and a pair of wolves by his side. All depictions of Wotan show his missing right eye.

entries.name: Worshipers
entries: Wotan is most beloved by jarls, wizards, and those who value wisdom. Among dwarves, the worship of Wotan the All-Father represents a step in life, beyond callow youth and into maturity and middle age. Older men and dwarves proclaim their loyalty at his shrines and feed his ravens bread, but some women revere Wotan as well, for the swift news his ravens bring or for the power of rune magic. In addition, Wotan has many followers among the ravenfolk. They see him as the greatest of figures, for his servants are feathered and wise, and Wotan is as wily as every ravenfolk wishes to be.

Wotan demands his followers be wise, canny in judgment, skilled in poetry, and quick to lead in honorable battle. Cowards and fools find no sympathy from the Rune God. Warriors pray to him, hoping to earn luck and victory in battle, or if defeat is fated, they pray to attract the attention of his Valkyries and a place in Valhalla.

entries.name: Symbols and Books
entries: Wotan's symbols are many, including the world tree Yggdrasil, the single eye, and the runes. Sometimes his favored animals, ravens and wolves, are taken as his sign as well. Wotan's two ravens are named Huginn (Thought) and Muninn (Memory), and his wolves are named Freki (Greedy) and Geri (Ravenous).

Writing is Wotan's favored form of recording wisdom. He expects all his followers to be literate so they may read his many sacred texts. Among these, the most prominent are the Lay of Mimir, the Tree of Knowledge, and the scroll called the Secret Runes. Fiercely guarded in the heart of Runaskr is the only known copy of Aldrunir—"Giant Magics of the First Age"—which contains lost enchantments Wotan seized from the jotun before the world was made.

entries.name: Shrines and Priests
entries: The greatest shrine of Wotan is in the dwarven hall of Stannasgard, where the chanting of the rune chorus never ceases, and the altar fires burn in his honor. This accolade may soon shift to the Hall of the Watching Eye in Wolfheim, which will be the largest temple to Wotan in the North once it is completed.

The kings and captains of the dwarven reavers are Wotan's priests or at least his devoted worshipers. His priests wear raven feathers to honor him. Possibly the greatest of his clerics is Brokk Kolisen of the Shrine of the Gallows Tree (Trollheim), a black-bearded human raised among dwarves, and loved and respected for his understanding of their ways. He leads many expeditions to fight giants in Jotunheim.

deity.name: Gullveig
deity.title: The Matron of Coin
deity.worshipers: Only scattered followers, mostly cultists and witches
entries: Gullveig is a vanished goddess of wealth and magic, and she is known in particular for her skill with illusions and transmutations. Though weakened in the ages since her disappearance, she was once widely worshiped by mortals and elves alike. Some fragmentary lore suggests the Silver Witch instigated the war between the Aesir and Vanir that resulted in Freyr and Freyja, the Twin Gods, being traded as hostages to the Aesir.

As punishment for her crime, the Aesir three times pierced the Silver Witch with spears and burned her body to ash. The first two times, she returned with a sly smile, holding a chunk of pure silver in each hand. The third time, the Aesir waited for her to return, but her ashes blew away on the North Wind, and she was not seen again, though Sif and Freyja both swear they heard the sound of Gullveig's laughter carried on that breeze.

entries.name: Worshipers
entries: At the height of her prominence, the Silver Witch was worshiped by landowners, community leaders, and merchants. Reavers cast silver shavings created by chopping jewelry into hacksilver into the water as they departed their homes to go raiding, hoping for easy wealth and little struggle.

As a patron of magic and those that wield it, Gullveig was a favorite of enchanters, illusionists, and transmuters. Many of her devout lived as druids in the forests, as often walking alongside the beasts in animal forms as they strode on two legs.

entries.name: Symbols And Books
entries: Gullveig's symbol is a silver coin.

The Silver Witch's holy tome is titled The Book of Smiling Silver. Few copies of this book exist, as the Silver Witch has long been silent, but some of her most devout followers claim she sometimes sends them messages impressed into the pages of their book in the blocky runes of the giants.

entries.name: Shrines and Priests
entries: After long years of absence, most of the Silver Witch's shrines have fallen into disrepair if they haven't disappeared completely. A single temple to her remains, located in a hidden valley in the mountains to the east of Huldramose. Her last high priest remains there, an ancient elf who is unwilling to travel to the Summerlands until her mistress returns to her place of supremacy among the gods.

deity.name: Norns
deity.title: Weavers of Fates
deity.symbol: A bloody pair of black shears beneath a pigeon with entrails spilling from its belly
entries: The Norns are a trio of goddesses who live at the foot of Yggdrasil, tending to the tree and weaving the threads of fate for every mortal. The three Norns are Uror, Verdandi, and Skuld, who are widely thought to be sisters, though neither they nor any of the other Aesir have confirmed the assumption. Similarly, though the Norns are claimed by the Aesir, they may have actually been of the Vanir, or perhaps they arose before either of those groups of deities were conceived.

Due to their prominence in the everyday lives of Northlanders and because their presence is a sign that all things are as they should be, there are few tales involving the Norns as protagonists, though they feature as truth-tellers and fate-spinners in many of the sagas.

entries.name: Worshipers
entries: The Wyrd Women are paid deference by almost all the people of the Northlands. Expectant mothers make offerings to them to pray for the healthy and safe birth of a child. Parents pray for the continued health and growth of their children. Farmers pray for good crops. Community leaders pray for safety from raiders. Warriors pray to either survive battle or to distinguish themselves enough to earn a place in Valhalla. Sages pray to them for wisdom.

entries.name: Symbols And Books
entries: The symbol of the Norns is a bloody pair of black shears beneath a pigeon with entrails spilling from its belly.

Of Warp and Woof is the holy book of the Norns. The tome holds all the prophecies that foretold the creation of the Aesir, the war with the Vanir, the many wars with the giants of Jotunheim, and the death and rebirth of the universe at Ragnarok. The book is written in a confounding, poetic fashion that scholars still find new ways to interpret.

entries.name: Shrines and Priests
entries: Temples to the Norns are rare, but shrines are commonplace. Few homes in the Northlands are without an effigy of the Norns at which the residents make a daily offerings of meat and mead, usually before the first meal of the day, though some traditions proscribe that the offerings must be made after sunset.

Priests of the Norns are called Seers by the people of the North. Many are women, but male seers are not unheard of. As healers and prophets, they hold positions of honor wherever they choose to make their homes, and the entryway of a Seer's home is rarely devoid of offerings from the local folk. From meat, to honey, to skilled works of craft and artistry, a seer is provided everything they might need to thrive.

Worship of the Norns touches every society in the North, with priests among even the clans of goblins and giants. In particular, the trolls of Trollheim have embraced the Wyrd Women and frequently produce talented haruspices who read the future in the entrails of birds, beasts, and occasionally, themselves.

deity.name: Ratatoskr
deity.title: Lord of Secrets
entries: Ratatosk is the clever runner, mischievous trickster, and laughing messenger of Yggdrasil. Responsibilities, rules, and orders fall forgotten to the joy of new sights, gathering secrets, and spreading rumors. Thought by many to be more of a nuisance than a deity, Ratatoskr knows much, trading as he does in information with the goodly eagles of the skies, as well as with the surly dragon Nidhogg among Yggdrasil's roots. When the other gods seek his knowledge before undertaking a journey or trial, their task seems easier and their success more assured.

Though he is little worshiped by mortals, numerous aphorisms, tales, songs, and curses inspired by the Messenger to Eagles have permeated the collective consciousness of the Northlands.
