entries: Some players may find their characters are far better at spontaneous rhyming insults than they are. To make this easier for those players, below are a series of words and their corresponding rhymes. Players can also use the Kennings in the section later in this chapter.

When using these tables, the Challenger must end their insult using a word on one of the rows. This allows the other participant to simply choose a rhyming word on the same row for their own response.
Both participants of the flyting must agree to either use the tables or perform freestyle.

entries.name: Kennings
entries: The cultures providing inspiration for the Northlands used a poetic metaphor called "kenning" in their riddles, poems, and songs. A kenning is a play on words that replaces a concept, usually a single word, with more figurative language. For example, a popular kenning for the sea was "whale's road." Often associated with skaldic poems, kennings draw on cultural and mythical knowledge. They are immensely useful and imaginative ways to add flavor and a unique cultural feeling to prophecies and games set in the Northlands.

entries.name: Using Kennings in Flyting
entries: Kennings can be amazing poetic forms for a flyting duel.

entries.name: Using Kennings in Prophecies
entries: Kennings are well-suited for creating prophecies because the wordplay inherent in their metaphors allows for a variety of interpretations. In a prophetic reading, the term "Night's Ship" could refer to the moon, a shadowy vessel, or perhaps a dream.

entries.name: How to Create Kennings
entries: The typical manner of making kennings is to combine a noun and a verb, or two nouns, in any order, to form a two-word phrase. This phrase is a descriptive phrase used in place of a more obvious or literal wording. Occasionally, three (or more) words are used to form a kenning if two words are insufficient to create the meaning.

variantrule.name: Prophecies and Omens
entries: The rules in this section reviews two types of prophecies (greater prophecies and prophetic blessings/warnings), gives helpful suggestions on how to construct prophecies, and introduces a way to reward players for using prophecies. This section also includes a table of omens and a few predetermined sample prophecies.

entries.name: Prophecies
entries: Prophecies at their core are predictions of events to come. They often contain cryptic language that leaves them open to a myriad of interpretations. While prophecies might hint at destiny, they are open to interpretation because, by their very nature, they are vague. Unless handed down by a deity or powerful entity, the prophecies most Northerners encounter are communicated to them by seers. As mortal beings, seers can only grasp at the complex weavings of the {@deity Norns|Norse|source}. This is why they speak in vague terms rather than in specific names, dates, and events. Prophecies given by seers are known as prophetic blessings or prophetic warnings.

entries.name: Greater Prophecies
entries: Greater prophecies are most commonly found in myths, legends, and tales, and they typically come directly from the {@deity Norns|Norse|source}, detailing information for major life or world changes. These prophecies cryptically speak of fixed and unchangeable events in the future. Fantasy literature features this sort of prophecy often. In the Northlands, greater prophecies are exceedingly rare, as the {@deity Norns|Norse|source} don't often reveal the weft and weave of their loom to mere mortals. When PCs seek out a seer to hear a prophecy, they never receive greater prophecies. These are purely in the hands of the GM to give or withhold and should have a major impact on the story or world. They also typically don't have the benefits or consequences used in prophetic readings (detailed later in this section). The effects of fulfilling a greater prophecy are much larger than bonuses enjoyed by a single person, as these are outcomes that change nations.

entries.name: Why Use Prophecies?
entries: Prophecies can serve many functions in a campaign. They can be the focal point of the entire narrative, though this should be done sparingly, as the PCs, not a cryptic omen, should be driving the story. They can be used to provide information the GM wants to release in an in-game way. They can foreshadow future events, giving players a wonderful moment of "Oh! That's what the phrase 'Void Monarch' meant!" They can function as a through-line or guidepost for the campaign. When the players feel lost or out of focus, they can turn to the mysterious prophecy given by the GM to get the momentum of the campaign back on track. Finally, prophecies can be used as the fodder of the antagonist(s) in the campaign. The evil wizard might be searching for an ancient prophecy about a powerful relic, or the hoard of fanatical cultists might be invading because they follow the prophecy of their bloodthirsty deity. Above all else, remember that a prophecy is not fate.

entries.name: Prophetic Readings (Blessings/Warnings) and Rewarding Fulfillment
entries: Prophecies are broken up into prophetic blessings and warnings. In many games or stories, prophecies are traditionally relegated to the background, perhaps foreshadowing a coming event or giving the PCs a trail to follow. But they don't have to be. Prophetic blessings and warnings are brief glimpses of the loom of fate given to PCs by seers or supernatural creatures.

entries.name: Prophetic Blessing
entries: A prophecy suggesting an action during a certain sort of circumstance.

entries.name: Prophetic Warning
entries: A prophecy warning the PC to avoid a certain action during a certain sort of circumstance.

Each blessing or warning features three parts: a trigger, an action, and an outcome. The trigger is a short, cryptic element, circumstance, or description that the PC can recognize during game play. The action is an act or activity the PC takes in response to the trigger. The outcome is the result of the PC performing the action in response to the trigger. Outcomes are seen more often in greater prophecies but can also be used to add flavor to a prophecy. By design, the trigger, action, and outcome are vague and non-specific, allowing them to be applied to a wide variety of situations. When a PC (or GM) decides a trigger applies to something occurring in a game, they can act to fulfill the rest of the blessing or warning. Doing so gives the PC a magical benefit or lets them avoid a potential consequence.

entries.name: Overview
entries: The specifics of this system are detailed later, but in general here is how it works.

items: The PC approaches a seer and asks a specific question.
The player makes a prophecy roll to determine the power of the reading and if it is a blessing or a warning.
A blessing comes with a benefit and a warning comes with a consequence.
The benefit or consequence can be selected by the player, be the result of a roll on a random table, or be chosen by the GM.
The prophetic blessing or warning is generated using the tables shown later and contains at least one "trigger."

entries: Later, the player or GM can decide if the trigger of their blessing or warning applies to a current circumstance in the game. If it does, they can attempt to fulfill it or avoid it.

items: For a prophetic blessing, the PC can perform the action described in the prophecy. If they do so, they gain the blessing's benefit.
For a prophetic warning, if the PC chooses to act in the way prohibited in the warning, they incur the warning's consequence.

entries.name: Prophecies and Omens are Vague
entries: When the PCs receive omens or prophecies in a game, the strange sighting or cryptic words absolutely need to be open to different interpretation. They should be "signs" that can be interpreted differently depending on the person, hindsight, and circumstance. They can mean different things to different viewers, or even to the same viewer depending on how the campaign unfolds.

From a GM's perspective, the vagueness of an omen or prophecy keeps your options open in case the needs of the campaign change. It does the game no good if a specific prophecy is suddenly rendered useless when a PC dies unexpectedly. Instead of calling out the specific name of the trollkin druid PC, a good prophecy might refer to "Child of Two Worlds" or "Seeker of Balance." The new dwarven cleric PC in the game might fit those same titles. It's all a matter of interpretation. Flexibility is the power of prophecy for a GM. If the PCs hear a prophecy, but the events of the campaign end up different than the GM expected, the prophecy wasn't incorrect—the interpretation of it was.
More examples are included throughout this chapter, but here are a few helpful suggestions when creating omens or prophecies.

items: Couch prophecies in symbolism and mysteriously vague titles.
Make omens seem out of the ordinary but not immediately threatening.
Keep dates and locations vague or unclear.
Use kennings or allusions rather than the exact creature, site, or phenomenon you plan on using later.
Use metaphors or pseudonyms instead of specific names (especially the PCs' names).
Make sure prophecies can unfold in a few different ways.
Make sure omens can be seen in different ways.
Limit the scope of prophecies so they hint about a limited event not the entire scope of someone's life.
Use omens to foreshadow and/or enhance the mood you wish for the table.

entries.name: Creating a Prophecy
entries: This section demonstrates how to create greater prophecies and prophetic blessings or warnings. If you are creating a greater prophecy, you can skip to Step 3: Generate the Prophecy.

entries.name: Step 1: Prophecy Roll
entries: The first step in creating a prophetic blessing or warning is the prophecy roll. When a seer or other entity gives a prophetic blessing or warning to a PC, the player must roll a prophecy roll to determine the power of the reading and whether it is a prophetic blessing or a warning. This roll is a simple {@dice d20} roll plus the PC's reputation modifier (see {@variantrule Reputation|NorthlandsWorldbook}), or half of the PC's {@variantrule Proficiency|XPHB|Proficiency Bonus}, whichever is higher.

entries.name: Step 2: Determining Benefits and Consequences
entries: The next step is to determine any consequences or benefits of a prophetic reading. Players can choose a benefit with their GMs approval, they can roll a {@dice d8} and consult the appropriate table, or the GM can choose it for them. Consequences are best chosen by the GM or determined randomly.

Each blessing/warning grants a game-specific aspect to the PC when the prophetic reading is fulfilled. Benefits and consequences are divided into three levels: Least, Greater, and Legendary/Dire. The relative power of the benefit or consequence increases with each stage.

Each benefit and consequence lists its duration. If a duration seems not to fit the listed benefit or consequence due to the specific circumstances of the game, the GM can change the duration. A GM can always choose to extend or end an effect, if doing so would better support the prophecy.

entries.name: Step 3: Generating the Prophecy
entries: The third step in the process features tables allowing GMs to select (or roll randomly to determine) the triggers, actions, and, optionally, the outcomes of the prophetic readings. GMs can also use the tables to generate a greater prophecy.
Prophecies (especially prophetic blessings or warnings) typically begin with either "When" or "If," and the trigger and action together should form a complete sentence.

entries.name: Trigger
entries: To determine the trigger, roll a {@dice d20} once for each column in the Trigger table, combining the outcome into a vague description. GMs can use a bit of poetic license to make the trigger sound better. For example, if the rolls determined the words "Dry/Wet," "Guardian," "Bellows," and "Holy Place," the resulting trigger might be "When the arid guardian bellows in the holy temple."

entries.name: Action
entries: To create the action, roll a {@dice d20} for each column in Action table and combine the outcome into a vague description. Due to the number of possible results, GMs should rearrange the results and/or add words as necessary so the action makes sense. For example, if the rolls determined the words "Run," "Relic," "Behind," and "Concealment," the resulting trigger might be rephrased as "Run from behind the concealed relic," with the word "from" added for clarity.

If the prediction is a prophetic warning, the action element must be described as something to avoid. Remember, the GM will be the one identifying a trigger as being active, but they might not share that information with the players. For example, if your rolls determined a different set of words, such as "Hold," "Relic," "Inside," and "Light," the prophetic warning might be "Don't hold the relic inside the light."

entries.name: Outcomes
entries: An outcome is a change to the world, for good or for ill. The Outcome tables below offer suggestions for changes, both large and small, that could occur when a greater prophecy is fulfilled. Prophetic blessings and warnings don't usually have an outcome because the benefit or consequence serves that role. If GMs wish to use an outcome with a prophetic reading, they should begin each outcome with the word "to," such as "To derive new knowledge..." Outcomes should be matched with the nature of the benefit or consequence. For example, the "gods bestowing a blessing" could be used for attacks having {@variantrule Disadvantage|XPHB} against you.

To create an outcome, choose a column in the table (or roll a {@dice d4} to determine it randomly) and then roll a {@dice d20} for that column. Reword the outcomes as needed to fit the prophecy's trigger and action and to form a complete sentence. Typically, prophecies only have one outcome, but GMs can certainly add a second for particularly momentous predications. Greater prophecies always have an outcome attached to them.

When presenting an outcome in a prophecy, the outcome should be phrased as an event that has not happened, yet also in a manner to fit with the "When" or "If" that began the prediction. Use words like "will," "shall," and "lest" to indicate a future tense.

For example, rolling a {@dice d4} and a {@dice d20} to choose a random outcome results in "Sleeping god awakens" (a societal change), giving us a prophecy that, if triggered, will cause a sleeping god to wake up.

entries.name: Final Prophecy
entries: After going through these steps, the trigger, action, and benefit/consequence (or outcome) should form a complete sentence. Using the samples we've seen so far, a prophetic reading with a greater blessing would be: "When the arid destroyer bellows in the holy temple, run from behind the concealed relic to gain {@deity Volund|Norse|source}'s protection." (Resistance to fire damage) Using the samples, a greater prophecy would be: "When the arid destroyer bellows in the holy temple, run from behind the concealed relic, and the sleeping god will awaken."

entries.name: Sample Prophetic Blessings and Warnings
entries: Presented here are several prophetic blessings and warnings along with possible interpretations to show how players can identify the triggers in different ways. Some elements of these samples are not found in the tables in Step 3, to demonstrate how GMs can invent their own.

entries.name: Least Prophetic Blessing
entries: {@i When the storm casts its shadow, seek shelter within the ancient to sip from Mimir's well.}

entries.name: Benefit:
entries: If you do so, you gain {@variantrule Advantage|XPHB} on Intelligence- and Wisdom-based ability checks for 1 hour.

items: Shadow of the storm could be a literal storm overhead. But it could also be a creature or situation. The fury of a giant could be described as a "storm," so then the giant's shadow might be identified as the trigger.

A player could "seek shelter within the ancient" by moving into an old structure. But "ancient" could also be a term for a mountain, so stepping into a cave would fulfill the action portion of the blessing. Similarly, moving beneath the branches of a mighty tree could be viewed as seeking shelter within the ancient.

entries.name: Legendary Prophetic Blessing
entries: {@i When the stars hide their faces, quench the wound-brand to strike like Sleipnir.}

entries.name: Benefit:
entries: If you do so, once in the next 24 hours, you can use an action to move up to twice your speed and make a melee attack. You don't provoke {@action Opportunity Attack|XPHB|Opportunity Attacks} when moving in this way. If you successfully hit a creature, the target is pushed 10 feet away from you and has the prone condition.

items: Stars hiding their faces could be a kenning for darkness. It could also be interpreted more literally as people looking away from a situation.

The most obvious meaning for "quenching the wound-brand" would be to take something on fire and extinguish it. But wound-brand could be a kenning for a sword or weapon, and quenching is a smithing term for plunging hot metal into water. So instead, a player might take that to mean they merely have to stick their weapon into water.

entries.name: Greater Prophetic Warning
entries: {@i When the light speaks in screams, don't answer the call with wyrd-craft, or suffer Thor's fate.}

entries.name: Consequence:
entries: If you cast a spell before the end of your next turn, you have the {@condition Poisoned} condition for {@dice 1d4} rounds. While you have the {@condition Poisoned} condition from this effect, your thoughts are muddled, so you can only cast cantrips.

items: The light speaking in screams could be something like a {@spell Fireball|XPHB}, which is bright and causes screams of pain. It could also be a glowing foe who is yelling.

The warning against answering the call with wyrd-craft is pretty straightforward as it is referring to spellcasting. That said, a player could instead decide wyrd-craft refers to an enchanted weapon, thus the warning would say not to attack the "screaming light."

entries.name: Dire Prophetic Warning
entries: {@i When an ancient roar fractures the land, don't spill the dew of slaughter, or your hand will betray your allies.}

entries.name: Consequence:
entries: The first time you deal damage with an attack at any point in the next 8 hours, you become cursed for 1 minute. While cursed, at the start of each of your turns, roll a {@dice d6}. On a result of 1 or 2, you must move and make a melee attack against a random creature. If you can't reach a creature with your movement, you can instead take the Dash action to move toward a random creature.

items: An ancient roar fracturing the land could be an earthquake, but it could just as easily be a yelling giant striking the ground with her club, or an erupting volcano.

The warning not to spill the dew could be viewed as meaning "don't spill a container or vessel nearby." The phrase "dew of slaughter" is a kenning for blood, so it could also be a warning not to spill blood, either your own or (more likely in this case) the blood of a foe.

entries.name: Sample Greater Prophecies
entries: Here is a complex Greater Prophecy crafted using the various tables described in this section. As shown here, GMs can roll several times on the various tables to make longer prophecies if they wish.

entries.name: Sample Greater Prophecy
entries: "When a great king withholds secrets, and the statue of the brave awakens in the village square, bind well the rune-carved blade with blessed steel, or the forbidden rite shall unearth the sleeping god. Should this come to pass, hope can yet be restored if the fractured binding is cast anew with bloody stone."

entries.name: Construction
entries: This complicated greater prophecy follows this format, with some additional words thrown in for clarity:

items: Trigger (great king withholds secrets)
Trigger (statue awakes in village)
Action (bind blade with steel)
Outcome (forbidden rite awakens a god)
Outcome (hope is restored)
Trigger (fractured binding cast anew)
Action (with bloody stone)

entries.name: Omens
entries: Small signs, portents, and sightings work hand-in-hand with prophecies to foreshadow future events. While not as informative as a prophecy, omens provide flavor and can increase the mystery and tension in a game. GMs can use them as much or as little as they wish, but a good balance is different for every game, campaign, and table. Include too many omens and the GM risks blunting their impact. Provide too few omens and the table won't have the tone or vibe the GM is striving for.

The tables in this section provide examples of three different types of omens to add into a game: hopeful, foreboding, and mysterious. Some are portents of good things, others are warnings of dire events, and some are just mysterious. GMs can use these suggestions as a base and invent their own omens.

In most cases, the GM should choose the type of omen they wish, altering the omen as needed to fit the circumstances of the campaign, but if a more random generation method is preferred, roll a {@dice d4} and consult the Omen Types table.

variantrule.name: Ships and Sea Combat
entries: The naval combat rules presented here are intended to make the ship a dynamic and exciting part of any conflict.

entries.name: Ship Siege Weapons
entries: In the real-world cultures that inspired the Northlands, longships typically didn't utilize ship-mounted siege weapons. Instead, the warriors aboard them made use of melee and ranged weapons they could carry, not relying on weaponized machinery to do their battles. Depending on your setting of choice, weapons such as ballistae or mangonels may be loaded onto a longship if it suits your style of play. For such times, siege weapons are included in longship entries in Chapter 5, which can be removed if they do not make sense for your particular game.

Ship-mounted weapon attack rolls are equal to the Strength or Dexterity modifier of the ship (whichever is higher). The damage bonus is also equal to the higher of the ships Strength or Dexterity modifier. A PC firing a ship-mounted weapon can choose to use their own ranged weapon attack bonus and damage bonus instead of the ship's if they wish, using the higher of their Strength or Dexterity.

entries.name: Ballista
entries: A massive crossbow that fires weighted bolts. A ship-mounted ballista can be loaded and aimed by the crew using the Operate Ship Weapon action.

entries.name: Naval Ram
entries: This metal and wood ram is mounted to the front of the ship at or below the water level. It can be used to smash a hole in the side of another vessel. If the ship moves more than 30 feet first, a ram deals an additional {@dice 1d10} Piercing damage.

entries.name: Ship Catapult
entries: A small ship-mounted catapult used to throw stones at enemy vessels. Loading and aiming a ship catapult requires a {@action Utilize|XPHB} action, and firing it uses another. Multiple crew can operate the same siege weapon to perform these actions in the same round.
Some of the possible siege weapons are described here.

entries.name: Movement (Sail and Rowing)
entries: Use the {@variantrule Speed|XPHB} statistic provided with the vehicle. If you draw from another source, and the only {@variantrule Speed|XPHB} provided for a vehicle is in miles per hour, a handy approximation of the number of feet the ship moves per round is to take the value given for the vessel's miles per hour and multiply it by 10. This assumes the ship is being piloted. For example, a galley moves at 4 mph with average winds, or 40 ft. per round. If you are playing on a grid, round to the nearest multiple of 5 when counting squares. The {@variantrule Speed|XPHB} listed for longships includes its sail speed and its Rowing {@variantrule Speed|XPHB}.

entries.name: Changing Direction
entries: Sailing vessels don't quickly turn. A ship changing direction without completing a shipboard action moves the first half of its {@variantrule Speed|XPHB} in the direction it is facing and rotates 45° before moving the second half of its movement. For example, a turning galley would move 20 ft. in the direction it began the round and then another 20 feet at a 45° diagonal to its previous course.

entries.name: Direction of Wind and Drifting
entries: The direction of the wind is of critical importance to sailing a ship, determining if it can easily move in a straight line or is forced to tack back and forth. These rules simplify the importance of wind direction, assuming that the crew is tacking and making other appropriate adjustments to the sails. If a ship is not controlled, it drifts in the direction of the wind at the start of each of its turns: 5 feet for light wind, 10 feet for average wind, and 15 feet for strong wind. If the ship is being rowed, it generally ignores the effects of wind and drift, unless in storm conditions.

entries.name: Turning Into the wind
entries: The one direction ships never want to go is directly into the wind. A vessel that turns into the wind and tries to move in that direction has its {@variantrule Speed|XPHB} halved. If the ship's speed is greater than 0 feet while moving into the wind, the crew member at the helm must succeed on a {@dc 12} Strength ({@skill Athletics|XPHB}) or Wisdom ({@skill Survival|XPHB}) check to turn the ship. If the crew member fails to turn the ship, or the ship's {@variantrule Speed|XPHB} was reduced to 0 feet., it drifts in the direction of the wind and is stuck until the wind changes.

entries.name: Wind Speed
entries: Distance traveled assumes average wind speeds. Over the course of days, this is likely to be the case. During a combat round however, that doesn't have to be the case. If there is no wind, sailing ships don't move. If there are light winds, halve the ship's {@variantrule Speed|XPHB}, and if there are strong winds, double it. Longships also make use of rowers.

entries.name: Sea Weather
entries: Traveling by sea in a fantasy world means encountering strange weather in addition to the normal variations of wind and visibility. Use the Wind and Precipitation tables to determine weather conditions. Effects on movement assume the ship is powered by sails. If it is rowed or derives its power from some other source, an effect might not be relevant.

entries.name: Naval Combat
entries: A ship-to-ship battle can be a thrilling addition to your adventure. Without using the rules in this section, GMs can run ship encounters like any other combat. At the end of each round, all ships involved in the encounter can maneuver as the players or GM wishes. This is certainly the quickest method of handling naval combat.
For GMs and players who want more involved ship encounters, here is an optional set of rules to help create electrifying ship combats.

entries.name: Crew Member Stat Blocks
entries: The average sailor has the statistics of a {@creature Bandit|XMM} or {@creature Pirate|XMM}. A quick stat block for an officer could be a {@creature Pirate|XMM} or a {@creature Viking|NorthlandsWorldbook} (see {@book Chapter 8|NorthlandsWorldbook|8|Trollkin}), while the captain might use a {@creature Wolf Reaver Dwarf|ToB1-2023} or {@creature Pirate Captain|ToB1-2023} stat block.

entries.name: Initiative
entries: Ships move and act last in {@variantrule Initiative|XPHB}, and their crews are assumed to be the ones performing the chosen action. Player characters and unique foes not concerned with running a ship roll {@variantrule Initiative|XPHB} as normal. However, determine {@variantrule Initiative|XPHB} between competing vessels each round.

To decide which ship acts first, determine which ship has the advantage of position by having the person at the helm of each ship make a Strength ({@skill Athletics|XPHB}) or Wisdom ({@skill Survival|XPHB}) check. The winner chooses whether to act first or delay. If the helm has no one assigned, that ship automatically fails the check.

entries.name: Using Ship-Mounted Weapons
entries: Unlike a standard siege weapon, large shipboard weapons require separate {@action Utilize|XPHB} actions to load, aim, and fire. In a raiding party, it's assumed that sufficient crew members have been hired to operate all ship-mounted weapons. The {@action Operate Ship Weapon|NorthlandsWorldbook} action allows the crew to reload and aim the weapon, but it still requires another action to fire it. If an enemy is in the firing arc of a weapon, generally 90° from the direction it is mounted, the gunnery crew can attempt to fire on it.

entries.name: Ship Damage
entries: A ship taking damage in combat can suffer various effects. This damage can come as the result of weapon fire, spells, or impacts with physical objects. Consult the {@table Damage to the Ship|NorthlandsWorldbook} table for the effects of damage to the hull.

entries.name: Targeting Crew and Casualties
entries: Ship weapons typically aren't used against enemy sailors. The opposing vessel is a much easier target. However, sailors might be injured as collateral damage from an attack. When an attack scores a {@variantrule Critical Hit|XPHB}, in addition to rolling the damage dice twice, determine the location of the ship that was hit using the Disable Station shipboard action.

Roll a {@dice d6} to determine how many crew members in that area are {@condition Unconscious|XPHB} and dying. If a PC or NPC with medical skill or magical healing does not take action to save them, 75 percent of them die in {@dice 1d4} rounds. If a PC is in the area hit, they take half the damage dealt by the attack from flying shrapnel. If the PC succeeds on a Dexterity save with a DC equal to the enemy gunner's attack roll, they instead take no damage from shrapnel.

entries.name: Actions During Ship Combat
entries: During a naval engagement, the PCs can act independently from the ship with its crew, or they can work with them as determined by the players.

entries.name: PCs During Combat
entries: PCs can choose to act as they would in any other combat. Throwing {@spell Fireball|XPHB|Fireballs} and raining down a volley of arrows remain effective tactics. Note however, that most engagements begin at {@dice (2d6 + 2) * 100|(2d6 + 2) x 100} feet, so PC attacks are not generally in range when engagements commence. PCs can also use their turn to perform a shipboard action. A PC doing so must use the {@action Ready|XPHB} action on their turn. Then, once the ship has moved at the end of the round, they can use their {@variantrule Reaction|XPHB} to do their readied shipboard action.

entries.name: Ship and Crew During Combat
entries: Ships and crew act at the end of the {@variantrule Initiative|XPHB} round. On its turn, a vehicle can move up to its {@variantrule Speed|XPHB} and use a shipboard action. The players should decide together what this ship action is going to be. PCs who delayed their actions on their turns can make additional shipboard actions. Unless noted otherwise, the same shipboard action can only be performed once per turn.

entries.name: Shipboard Actions
entries: There are a number of actions the crew of the ship (and potentially the PCs) can take in ship-to-ship combat.

variantrule.name: Raiding
entries: In the culture of the Northlands, raiding other communities dates back to the Reaving. These expeditions served a variety of purposes depending on who conducted them. For some, they were a method of earning glory, training young warriors, punishing foes, or (more typically) securing badly needed resources. Historically, raids involved securing a ship, gathering a crew, sailing often great distances to a location, attacking it, and returning with treasure. Played out fully, a raid could be a campaign all by itself, and GMs are certainly free to run them that way. These optional rules, however, allow various portions of the raiding journey, or even the entire raid, to occur "off-stage" by abstracting them. This keeps raids feeling fast and thrilling.

entries.name: A Word About Theft and Raiding
entries: For a Northlander, raiding is not the same as thievery. To steal something from someone is not honorable and violates the various rules of hospitality. Raiding, however, is not "theft" because you are fighting someone for their treasures. Even if the "battle" consists of sneaking up on a location, setting it on fire, and cutting down the inhabitants as they flee the blaze, it's considered a fight and thus an honorable means to seize the rewards. The general guideline for a reaver is anything goes, as long as it doesn't stain their honor.

The typical goal of a raid isn't to take territory or inflict the most damage. Instead, it is to gather the most resources or treasure without losing too many warriors or your own supplies in the process. Thus, raids tended to be lightning-fast assaults rather than sieges.

entries.name: Using Raiding Rules
entries: These rules break raids down into abstract phases—preparation, journey, raid, and return—with each phase determined by rolling dice and consulting tables. Successes or failures from each phase affect the next subsequent phase. A few other aspects are also abstracted for ease of play.

entries.name: Cost
entries: To participate in the raid, a PC must spend coins, as determined by the target of the raid (see the {@table Raiding Target|NorthlandsWorldbook} tables). This is an abstracted cost reflecting a share of the cost of outfitting the expedition, but in return, the PC gets a greater share of plunder taken.

entries.name: Time
entries: Raiding activities are typically measured in weeks, each of which is roughly assumed to be at least 5 days, where 8 hours per day are spent pursuing the current activity. Each phase of the raid indicates the amount of time in "weeks" that occurred.

entries.name: Distance
entries: While it is important for the GM to know how far the target of the raid is, the exact distance is somewhat meaningless for the purposes of these rules. More distant targets chosen during the preparation phase may require GMs to adjust the tables in other phases to account for the particulars of various climates, hazards, flora, and fauna found in those locations.

entries.name: Raiding Roll and Spoils Dice
entries: Just as the time and distance of the raid are handled abstractly, the actual raid and the amount of plunder taken is abstracted in a mechanic similar to rolling attack and weapon damage in combat. While raiding, PCs make a raiding roll against a DC determined by the size of the target (plus any additional modifiers). If successful, the PCs then roll a spoils die to determine how much plunder is gained.

In general, 1 spoil is worth 500 GP, regardless of it being a bag of grain, bars of steel, a pouch of gems, or a crate of chickens. This isn't a replacement for standard treasure; instead, it serves as a shorthand for the "wealth" taken during the raid. The spoils gained in a raid reflect what goes directly to the PCs. This assumes NPCs already received a separate share of the proceeds of the successful raid.

The abstractions presented by this system provide a way for PCs to track the costs and rewards of a raid without getting bogged down in the minutia of weights and cargo lists. However, any phase can be replaced with actual in-game play according to the needs of the GM. For example, the preparation, journey, and return phases could be handled abstractly, but the raid itself could be a full combat encounter.

entries.name: Raiding Phases
entries: The four phases of a raid are preparation, journey, raid, and return, and they are detailed here.

entries.name: Preparation
entries: In the first phase, the PCs determine the following aspects.

items.name: The Target
entries: Choose the place to be raided.

items.name: Ship Upgrades
entries: Pay for additional upgrades for the ship.

items.name: Additional Raiders
entries: Recruit a crew of hearty warriors.

items.name: Special Resources
entries: Gather provisions, ship repair materials, and deal with other details for the journey.

items.name: The Cost
entries: After calculating the total based on their choices, PCs each pay a share to fund the raid.
Making wise choices during the preparation phase can mean the difference between a successful raid and an abject failure.

entries.name: Journey
entries: In the second phase, the PCs must contend with the voyage to the raiding target, overcoming hazards and obstacles. Success or failure when doing so can grant bonuses (or penalties) during the next phase.

entries.name: Raid
entries: In the third phase, the raiders reach their destination and conduct a fast assault on the target before additional defenders can be mobilized to oppose them. The PCs make a raiding roll and roll the spoils die to determine the level of the raid's success and the amount of plunder taken. How things go here can directly impact the ease (or difficulty) of their trip home.

entries.name: Return
entries: In the fourth phase, the PCs return home, hopefully with their ship laden with spoils. Much like the journey phase, the return features hazards and obstacles. This phase can be more difficult if the raid went poorly.

entries.name: Outcome
entries: Once all of the phases are complete, the GM tallies up the positive and negative results of the entire voyage to determine the final spoils of the raid.

entries.name: Preparation Phase
entries: The preparation phase involves recruiting warriors, upgrading a ship, and gathering supplies for the raid. But the first decision to be made is to choose a target.

entries.name: The Target
entries: Raids can be carried out on various targets, from small hamlets, to forts, to major cities. The dangers the reavers might face, including armed defenders, increase with the scale of the target, but so do the possible rewards.
The PCs can use the Raiding Targets table to choose the target of their raid, as well as the types of loot typically found in the listed communities.

If the GM plans to run the raid phase as an encounter, a table of different settlement sizes has been provided to show the average number of defenders. The number of reavers needed to raid various settlements detailed in the abstracted table is the same here.

entries.name: Ship Upgrades
entries: The choice of ship, number of warriors, supplies, and so forth are abstracted in this system. The funds paid by the PCs to participate in the raid include an appropriately sized ship crewed by enough warriors to attempt the raid against the chosen target settlement.

If the players and GM wish to explore ship options in more detail, consult the Naval Combat section earlier in this chapter. Additionally, Chapter 5 contains specific information about the most common vessels used in the North. As a reminder, all crew members are expected to operate the vessel as well as participate in the raid itself.

As part of the preparation phase, the PCs can choose to enhance their ship with a variety of options. Each of these enhancements gives the PCs a bonus to their raiding roll, spoil dice, or other mechanics, but using them also increases the cost each PC must pay to participate in the raid. Each upgrade is only usable once during this raid to give a bonus in one phase. If an upgrade is not used, it is wasted. These upgrades don't have any mechanical function in naval combat.

entries.name: Additional Raiders
entries: A contingent of warriors large enough to tackle the chosen target comes with the funds paid by the PCs. However, some parties might wish to bring more warriors along to ensure victory. The PCs are not going to be able to empty a village of warriors to crew their longship. At best, they'll convince half of a community's able-bodied reavers to sign on. Raiding is a risk not only for those participating but also for the communities they leave behind. Every raider lost during a raid means one fewer warrior to defend the village against monsters or raids, as well as one fewer worker to do the vital tasks to keep the settlement going.
In general, the size of community hosting the raid (or the place where the raid leaves from) directly relates to the number of extra warriors available to be recruited.

Additional warriors can be hired in bands, ranging from 5 to 100. Each group gives a bonus to the raiding roll during the raid phase, but it also comes with an associated cost added to the sum the PCs pay to fund the raid (see the Extra Warriors table). Only one group of extra warriors can be added to each raid.

entries.name: Special Resources
entries: The base level funds provided by the PCs provide a decent amount of provisions, repair materials, and other supplies for the raid. Aside from that, there are special resources PCs can purchase (see the Special Resources table). Similar to ship upgrades, these resources give bonuses to raiding rolls, spoils dice, and other game elements. Each special resource is only usable once during a raid to give a bonus in one phase. If a special resource is not used, it is wasted.

entries.name: The Journey
entries: In the second phase, the PCs must contend with the voyage to the raiding target while overcoming hazards and obstacles. Success or failure can grant bonuses (or penalties) during the next phase. The PCs make a group roll on the Sea/Land Journey table for each week of travel (see Abstracted Time/Distance in this section). GMs can choose to add additional rolls on the Sea/Land Journey table as they wish. To emphasize the epic themes of the raid, the GM should be as descriptive as possible.

entries.name: Abstracted Time/Distance
entries: Rather than delve into the minutia of travel speeds and distance, those aspects are abstracted in the journey phase to 1 week of time for most destinations. The GM can always add time to the voyage to account for things such as setting elements or for more distant destinations.

entries.name: Land Raiding
entries: Not all raids need to be conducted via the sea. The communities of giants to the North offer tantalizing targets for metal, rare resources, hides, and relics. Due to the geography of the Northlands, most reavers utilize ships for direct assaults on raiding targets or to travel to a landing site near the target for an overland attack. Raiding PCs aren't required to use ships if their target is reachable by marching, though most groups of warriors won't want to trek hundreds of miles across frozen mountains when they could just sail there.

entries.name: The Raid
entries: In the third phase, the PCs reach their destination and conduct a fast assault on the target before additional defenders can be mobilized to oppose them.

entries.name: Raiding Roll
entries: The moment has come! Screaming their battle cries, the reavers leap from their longboats or charge through the snow-covered field toward the (hopefully) unsuspecting settlement. Determining the result of a raid requires the players to make a group raiding roll against the DC of the target settlement.

The raiding roll is equal to {@dice 1d20}, modified by any bonuses or penalties gained during the previous phases. If the result of this roll meets or exceeds the DC, the raid succeeds and grants a bonus to the spoils die, as well as additional benefits. However, a result lower than the DC indicates the raiders were driven off but still managed to grab some plunder on the way out. Rolling below the DC gives a penalty to the spoils die and may result in other complications. The Raiding Roll table displays all of these results.

entries.name: Important NPC Captives
entries: If the raid captures an important NPC, that individual can be ransomed back to their family or community. The negotiations and exchange can take some time, but many Northlands jarls are more than pleased to take such captives off the PCs hands in exchange for favors, like gaining renown or learning hidden lore, or for a lump sum of gold, a magic item, or another reward determined by the GM.

entries.name: Spoils Die
entries: Once the raiding roll is resolved, the PCs can roll the spoils die for the target settlement, adding any adjustments incurred during the current and previous phases. As a reminder, the result of this roll is the share of plunder going directly to the PCs. The raiding rules assume NPC warriors receive a separate share from the total among of loot taken.

entries.name: The Return
entries: In the fourth phase, the PCs travel home (hopefully) laden with spoils from a successful raid. Repeat the journey phase, adjusting rolls as necessary. This phase can be more difficult if the raid went poorly, and failures here can cost the PCs a portion of their spoils.

entries.name: Outcome
entries: Once all of the phases are complete, the GM and the players tally up the positive and negative results of the entire voyage to determine the final spoils of the raid.
The total spoils handed to the PCs can be immediately exchanged for gold pieces or standard equipment of equal value. One spoil is worth 500 GP.

With GM approval, PCs can instead exchange their spoils for magic items. The availability of items depends on the size of the settlement the PCs return to after their raid is complete. Typically, this is the same location they left from, but that isn't a requirement. The Spoils Exchange table shows the number of spoils that can be exchanged for magic items of different rarities, as well as the minimum size of the settlement likely to have such an item.

The exact nature of an item gained by the PCs should be a discussion between the players and the GM. Since magic item rarity offers a wide range of value for items, not every item will be available just because they have enough spoils to exchange for it. Settlements might also charge more for certain items than is shown on the table, due to campaign circumstances. The GM makes the final determination on all magic item availability and cost.

entries.name: Who Leads the Raid?
entries: Are the PCs leading the raid themselves? Or are they joining a raid led by an NPC? Either way, the players are the ones making decisions for the raid and will exert a degree of narrative control over all of the NPCs involved in it. If the PCs join a raid led by an NPC, the cost they pay up front is a bit like investing in the expedition. If it is successful, the PCs get a larger share of the plunder than the average warrior. GMs can, of course, have NPC leaders push for larger shares, perhaps setting up some fun roleplaying confrontations.

entries.name: Raids as Downtime Activities
entries: The raiding rules presented in this chapter can be used as downtime activities. Typically, this works best if all of the PCs choose to embark on the raid together, especially since most raids take at least two weeks to conduct. GMs can shorten this time by giving the raid expedition a few of the ship upgrades or special resources that reduce the sailing time. This might be advisable if some of the PCs go raiding and others stay behind. That way, everyone is on the same time frame.

variantrule.name: Northlands Weather
entries: As mentioned in {@book Chapter 1|NorthlandsWorldbook|1}, the North is generally a cold environment, with most areas experiencing extreme cold during winter. The following rules feature optional game elements for environmental obstacles in the Northlands.

contents.name: Overview of the North
headers: Land of Deadly Beauty and Epic Adventure
Timeline—The Land of Frost and Bears

data.name: Welcome to the Northlands
entries: Heill þik!

That's "Hail to you!" in your tongue, brave traveler! Epic sagas and thrilling trials await you in the North. As you set off into these windswept, storied lands, this tome offers sagas, prophetic runes, and sage council to guide you through ice-choked fjords and fell forests, over frost-rimed peaks and ancient halls of frost giant jarls, and onto the wave-washed decks of reaving longships.

The Northlands is a realm of contrasts. Towering jotun scheme within their primordial bastions, trolls lurk among the hills, and ancient evils stir beneath glacial ice. Yet it is also a place of grim determination, voices rising in song, laughter around the fire, and mugs of honeyed mead. The stories of the Northlands are as broad as your boldest dream.

This worldbook reveals the sweep and splendor of Northern-inspired fantasy, inviting you to explore the mood and flavor without needing to leave your setting behind. One adventure might see heroes confront werekin raiders in Vargrike, and the next might bring them to bargain with storm giants atop the sky-anchored peaks of Jotunheim. They can set sail from the harbors of Trollheim or Wolfheim to go a-raiding for glory and plunder, or delve into the forgotten vaults beneath the Bleak Expanse, where the North Wind plots to cover the world in ice. The Northlands is rooted in epic sagas and open skies, ready to test their strength and spirit alike.

entries.name: Overview
entries: Why do we gravitate toward myths and legends of the North? Because these stories shine with the fierce determination of brave mortals who carry on against monumental obstacles to spit in the face of fate itself. In their words we sit on timber benches as oars dip and dig into the waves, propelling our longships across deep oceans, icy fjords, and shallow bays. They propel us into the heart of battle, our bloody hands firm upon the hilts of our axes. With a turn of the page, we stand before bearded jarls in smoke-filled longhouses, raising our horns of mead high.

The Northlands Worldbook is your guide to this realm of myth and ice, of squabbling gods and the Great Wolf destined to consume the world. This book is vast, containing everything from new player options and spells to rules for raiding, contests of insults, and prophetic runes.

Northlands adventures are intended to feel epic, no matter if they are episodic or campaign-length. Whether your saga stays in a single jarldom or roams from fey-haunted groves to ice-wreathed citadels, the North holds titanic dangers, survival struggles, political clashes, and mythic journeys. In tone, the Northlands echo screen tales such as The Northman, The 13th Warrior, Vikings, and other tales set in Ragnarok-threatened lands.

entries.name: Campaigns in the Northlands
entries: The Northlands is a flexible addition to any existing home campaign; indeed, it fits comfortably in the Midgard setting or within any published setting. You can just as easily use it as a stand-alone realm or weave it into a broader story world. It might serve as a place of pilgrimage, an ancestral homeland, or a crucible for legends yet unborn. The lands themselves—Vargrike, Bjarmia, Kaldrgard, Trollheim, Blodejord, and more—are described in {@book Chapter 2: Regions of the Northlands|NorthlandsWorldbook|2}. Meanwhile, the looming threats and howling foes are explored in {@book Chapter 8: Monsters of the Northlands|NorthlandsWorldbook|8}.

entries.name: How to Use This Book
entries: As a player, if your hero comes from another realm and is drawn into the Northlands for the first time, you may want to keep your eyes off these pages and let the wonders and mystery unfold in-game.

If your character hails from these shores, then {@book Chapter 3: Factions of the North|NorthlandsWorldbook|3} and {@book Chapter 4: Heroes of the Northlands|NorthlandsWorldbook|4} will be for you. Whether you are mischievous ratatosk, a hearty dwarf, a cunning ravenfolk, a storm-touched giantkin, or a clawed werekin, this book has options for you. The list of new subclasses is equally expansive, from raging {@deity Fenris|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} Druids to trickster Warlocks to brave viking Fighters and Norn-blessed Clerics.

Spellcasters and reavers alike will want to delve into {@book Chapter 5: Magic and Miscellany|NorthlandsWorldbook|5} for magic and equipment from the land of frost and bears. New spells, rituals, and magic items await, alongside various longships, weapons and gear. Devout characters will find rich lore in {@book Chapter 6: Gods of the North|NorthlandsWorldbook|6}, including {@deity Wotan|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook|Wotan the All-Father}, hammer wielding {@deity Thor|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}, the ever-sly {@deity Loki|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}, and the jotun deities plotting their demise.

Game Masters will find a host of lore and adventure hooks in {@book Chapter 2: Regions of the Northlands|NorthlandsWorldbook|2}, and {@book Chapter 3: Factions of the North|NorthlandsWorldbook|3}, which detail schemes, enemies, and opportunities for player-driven conflict. For terrifying foes, see {@book Chapter 8: Monsters of the Northlands|NorthlandsWorldbook|8}. For new rules on survival and prophecy, and a complete raiding system, turn to {@book Chapter 7: Running Northlands Campaigns|NorthlandsWorldbook|7}.

entries.name: Find Your Destiny
entries: No matter how far you roam across glaciers, snowfields, or among ice-choked seas, there is always more to discover. The Northlands cry out for heroes with a sharp blade, a strong voice, a steady heart, or a hand raising a rune-marked stone in defiance of fate.
So gather your warband, ready your longship, and call upon your shield-maidens and reavers. Step into the sagas and marvels of the Northlands and see what glories await you.

{@i O, Wanderer! I see you gaze with wonder at our fjordlands and well you might. For the North is indeed a place of wonder, yet it is also full of dangers. So come, sit by my fire for a time and mind not my hollow eye; I see well enough without it. As the flames ease the chill from Boreas's rattling winds, let us speak of gods and ice, of the honor of men and monsters that lurk, of the beginning times and of Ragnarok, the end of all. These and more await you, wayfarer, in the lands of the North}!

entries.name: Land of Deadly Beauty and Epic Adventure
entries: The {@i Northlands Worldbook} is a campaign setting inspired by the epic tales and sagas of poetic eddas, skaldic stories, and rime-bound mythology, ready for any fantasy world using the rules for the oldest roleplaying game. Here, nature is more dangerous than the most brutal band of raiders. Deadly creatures lurk in dark pine forests, blizzards and snowdrifts can isolate farms and towns for months at a time, and the temperature plummets to a deadly chill during the winter months. Even daylight, the oldest defense against ghosts and skulking horrors, dims as the year ends. It dooms folk to huddle around their fires and stare nervously into the dark. Yet, for all its harshness and hazards, the North is indisputably, breathtakingly beautiful. Frost glitters in the morning sun, making the world shine as if coated in diamonds. Waterfalls thunder over cliffs, cascading down through an unearthly haze of mist and rainbows. The land's beauty inspires countless poems and songs, but for those lost and starving in the wilderness, the allure is a deadly trap, dulling the mind to approaching danger.

Readers familiar with the Midgard Campaign setting will find many familiar locations in this book, as well as new surprises, but these areas are designed to be easily added to nearly any campaign setting. Readers yearning for epic adventures in ice-shrouded lands, or upon serpent infested waters, will find enough thrills, mysteries, lore, and wonders to populate their own epic stories for years to come.
Welcome to the Northlands.

entries.name: Seven Secrets of the Northlands
entries: At first glance, the Northlands setting might seem familiar, with themes drawn from Norse mythology, Scandinavian history, and Viking Sagas, mixed well with a medieval level of technology, and filled with magic and lineages taken directly from the greatest fantasy traditions. Looking beyond the common tropes reveals surprising twists and surprises. These seven foundational mysteries provide a quick summary for the game master (GM) who wants to plan out a short campaign or a long arc.

entries.name: Going Viking
entries: The drums of war beat in the hearts of Northlanders. The raiding culture of the North is firmly woven into its social, political, and religious fabric. Raids provide not only sorely needed grain, but also offer the opportunity to earn glory and respect in battle. Bands of raiders descend on neighboring Northlands realms almost as often as they venture across the seas. Defending kin or community is considered just as honorable as raiding. Northerners embrace a level of brutality that would disturb those who dwell elsewhere, accepting as normal behavior what more "civilized" societies decry as wicked.

entries.name: Honor and Reputation
entries: Northerners believe that death awaits everyone, but honor is eternal. Their god {@deity Wotan|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} says, "Though you are but mortal, honor and reputation never die for the one who earns them." To a Northerner, an honorable life is earned through bravery, heroic deeds in battle, loyalty to family or clan, cleverness and wit, prowess and skill, upholding oaths, sound judgement, and generosity in hospitality. They believe Valhalla awaits the honorable, so even death shouldn't be feared; instead, it is welcomed as the reward for a life well lived. With so much at stake, personal honor and reputation are paramount. The loss of face or perceived insult often leads to vengeance or blood feud, binding entire families, clans, and communities into a cycle of retribution.

entries.name: Fate, Luck, and Prophesy
entries: Everyone knows the {@deity Norns|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} weave the strands of fate for each life, dictating certain outcomes, such as death, to be predetermined and unavoidable. So Northerners generally have a cheerfully resigned attitude and risk dangers others might shun. Yet while destiny has already been woven, how these predetermined outcomes are navigated, and sometimes their results, can be influenced by luck. To aid their decisions, Northlanders look to signs from the gods and prophesy. For what is woven can be rewoven, and those who find their path descending to darkness can sometimes persuade the {@deity Norns|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} to alter their fate with heroic deeds and acts of honor.

entries.name: Influence of the Gods
entries: The gods of the North are not distant and detached observers of the mortal world. They dabble and plot, answer prayers, reward offerings, punish transgressions, and constantly meddle. The gods feud, argue, love, and even die. Their hatreds and rivalries spill out from Asgard into the streets and homes of the North. With the divine so regularly among them, Northlanders know the gods observe who is honorable (and has earned a seat in the afterlife) and who is not. So they are quick to offer prayers, rituals, and ceremonies to their gods, for aid may be but an offering away.

entries.name: Deadly and Liminal Wilderness
entries: The Northlands are indisputably, breathtakingly beautiful. Countless poems and songs have been inspired by their allure, but for those lost and starving in the wilderness, nature is more dangerous than the most brutal band of reavers. Snow and ice slay swifter than the blade. The God of the North Wind seeks to spread his frozen influence across the world, and the sun hides from view. In this twilight and darkness, fallen warriors stir in crumbling barrows, giants descend from frozen fortresses, and ancient threats arise anew to endanger communities' villagers who huddle around their fires like beacons of light in the gloom.

entries.name: Magics of the Giants and Forgotten Runes
entries: The Northlands are steeped in secrets and mysteries, both current and ancient. In the dark forests of the taiga, ancient entities once worshiped like gods lurk beneath barrow mounds and within stone circles. The glaciers gleam with the power of eternal ice, and the seas writhe with the encircling World Serpent. Jotunheim, the realm of the giants, overflows with enchantments devised in the world before. To combat these threats, the gods gave runes to mortals. These magical symbols, cut into stone and bone, act to combat the darkness and pierce the veil of destiny to show what is to come.

entries.name: Power of Poems, Stories, and Sagas
entries: These lands overflow with epic tales of warriors and monsters, giants and serpents, old gods and newly crowned kings. These are sagas—timeless songs of heroes. The skalds hold the sagas as they do the history of the Northlands. Holding an important social and cultural role, these writers, poets, and musicians bear witness to great deeds and wicked betrayals, and in their works lies immortality. A Northlander knows they will never truly die as long as their stories are sung around the crackling hearth of a campfire or their deeds are marveled over by new blades and old sailors.

entries.name: Life in the Northlands
entries: Life is harder in the North. In the fjordlands, running out of firewood doesn't mean a chill night, but exposure to bone-wracking cold or a trip into the dark and dangerous forest for kindling. Everyone from king to lowly karl must work hard daily to survive. A life of indolence is unheard of and impossible without help from powerful magic. Work-shy characters aren't just lazy; they're ostracized as threats to the community.

People of the North are practical and independent, energetic, and inured to the hardships of life. No central authority demands taxes or a cut of loot, but at the same time, no one reins in the excesses of monsters and unscrupulous rulers. When bandits or trolls or the jarl's bullying huskarls come prowling, it's down to each family and their friends to choose fight or flight. Death comes to all sooner or later, for no matter how well-prepared and defended, nothing lives a moment longer than it's fated.

entries.name: Climate of the North
entries: In other lands, weather is an inconvenience to endure. Not so in the North. The arctic winds cut as deep as a blade. Blizzards blind. Snowdrifts isolate farms and towns. Falling temperatures turn blood to ice. Since the days of the Reaving (discussed in the {@area timeline|03d|x}), the climate of these lands has grown steadily colder. The inhabitants of these frigid lands have learned to adapt to the dangerous climate, but those who take it for granted typically perish.
The following tables outline the general climate conditions of the Northlands broken down by season and region:

items: {@b Fjordlands}. Skaldholm and the coastal areas of the Reaver kingdoms.
{@b Tundras and Hills}. Inland regions of the Reaver kingdoms and tundra areas of Thursrike and Vargrike.
{@b Mountains}. Jotunheim, the mountainous regions of various kingdoms, and the northern areas of Vargrike.
{@b Far North}. The glaciers and ice fields of the Bleak Expanse.

entries: Specific locations may have different conditions depending on altitude and other factors.

entries.caption: Northlands Seasonal Climate (Spring)
rows: Steady winds, light snow, heavy melt-off mid-season
Heavy meltwater and mud; planting season
Light winds & snow, moderate melt-off mid-season
High gusts, heavy snowfall, avalanches common
Cliffs and slopes shed winter ice

entries.caption: Northlands Seasonal Climate (Summer)
rows: Coastal breeze, no snow below 5,000 feet
Long days, trading and raiding season
Wind in mountain passes, snow above 5,000 feet

entries.caption: Northlands Seasonal Climate (Fall)
rows: Coastal gales, rain turns to snow by late season

entries.caption: Northlands Seasonal Climate (Winter)
rows: Boreal Dark, only 5 hours of sunlight

entries.name: Boreal Dark and Midnight Suns
entries: In the Northlands, even the daylight seems to dim during winter months. Evenings last a long time in these lands, and the sun is often hidden behind its cyclopean mountains, allowing nocturnal beasts to haunt the shadows long before night's true arrival. In winter, the sun seems to abandon its course completely, arching lower and lower until it ceases to rise beyond a glimmer on the horizon—a grim time known as the Boreal Dark. This phenomena lasts longer the farther a traveler moves north, so that the valleys of Jotunheim endure around two months without true daylight and half that in perpetual night. The Bleak Expanse sees even more Boreal Dark, and beyond that, the sun rises and sets only once each year. In summer, this distortion of day and night is reversed, hours of sunlight lengthening until the nights are no dimmer than twilight. These are the days of the Midnight Sun, sacred to {@deity Baldur|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} and a welcome respite from the horrors of the night.

entries.name: Climate and Survival in TTRPGs
entries: Traveling or exploring in the Northlands without a steady source of food or shelter might be as dangerous as the monsters encountered along the way. In most TTRPGs, matters of survival tied to climate are typically reduced down to a simple check, when they come up at all. Conditions in the Northlands can similarly be handwaved for ease of play. {@book Chapter 7|NorthlandsWorldbook|7} of this book includes rules for climate and survival, as well as more robust optional rules for those GMs and players who wish to indulge in more environmental challenges.

entries.name: Daily Life in the North
entries: Northlanders believe life is not lived—it is endured, contested and claimed. From the fjordlands to the farthest glaciers, brave folk survive in defiance of the weather and threats from monsters. Among these hearty inhabitants, honor and hardships are the daily meals, and even the lowest karl may rise through valor to greatness. Stories of the Northland reavers strike fear in the hearts of southerners and for good reason. Life in the North is more than just reaving, but understanding the mindset behind the raiders opens the window to view the depth of the Northlanders.

entries.name: The Reaver Mentality
entries: The so-called "reaver mentality" is not about raiding and pillaging, despite what those in the southern lands might believe. It is a philosophy of life framed by honor, sharpened by fate, and formed by hardship. Life in the North has been shaped by disasters like the Reaving and the gradual cooling of the climate. The subsequent loss of farmland meant that raiding became less about plunder and more about survival of the clan, family, or felag. It is not a crime to go raiding; it is a part of the social fabric. A successful reaver is admired for their courage, cleverness, and generosity with the spoils, not some southern concept of right or wrong.
Time has honed these factors into a series of axioms summing up what it means to be a reaver.

items: Face the odds with acceptance, a grin, and a bloody blade.
Express your honor through bold deeds, loyalty, and matching beliefs with action.
Earn your reputation through deeds, not by blood or bought with coin.
Fight with courage and never break an oath.
Treat guests as family.
Ensure you die well and earn a place in Valhalla, for Fate is already written.

entries.name: Social Structure
entries: Outside of family and clan, felag is the strongest bond in society. It means "fellowship" and "partnership" and is linked to the power of the {@i Fe} rune, which represents division of wealth. A felag oath-taker swears to loyally support their lord and fellow warriors in a sacred bond between companions. This oath defines the felag's aims, its right to depose and elect leaders, and fair division of the spoils.

Social order in the North is fluid and defined by one's actions. Kingship and jarldom are forged through skill, war, and adventure, not guaranteed by bloodline. Most Northlanders are karls (free farmers), crafters, artisans, and part-time raiders and traders—who answer only to themselves. Unlike their counterparts in the feudal hierarchies of the south, homesteaders aren't bound to a local lord by anything but their own choices and oaths. Karls who directly serve a lord are known as huskarls ("karls of the house") and make up a lord's allies, administrators, and personal bodyguard. A wise lord is free with gifts and opportunities for glory, else a few karls may look elsewhere for a patron. The blandishments of {@deity Loki|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}, {@deity Boreas|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}, giants, or the trollkin sometimes win over a karl far out on the cold margins of civilization.

Above karls are jarls and kings—nobles defined not by bloodline or divine provenance but followers, ships, and estates. Sometimes a kingdom of the North has many kings, and sometimes it has but a few. Royalty attracts more than enough rivals, invaders, and pretenders to stymie any ruler's power, and successions are always disputed. Kingship is not regarded as especially sacred or special. Some rulers might claim descent from a hero or god (occasionally backed up by genuine divine favor), but success is the only real measure of nobility in the North.

entries.name: Seers, Prophecies, Omens
entries: Existing outside of the traditional social order are seers. These individuals are blessed, or some say cursed, with the ability to give prophetic readings. They use rituals, runes, and the ingestion or inhalation of various substances to catch a glimpse of the {@deity Norns|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}' great weaving of fate.

What a seer foretells is neither clear nor straightforward. At best, it is a hint or guideline, and it is never guaranteed. Prophecy in the Northlands isn't a method to avoid fate; instead, it is a way to guide someone toward fulfilling their destiny. This may seem like a subtle difference, but it is a significant one. Fate is largely unknowable, except for the {@deity Norns|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} and their weavings, yet it is also inescapable. Despite appearances, this doesn't take agency away from the characters. In truth, there isn't much difference between free will and an unknown fate, except in terms of mindset.

Seers tend to live outside of established settlements, in caves, isolated cabins, or crumbling ruins. This ostracism is as much their choice as it is something forced on them by others. The path of the seer is plagued by false visions, hallucinations, and mental instability. This is the price they pay to the {@deity Norns|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} for their glimpses at fate. Seers are greatly valued and feared by Northlands communities in equal amounts. For every jarl or would-be hero who wishes for a hint about their fate, there are those who shun the seer for the same reason. An accepted truth is that to harm a seer is to risk angering the {@deity Norns|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}, and even mindless monsters seem to avoid harming them.

items.name: Visiting a Seer
items.entry: When a character visits a seer to receive a prophetic reading, they participate in a two-hour ritual that culminates in the reading. As payment for the ritual, a seer typically accepts hacksilver or goods equal to the character's level multiplied by their proficiency bonus, in gold pieces. GMs should alter the price for prophetic readings depending on the importance or accuracy of the result.

entries: {@area Chapter 7|4e8|x} details rules for creating prophetic readings.

entries.name: Customs of the Northlands
entries: The unyielding landscape hammered Northern culture into its current shape. The surroundings define its people far more than species. Different species approach life with the same bullish mindset, worship in a similar fashion, and follow roughly the same customs. Humans can travel to a trollkin steading or a goblin hall with reasonable expectations of proper etiquette.

Still, each species exhibits prejudices and preferences, muddying the waters of tradition and adding unexpected twists that can form the basis of adventures. {@creature Jotun|NorthlandsWorldbook} rarely think it unfair to challenge guests to giant-sized games of strength for example, while kobold althings (see {@area The Althing|01e|x}) are notorious for backstabbing politics, and what's on the table at a troll feast might not be palatable to other races, though it's still rude not to eat. The most common shared customs involve honor and reputation, hospitality and feasting, the althings, wergild and duels, and the infamous reaver raid.

entries.name: Honor and Reputation
entries: Reputation and honor are everything. Warriors tell tales of old comrades and adventures, and skalds sing of deeds both valorous and vile. Passing news and gossip is a common pastime from karls to kings. Desire for a good reputation compels people to acts of generosity, valor, and hospitality, while ill-repute is rightly feared, and the taint of dishonor is difficult to shed. Northlanders have a prickly sense of honor: A good name is all that remains after death, so most people don't just want to do the right thing, they want to be seen doing it.

Honor isn't the same as goodness, however. Wicked reavers are considered honorable, and some good Northlanders are known as nithingr (honorless) for abandoning the crueler Northern customs. Regardless of alignment, an honorable person is generous in gifting and hospitality, fair-minded in judgments, and fearless in battle. The ability to uphold such values can keep even the truly malevolent in good favor with the gods, and the ability to subvert such customs to meet one's goals draws the favor of the more devious among the deities.

Cleverness and wit are also essential; Northlanders should be able to recite poetry, evade the tempers and tantrums of the gods, and be considered cunning by allies and enemies alike. Northlanders take life stoically, calm in even the worst of circumstances. They know well that the {@deity Norns|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} control fate, and the best one can do is be honorable, live up to the fate written for them, and (hopefully) take their place in Valhalla.

The {@variantrule Reputation|NorthlandsWorldbook} rules in {@area Chapter 7|4dd|x} present optional rules on how to include reputation as a mechanic during gameplay, as well as a simplified version for GMs not wishing to track the PCs changing reputation.

entries.name: Fate and Fortune
entries: The {@deity Norns|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} weave destiny for gods and mortals alike, and none escape their final doom. Everything in the world has a fate that cannot be evaded or denied. {@deity Baldur|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}'s dreams foretell his death, and a hall awaits his coming in the Underworld. {@deity Wotan|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} learns of Ragnarok many years before it will come to pass and knows that he will die with the jaws of the {@deity Fenris|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} Wolf around his throat. For those who are not gods, fate is predetermined, but it isn't incredibly specific and, more importantly, though their fate has been written, they don't know what that fate is. Whereas a character from elsewhere in the world might be worried about "changing" their fate, a Northlander might consult a seer for aid to achieve their fate. Generally, however, they go about their lives without any such concern. Why worry when it is already written?

Northlanders don't believe in coincidence. When old friends or enemies meet, they give a knowing nod at their destined reacquaintance. When an expedition is lost at sea or a companion killed, it was destiny. People's actions are predestined, and their choices already woven, but Northerners travel through life with a cheerfully resigned attitude: It was meant to be, and good people struggle on as best they can and hope that a better thread of fate awaits them tomorrow.

The concept of fate in the Northlands can best be described as a series of specific set events stretching from birth to death. These events only cover major life changes. The events in between are not necessarily covered by preordained fate. That's where luck comes in.

entries.name: Luck
entries: A human warlord is destined to fall in a certain battle in their 44th year. That is a set point in time. But the details matter. Are they entering that battle as a common warrior? A jarl leading their hand-picked soldiers into war? Are they cut down trying to flee the battle? Or do they accomplish great deeds in that battle and thus earn their place in Valhalla? If fate determines a person's life, luck is the factor that fills in the gaps between the preordained signposts of fate and influences the manner by which they come to pass.

Being "lucky" isn't random. It is tied to fate and to the individual's own actions. Luck can even grow with honorable deeds, reputation, and honors, or diminish through cowardice, betrayal, or vile acts. Because lucky men and fortunate women are signposts of fate, Northlanders ally with those folk. Likewise, they distance themselves from unlucky people and items.

entries.name: Acceptance of Fate and Death
entries: How the acceptance of this fate is embraced is key to the reaver mentality and the source of the Northlanders' fierce reputation. Warriors know they cannot avoid death. They know it is meant to be, just as they know water is wet. This nurtures an aggressive, even joyful fatalism. Where others might shy away from danger, Northlanders charge ahead without a pause. They know they can't avoid their predetermined death, but they try to ensure their death is worthy so they can earn a place in Valhalla.

Death comes to all, sooner or later, for no matter how well-prepared and defended, no one lives a moment longer than they're fated. Although the heroic dead may earn a place in Asgard, for most, all that remains after they've gone is their name and reputation. Death comes to Player Characters like everyone else. Although {@spell Raise Dead|XPHB} and other magic might see a PC return from death, most Northlands characters consider a heroic end to be a fantastic outcome, since it would earn them a place in {@deity Wotan|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}'s Hall, and many heroes might not want to return.

Both PCs and NPCs have the option of accepting a "good death" as a worthy end. Gone but not forgotten, dead PCs live on through tales told by the friends and allies they made, their reputations (which might inspire feats or traits for later PCs), tales sung by skalds and their comrades, and even high-level visits to Valhalla. For less honorable characters, Niflheim is the unwelcome destination. {@deity Hel|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}'s hall is a virtual prison—one that characters might infiltrate in order to rescue a nefarious comrade. {@deity Hel|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} is always open to a bargain.
Returning from the dead isn't seen as avoiding fate. If it is successful, the individual was simply not fated to die at that time.

entries.name: Feasting and Hospitality
entries: The communal meal is a cornerstone of Northern culture, from the farmer sitting down with family members and hired hands each night, to a reaver captain hosting her shield-maidens and huskarls, or a king celebrating a major religious festival. At the feast table, warriors get to know one another, deciding issues of status and building the camaraderie needed to survive as a warband or army. Outside martial groups, feasts mark harvests and other important calendar days, offer praise to the gods, and help bind families and communities together. The day's events are discussed, gossip spread, and deals brokered from betrothals to barter to raids.

entries.name: Law of Hospitality
entries: Providing hospitality is one of the most important obligations of honor. A warm hearth, a hearty meal, and stout walls are the only respite from the dark and dangerous wilderness, and welcoming guests is one of the few ways to learn foreign news and gossip.
