How someone acts as a guest or a host is considered a telling mark of character. In exchange for the host's generosity, guests pay them back not with coin but by behaving themselves, defending their host from attack, and giving their own gifts (or aid in time of need) while staying beneath the host's roof. Even deadly enemies and monsters adhere to the laws of hospitality—or at least the letter of it. It is a mark of great dishonor to attack a host, but it is perfectly fine for a warrior to take their leave of their host and then ambush them outside of town.

Across the Northlands, feasts share some common elements. Ale and mead are served in vast open barrels, ladled out by servants and ferried to drinkers who sit in order of reputation. Those most favored sit near the lord of the hall, who sprawls on a thronelike chair, or thrones in the case of married rulers. Guests' weapons are kept nearby but not permitted at the feast; they would offer too many temptations for drunken diners to violate hospitality, bringing dishonor upon all concerned.

entries.name: The Althing
entries: The democratic traditions of the North surprise many outlanders. Families and neighbors sort out local matters among themselves, but every region also has a regular meeting called an althing that combines court and trade fair. Northlanders meet to settle quarrels, make vows of peace or war, forge new alliances, celebrate great deeds, and invoke ancient laws. A council of wise law-speakers and jarls oversees debates and attempts to broker satisfactory settlements, but all the discussions are public, and all free people can have their say.

Much in the North is decided by the influence of local lords and bullies, but big decisions need public approval—although intimidation and backstabbing goes on behind the scenes. Even peaceful times see arguments to settle and feuds to avert, so the althing's law-speakers constantly rule on hunting and pasturage rights, debts unpaid and stolen property or cattle, and even kidnapping and murder. If agreement and recompense cannot be reached, injured parties rely on the sanctity of the duel or the declaration of a feud.

The althing also provides an opportunity for trading and the disposition of raid booty. Families bring slaves, cloth, fine weapons, salt, wax, hides, raw materials, or a variety of hand-crafted household goods to offer in trade. Artisans, rune masters, and wizards also search the althing for customers, and in a region with few cities, it's the best opportunity for wealthy Northlanders to lay their hands on exotic or magic items.

Distant kings and powerful jarls sometimes send both warriors and silver-tongued bards to the althing to safeguard their interests. Locals despise such sly emissaries, and it's not uncommon for such folk to have their heads removed and sent back to their lords as a message that communities prefer to manage their own affairs. These actions and duels are the only violence permitted at the althing, though most attendees consider it a poor event if fewer than three or four people travel The {@deity Hel|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}-road during a moot. Death is great entertainment, a fine sacrifice, and a good way to remind everyone of the usefulness of the peace of the althing.

Most althings take place at a traditional spot: a jarl's longhouse, sacred glade, blessed rock, World Tree, or other hallowed location. Borders are a common locale, allowing rival regions to remain separate between debates. A nearby hall might host prominent visitors, but most people camp in the surrounding fields. Divinely sent afflictions and public condemnation await those who break the truce of an althing.

entries.name: Northern Economics
entries: Gold is relatively rare in the North and has a reputation as a provoker of men to unwise acts of violence or greed. Silver, however, is commonplace. Most native Northern coins are silver, often large enough to be worth five or ten times a Southern silver piece. Dwarves, especially, prefer to create valuable goods rather than coins (and are notoriously easy to offend if offered coins), but to some extent, all Northerners are distrustful of it, preferring more substantial and beautiful treasures, something worthy of a song or tale.

A common type of wealth is hacksilver, consisting of simple pieces of jewelry, like rings and armbands, designed to be used in place of coins and to be broken into chunks when smaller amounts are needed. Most traders judge coins and hacksilver by weight. More valuable objects are also used as currency, especially when it comes to gifts.

Almost all trade is done through barter, conducted face to face and inevitably involving small talk, haggling, and ale to loosen the tongue and purse-strings. Most commoners aren't paid wages as such; instead, they are provided with hospitality and an appropriate value of gifts for their work. Adventurers are the exception to this practice, as it is typical to reward such heroes for their deeds.

entries.name: Justice
entries: A Northlander's concept of justice can be hard to define. Relatively few actions are considered crimes. Most involve theft or dishonoring someone's good name, and "justice" is synonymous with compensation or avoiding a feud, not some abstract idea of right or wrong. Assuming the wrongdoers have not committed an especially heinous crime (treachery, for example), the accused might not be treated as criminals by the populace at large, or even by their victims. Fines known as wergild are the usual punishment, paid by the offenders to the victim or their family (traditionally in the form of silver rings or hacksilver), and in exchange, the victim and the victim's kin both swear to let the matter drop. An insult to a family's honor must be answered regardless of how many generations pass. Often, these rivalries are put aside during raids or other common causes when the goal of the endeavor is more important than settling an individual grudge.

Traditional reaver culture abounds here and permeates most aspects of life. The legal system centers on honor and revenge, with the Jarl's word and holmganga duels acting in place of advocates or juries. Punishments for lawbreakers tend toward servitude or imprisonment for minor offenses, but can reach ritual scarification or even death for major crimes. The most violent aspects of the worship of {@deity Thor|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}, {@deity Volund|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}, and others are commonplace, and most religious services involve some manner of ritual sacrifice (though seldom of sentient beings).

entries.name: Dueling
entries: Questioning someone's honor, accusing them of a crime or of cowardice, or falsely claiming credit for heroic deeds is asking for a fight. Sometimes, this is resolved through a flyting, a contest of insults, but more serious matters can only be decided through a bloody duel called a holmganga.
{@area Chapter 7|4e5|x} includes rules for running flyting contests and holmganga duels.

entries.name: Feuds
entries: If debate or holmganga cannot resolve an issue (or neither party is interested in trying them), then a feud can erupt. Immediate and extended family, neighbors, and the victim's friends are expected to avenge them by inflicting the same woes on the criminal and all nearby kin. Sometimes the motivation is a genuine sense of justice; more often, it's an excuse for robbery and murder. Feuds rapidly get out of hand as each side calls in debts, creating an ever-expanding circle of violence (and more wergild needed to settle it) that can go on for generations.

Pressure from the althing can sometimes end feuds, but otherwise, they continue until one side flees the area, is destroyed beyond capacity to strike back, or—rarely—both sides weary of continual bloodshed. All factions court adventurers to aid them, both officially and unofficially, and the call for allies or the duty of guests to their host are easy ways to embroil honorable characters in a conflict, sometimes on the wrong side. Even intervening to break up a fight can cause an unwilling party to become part of a feud—or the cause of a fresh one.

entries.name: Outlawry
entries: Outlaws have been banished from honorable society. They are outcasts, sometimes by choice or circumstance but more commonly as a punishment. Beggars as well as respected jarls are declared outlaw for crimes. Literally "outside the law," they can be killed without penalty or fear of wergild or feud. Their families are supposed to treat outlaws as if they were dead, while strangers should not offer them hospitality or aid, treating them as they would a wolf scratching at their door. Sometimes a bounty is offered by the outlaw's victims, and jarls reward anyone who kills a known outlaw.

Outlawry is sometimes for life and sometimes for a set period—a year or three years or until the king or jarl who declared it is dead. Outlawry applies only in the outlaw's local althing or kingdom. Depending on the crime, an outlaw might be ignored or even welcomed in neighboring lands. Outlawry doesn't carry much stigma (it's an occupational hazard for most adventurers), but the deed behind it might reflect significantly on the outlaw's reputation.

entries.name: People of the North
entries: The Northlands has always been home to a variety of different species, all of whom follow Northern traditions, instead of having a variety of highly specialized customs. Small differences exist, but for the most part, the true measure of a person in the North is their courage, truthfulness, and honor. Industriousness, perseverance, and self-reliance are prized and revered traits. Hospitality provided to travelers and kin is not only expected but a matter of personal pride. While many people differ on what those values mean specifically, no one doubts they are the key to survival in the North.

entries.name: Major Species
entries: Blessed by powerful patron gods and holding widespread influence, the major species have a long history in the lands, and most have nations of their own or large populations in various realms.

entries.name: Bearfolk
entries: Found in the northerly climes of Bjornrike, the bearfolk are broad-shouldered, bipedal humanoids that strongly resemble upright bears. Their hands lack a bear's sharp claws and are as dexterous as those of any human craftsman. They are covered in shaggy black or brown fur and often have light frosting on their chest, shoulders, and upper back. The color of their fur sometimes gives clues as to a particular bearfolk's heritage and what tribe they hail from. As they get older, the fur around their muzzle begins to silver, giving them a distinguished look.

Bearfolk stand against both the challenging environment of the North and more fearsome neighbors with their size and might, often using their great strength to excel as warriors, druids, and shamans. While their fangs, fur, and size may make smaller races nervous, most bearfolk prove to be honest and loyal friends. Many bearfolk societies consist of tight-knit families, and most bearfolk acknowledge the Bear King of Bjornrike as their ruler regardless of where they reside.

entries.name: Dwarves
entries: The Northlands dwarves are keepers of the old ways and the old gods, smiths and warriors, farmers, traders, and reavers. Stout, strong, and able to down a barrel of ale in one sitting, they keep busy fighting the giants or the werewolves and worgs, or each other. Dwarves are especially accomplished at ring-making and smithing, and their metalwork is exceptional. Most dwarves embrace the reaver mentality, waiting with eager anticipation for the sea ice to clear. When spring is in bloom, these dwarves put aside their tools and crafts to take to the sea in their longships and raid the coasts, from nearby villages to distant cities in southern lands.

The Northern dwarves possess the same traits as dwarves found elsewhere in the world. A small variant lineage of dwarves called Baudsmidr can be found in the heart of dwarven holds across the North, but they rarely venture into the outside world.

entries.name: Giantkin
entries: Descendants of the unlikely pairing of giants and humans, giantkin tower over most other Northerners, their physical characteristics showing the signs of their ancient heritage. Standing 6'5" or taller, they carry the blood of their forebears and the grit of the Northlands in equal measure. Neither fully giant nor truly human, giantkin walk between worlds: mistrusted by some, respected by others, but always seen as formidable. While not as common as humans, giantkin are found from glacier to fjord, living hard lives of labor, warfare, or wanderlust.

Each giantkin bears physical traits tied to their lineage, such as fiery hair from fire giants or grayish skin from stone giants. Despite these differences, all giantkin share the strength of their bloodline and a sense of fate tied to ancient powers. Giantkin deal with their ancestry in personal ways; some choose to engrave jotun symbols into their gear or seek out lost relics from the Vanir Wars, while others try to put their blood behind them. Whether wielding axe, bow, or spell, the giantkin embody the raw, wild power of the North.

entries.name: Humans
entries: Humans are the youngest people of the world, and their tenacity and flexibility has allowed them to quickly spread. Humans are diverse in appearance and culture, so it's not surprising that their creation myths are similarly varied. Despite, or perhaps because of their tangled history, humans leave their stamp wherever they go. A natural drive fills their lives with dreams of long-lasting achievements. More than a few reach those dreams. The humans of the Northlands can be found in nearly every environment and in nearly every form of community. Two main heritages of humans can be found in the North. Both speak the Northern tongue, and many also speak Dwarvish or Trollkin.

items.name: Northlanders
items.entry: Pale, tall, and strong, the Northlanders are a race of survivors and warriors. Their hair runs to pale blond or even white, sometimes with golden or red streaks. Their eyes are often a piercing blue or purple.

items.name: Plainsfolk
items.entry: Hailing from the great steppes and plains to the east of the Northlands, the Plainsfolk are a proud people with olive skin and dark hair. Some humans of the North can claim descent from Plainsfolk immigrants, but by and large, they adhere to Northern customs.

entries.name: Trollkin
entries: In ancient times, ogres, trolls, and fey would sometimes take humans as mates. The children of these unlikely unions are known as trollkin, lanky and hulking humanoids who bear the traits from both sets of their ancestors. Trollkin are strong in body and mind, warriors and raiders known for ferocity, courage, and persistence. They have carved out a reputation for violence and for being powerful, if unreliable, mercenaries.

In the past, trollkin were rarely accepted in the so-called civilized regions. Their clans inflicted untold misery on the North's isolated villages and farmsteads. Recent years, however, have seen an influx of trollkin migrating to and integrating with communities across the Northlands, especially in Trollheim, Wolfheim, and even Vargrike.

entries.name: Werekin
entries: Born of ancient bloodlines and touched by the wild essence of {@deity Fenris|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}, werekin are humanoids who bridge the worlds of beast and man. Descendants of those once cursed—or blessed—with natural lycanthropy, they now breed true as a species. Werekin don't suffer the madness of the full moon as their ancestors did, but they retain the ability to shift between humanoid form and a lupine hybrid state. In their shifted form, they grow fur and claws, and their eyes gleam with predatory cunning.

Werekin are common in the harsh Kingdom of the Wolf, where the law of fang and strength governs all. They are hunters, scouts, warriors, and survivors, filling the ranks of the great lupine packs that roam the taiga. Ignorant outsiders distrust them, mistaking them for full-blooded werewolves, but werekin are fiercely proud of their heritage and gladly embrace the beast within, proving each time that rather than being a curse, it is power and freedom.

entries.name: Minor Species
entries: A number of other species live in the civilized lands of the North, and many more in its wilderness and wastelands. These include beastkin, elves and elfmarked fey, gnolls, goblins, halflings (winterfolk), kobolds, ratatosk, and ravenfolk. Most have some presence in the larger realms or have claimed small regions of their own. Some, such as the dragonborn, are barely known. Others, like the aasimar or gnomes, are simply rare, or at least rarely seen. Even those with some weight of numbers, such as the ratatosk and ravenfolk, are too insular to bend history to their will.

entries.name: Beastkin
entries: Born between civilization and the wilds, beastkin are as varied as the animal kingdom itself. Sometimes called wildkin, beastkin universally share the bipedal form of humans, elves, or dwarves, but have pronounced traits of a specific beast, such as hawk wings, a scorpion's tail, rabbit ears, owl eyes, a crab-like carapace, razor-sharp shark teeth, or bony ox horns. Some beastkin show only slight bestial features, while others resemble bipedal versions of their animal kin.

Some beastkin believe they are relatives of the intelligent beasts that hold court in the fey realms. Others claim they are descendants of lycanthropes or other magically transformed beings. Whatever the case, all beastkin share a tie to the natural world, and many choose to live alongside the animals they resemble. Young beastkin are often driven by curiosity to seek out other civilizations and far-flung environments. While all beastkin contend with primal urges, they are quick to form unshakable bonds with those who show them compassion and loyalty, whether humanoid or beast.
Though small in number in the Northlands, most beastkin can be found in Bjornrike, Skaldholm, and (perhaps oddly) Thursrike, where they have carved out a place among the giantfolk.

entries.name: Elves and the Elfmarked
entries: The elves are a people apart, as they are quick to remind others. They say they taught arcana and civilization to humans and dwarves and others—a claim the dwarves loudly dispute. Pushed out of the Northlands by the surviving dwarven holds after the Reaving, the elves established a wondrous empire in southern lands. Its magical roads, slim towers, and speedy and lethal armies were a wonder for the ages until a few centuries ago when the majority of the elves, and those who served them, left the mortal world during the Great Retreat. The few elven courts in the North were abandoned and left to ruin. Some of these courts are still inhabited by a handful of gnomes, elfmarked, or even a solitary elven caretaker; others are entirely left to ghosts, phantoms, banshees, or wild animals.

In the Northlands, elves are exceedingly rare. The few individuals who claim descent from the elves of old, called "elfmarked," are slightly more common, but are as much human as elf. The true elves are rarely seen, and in the North, they are defined by three lineages: the elusive Alfar, the wild Ice Elves, and elven visitors from southern lands.

items.name: Alfar
items.entry: Also called "hidden elves," these isolated and insular elves remained behind during the Great Retreat to protect their ancient holy sites.

items.name: Ice Elves
items.entry: Nomadic bands of wild elves roam the glaciers and hills of the far north. They shun "civilized" lands but sometimes trade with others.

items.name: True Elves
items.entry: When found in the Northlands, true elves are usually visitors, recently arrived from other regions of the world.

entries.name: Halflings (Winterfolk)
entries: Unlike their southern counterparts, the halflings of the North (also called winterfolk) are a determined people so used to the rugged life of ice and fang that they seem to relish hardship. Some winterfolk live in isolated communities in the lowlands of the Tunturi Range or pockets of the Reaching Mountains. Others choose to dwell for a time in towns and cities in the Northlands, but they never stay for very long. Community and family remain a strong cultural bond for winterfolk, and they give no quarter to any creature seeking to threaten the freedom and security of their people. Winterfolk are often superstitious and have many cultural rituals they follow on a daily basis.

Life can be tricky when you are three feet tall in a world of 12-foot-tall snowdrifts. Winterfolk believe they must be twice as strong as the "big folk" to survive, and they seek out challenges with a zeal that appears suicidal to others.

entries.name: Kobolds
entries: Once enslaved by the reaver dwarves, kobolds are the only scaled species to have adapted to life in the North. Often dismissed as harmless, they thrive in the shadows of dwarven society as miners, scouts, and tinkerers. Many kobolds worship {@deity Loki|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}, fiercely defending dwarven mines while keeping up the ruse of servility. Survivors at heart, their keen senses, clawed agility, and sheer numbers help them endure where others fail. Kobolds are skilled miners, gearsmiths, and modest alchemists. When not integrated into a larger community, their society is clan-based, matriarchal, and places great emphasis on working closely with one's clutch-mates. Exiled or grieving kobolds may become adventurers, adopting new companions as family.

entries.name: Ratatosk
entries: In recent decades, the squirrel-like beings called ratatosk have grown bored with simply safeguarding the World Tree and have ventured into the mortal world, especially with the arrival of Hrafnheim. Often exuberant individuals with large personalities, ratatosk can be insatiable tricksters. Sharing gossip from across the planes, many delight in learning secrets and spreading those tidbits of information in mischievous ways. They are squirrels with sleek fur and small tusks, and they form close matriarchal familial units called drays within larger communities called scurries. More adventurous ratatosk often act as planar guides and guardians, though it is not uncommon to find squirrel-folk offering their services as couriers, thieves, or even spies.

entries.name: Ravenfolk
entries: Also called huginn or heru in southern lands, these ravenlike humanoids are found in large numbers in Hrafnheim, but they also have small presences in Trollheim and other kingdoms. Old superstitions unjustly cast them as spies, informers, and troublemakers, but when most ravenfolk swear an oath, they abide by it.

Ravenfolk have long held a role as messengers for the gods. They hear the words of {@deity Wotan|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} most clearly, but they also claim to speak for {@deity Thor|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}, {@deity Loki|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}, and {@deity Sif|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}. Occasionally, they bring dark tidings from {@deity Boreas|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} or blood-smeared missives from {@deity Chernobog|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}, but these are rare, and the poor ravenfolk chosen to deliver divine messages and prophecies from dark gods are often shunned even among their own people.

Ravenfolk claim to have invented or at least shared the runes of the All-Father. Though their understanding of prophecy and shadow are excellent, their magic wins little renown in the wider world, for they guard it jealously. They are keen scouts and powerful oracles, and they demonstrate an uncanny ability to bend runes to new uses.

entries.name: Visitors from Distant Lands
entries: Other species, such as goliaths, orcs and tieflings, live in the North, but they are of limited number. The traditional roles of goliaths and orcs in this book are taken up by the trollkin, so members of those species found in the North are most likely just called "trollkin" by the locals.

Northland traders and reavers venture into far distant seas, so it is feasible to add virtually any species to this setting, though some discussion should be had as to how and why they came to these icy shores.

entries.name: Other Species in the Northlands
entries: The North is home to many other species. Vast numbers of giants are its most well-known inhabitants, claiming Jotunheim, a land that bubbles with primal energies. Various types of fey claim they have always been in the ice-shrouded woodlands. Clans of white-furred gnolls roam the glaciers and wild places of the far north, and clutches of goblins scramble for a place in the forgotten corners of various kingdoms.

entries.name: Fey
entries: The fey are ubiquitous throughout the Northlands, from Bjornrike to the shores of the Haamu Hills and as far north as anyone has dared to travel. It is a rare stretch of woods, lake, river, or stream that lacks a resident faerie creature, or a whole host of them. Certain varieties of fey are particular to the north: ice maidens wander the high frozen places, some with bands of fraughashar to do their bidding; hags lurk in the cold bogs, hatching their vile plots against the innocent; and rum gremlins wreak havoc along the piers and docks or from hidden burrows beneath mead halls. Travelers are advised to learn the proper ways to pay their respects or otherwise avoid the endless variety of hazards and entanglements one risks when dealing with fey creatures.

entries.name: Giants
entries: This world is but a poor replacement for the world created by Aurgelmir, or so the giants claim. That first world was destroyed by the gods at the end of the First War, when the Aesir and Vanir joined forces to crush the giant's dreams of glory. The giants took the far reaches of the North, while the followers of the hated gods spread out across the world.

Giants roam the Northlands in increasing numbers, and the ruins of isolated farmsteads offer mute testimony of their destruction. Aside from their holdings, giant-sized geography and architecture, an understandable obsession with strength and size, and a hatred of the gods of Asgard, life in the giant's realms is much like anywhere else in the North in its mundane details. Many types of giants can be found in the North. The following is a brief description of the most common varieties (arranged by height).

items.name: Thursir
items.entry: Smallest of the giants at only 10 feet tall, the thursir are crafters with an affinity for metalworking and are known for their gluttonous appetites.

items.name: Hill Giants
items.entry: Industriously dim, hill giants are 16 feet tall. They tend to be blunt and direct, enjoying the simple things in life.

items.name: Stone Giants
items.entry: Gray-skinned giants that stand about 18 feet tall, stone giants hold a lesser social status among other giants due to an ancient crime no one remembers.

items.name: Fire Giants
items.entry: Dark-skinned and flame-haired fire giants stand about 19 feet tall. They enjoy smelting and smithing but are typically too temperamental for fine artistry.

items.name: Frost Giants
items.entry: Ice-skinned giants that stand about 21 feet tall, frost giants live on glaciers and hunt vast herds of mammoths and other megafauna.

items.name: Cloud Giants
items.entry: Elegant and stately 24-foot-tall blonde giants with sky colored skin, cloud giants live in floating towers and high mountains peaks.

items.name: Storm Giants
items.entry: Crackling with lightning, these 26-foot-tall reclusive giants seek lives of solitude but are easily roused to furious anger.

items.name: Jotun
items.entry: The oldest and mightiest of the giants, jotun are 60 feet tall and nearly immortal. Some possess powers rivaling demigods.

entries.name: Gnolls
entries: Gnolls are more common in southern lands, but clans of tundra gnolls range the glaciers and windswept ice of the far north as hunters and scavengers. Known to be expert rangers, scouts, and trackers, their matriarchal culture is violent and largely unfriendly to outsiders. Some clans bend their knees to {@deity Boreas|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} or powerful giant jarls, while others avoid entanglements with the powers of the world and merely want to be left alone.

entries.name: Goblins
entries: Alone among the shorter races, goblins refuse to be conquered or adopt even the pretense of diplomacy, and so they are treated as vermin and exterminated wherever dwarves and men encounter them. Driven into the wilderness by larger races, goblins are opportunistic scavengers. Many goblin tribes fall under the sway of worgs and nightgarms, which they worship as totem beasts. The relationship between goblins and worgs reverses expectations: the goblins are pets and servants of the lupine lords, not the other way around.

entries.name: Ogres and Trolls
entries: Ogres, trolls, and other types of so-called "minor" giants dwell in great number in the Northlands. Ogres and trolls especially inhabit a wide variety of environments and locations, from sea to swamp to ice. Some clans form their own communities and exist by hunting and raiding. Others are drawn into nearby communities of larger giants or are powerful troops in the armies of warlords, mystics, or cultists.

entries.name: Festivals and Holidays
entries: Life in the Northlands encompasses more than reaving, winter storms, and rampaging giants. People come together to celebrate the progress of the year, thanking their gods for the good times or appealing to them to help in darker moments. In these ceremonies, sacrifices of food, mead, or (rarely) animals made to specific deities are common. The following section details the important annual events shared by the folk of the North.

entries.name: Major Events
entries: Over the course of the year, the holidays of the calendar mark festivals, rites, and religious ceremonies meant to signal the changing seasons, to mark great times of victory, and to give the pious an occasion to make obeisance to the gods.

items.name: Skjoldnott "Shield-Night" [Midwinter]
items.entry: A joyful communal meal with offerings and prayers made to {@deity Thor|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} for survival and good fortune through the harshest part of winter.

items.name: Varvaka "Spring Vigil" [Early Spring]
items.entry: Held when the last snow of winter melts, this outdoor procession offers prayers to {@deity Freyr and Freyja|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook|Freyja} to bless the sowing season and seek fertility for crops and animals.

items.name: Vaeringrfest "Warrior's Feast" [Spring]
items.entry: A communal meal with music and dancing marks the beginning of reaver season. Jarls and other leaders choose the crews for their longboats while sacrifices are made to {@deity Wotan|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} for victory in battle and good fortune on raids.

items.name: Saelgrod "Joyful Harvest" [Midsummer]
items.entry: A celebration of warmth, trade, oaths, and friendship, the Summer Festival occurs at the solstice. The Summer Festival is a popular time for marriages and betrothals, horse trading, and fair dealings with strangers and old friends alike. Offerings are made to many deities, especially to {@deity Sif|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} and {@deity Freyr and Freyja|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook|Freyr}. Priests of {@deity Volund|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} are also sought after to bless anvils and livestock, hold funds for wagers, and negotiate marriage contracts.

items.name: Tidaskal "Season's Cup" [Autumn]
items.entry: A lively celebration marks the end of the harvest. Offerings of food and wine are made to {@deity Freyr and Freyja|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook|Freyr}, giving back some of the bounty of the year for the god's blessing for the coming winter.

items.name: Sununingrar "Turning Year" [Midwinter Solstice]
items.entry: During the longest night of the year, candles are lit, and toasts are made to many deities: {@deity Wotan|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} for victory, {@deity Njord|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} and {@deity Freyr and Freyja|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook|Freyr} for peace and plenty, and {@deity Thor|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} and {@deity Sif|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} for good weather. This ceremony marks a time to honor the dead.

entries.name: Regional Festivals
entries: These smaller celebrations are only in certain parts of the Northlands at various times of the year.

items.name: Askrhlattr "Ashen Echo" [Skaldholm, Early Winter]
items.entry: A day of misrule, satire, and folly held in {@deity Loki|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}'s name when the students at the various skaldic colleges take on the role of teachers and lead improvisational classes.

items.name: Bear King's Challenge [Bjornrike, Spring]
items.entry: Each year, the Bear King calls the strong and the wise to participate in a set of challenges, and the winner of the contests is crowned the King of Bjornrike. No one has ever defeated the Bear King. It is a festival much recounted in song and skaldic poetry, though the actual gathering is smaller than some.

items.name: Bloddagr Aurgelmis "Blood-Day of Aurgelmir" [Sengajordensblod, Midwinter]
items.entry: Jotun gather at the Temple of the Skull to recount the murder of the First Giant. Each lord renews their vow to someday repay the hated gods for their dark deed.

items.name: Eldskorinn "Fire-Cut" [Kaldrgard, Early Winter]
items.entry: In a ritual honoring {@deity Bergelmir|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}, giant warriors inscribe their deeds in runes of frost, then sear them into their skin with heated iced steel. Each scar becomes a living record, read aloud in feasting halls across the frost giant realm.

items.name: Hlijodfall "Chimefall" [Hrafnheim, Autumn]
items.entry: A solemn festival honoring {@deity Wotan|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} and {@deity Ratatoskr|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} when scholars and speakers share the year's omens and insights.

items.name: Hrimhringr "Frost Ring" [Bleak Expanse, Winter]
items.entry: A brutal contest of blood and strength held at the top of glaciers in honor of {@deity Boreas|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}. The winners gain the North Wind's favor, and the losers are thrown off the glacier.

items.name: Manargaldr "Moonspell" [Vargrike, Late Spring]
items.entry: The lycan folk conduct sacred howling rites under the full moon with offerings made to {@deity Fenris|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} and {@deity Angrboda|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}.

items.name: Myrkrgrot "Dark Soil Feast" [Thursrike, Autumn]
items.entry: On the cusp of winter, sacrifices are made to {@deity Angrboda|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} by the herders of Thursrike. Animal blood is fed into the soil to ask for protection over the coming season.

items.name: Njordarleikr "Njord's Games" [Trollheim, Midsummer]
items.entry: A celebratory festival honoring {@deity Njord|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} involving boating races, swimming contests, and other maritime games.

items.name: Stjarnaveizla "Feast of Stars" [Bjarmia, Summer]
items.entry: Held under the shining aurora, this feast to Aurgelmir celebrates knowledge, magic, and celestial wonder with eldritch demonstrations and arcane duels.

items.name: Svidnarsonr "Forging Rite" [Blodejord, Midsummer]
items.entry: Young fire giant crafters and warriors are tested by the fortress commanders and clerics of {@deity Bergelmir|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}. Those who fail are exiled to the ash wastes until they redeem themselves through acts of bravery.

items.name: Volundsmot "Volund's Meet" [Wolfheim, Late Winter]
items.entry: This annual smithing and forging competition honors {@deity Volund|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}. Grand prizes of hacksilver and rare ore are awarded to the winners.

entries.name: Timeline—The Land of Frost and Bears
entries: The history of the world varies according to the teller. This recitation is meant to provide a useful history of the Northlands, from the long-ago eras before scholars assigned dates to events, to the current struggles against giants, dragons, and horrors from the dark.

entries.name: An Abridged History
entries: Detailed here is a portion of the Bard's Chronology, as told among the schools at Skaldholm. These historical events can be used as shown, or they can be inserted into campaigns as needed when using the material presented in this book.

entries.name: The First Age of Creation: From Blood and Bone

items: Aurgelmir, the first giant, is formed from the Void. Gods and giants are born from him. Aurgelmir creates a world for his children to inhabit.

The gods fight the giants for control of the first world. When Aurgelmir sides with the giants, the gods slay him and break the branch connecting the mortal plane to Yggdrasil the World Tree. The first world is destroyed, killing all but two of Aurgelmir's firstborn children. Other lesser giants such as jotun survive.
The gods create a new world from Aurgelmir's corpse, and they hang it on Yggdrasil's broken branch.

The Vanir, gods of nature, war against the Aesir, gods of glory. During the conflict, dwarves and elves are created to fill the armies of either side. {@deity Wotan|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} brokers a truce, ending the war. The Aesir and Vanir become one pantheon and make their home in the plane of Asgard.
In what is now Vargrike, the Court of Masks is abandoned when its fey lord Reynard is forced to flee back to the Fey Realm.
Sengajordensblod Founded. The great jotun city is constructed around the heartstone, believed to be Aurgelmir's heart.
There are scattered small wars between the gods and the jotun lords. The massive redoubts of Drekholl, Jarnskul, Kjothall and Kupparsheim are constructed.
The jotun lords exile the majority of stone giants from the Northlands for a transgression they refuse to speak of. Most flee to southern lands, but a few isolated clans remain behind.
{@deity Bengta|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook|Bengta the Bear Maiden} transforms some northern bears into the first bearfolk.
Tanserhall and the first dwarven holds are established, forming the heart of an empire spanning what is now the area covered by the Nieder Strait.

Elven communities are either dominated by the dwarves or pushed to the south. The giant clans flee northward. Werewolves are contained in the northeast edge of the empire. Kobold communities are pressed into service as indentured workers in dwarven mines.
The Dwarven Empire pushes the fire giant jarls out of their ancestral holds near Bragafjall Mountain and establish Ishamagard. A clan of dwarven druids begins to tend to the mountain's slopes.
Bjarmia Founded. The goddess {@deity Gullveig|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} teaches cloud giants the art of cloud weaving and aids them in the construction of a majestic flying city.
Elves plant a branch of Yggdrasil on mortal soil, growing the first World Tree. Others soon follow in distant lands, all magically connected to Yggdrasil itself.
The giant goddess Mengloth imprisons herself within a hollow mountain but refuses to reveal why.
Mesikammen, a fey lord, arrives via a World Tree and settles among the bearfolk.
Dwarven vampire lords secretly take control of Glymshall.
The god {@deity Thor|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} destroys the jotun hold of Gatusalr to steal a pair of magical goats.

High King Vaknir Grathegn crafts the Dominion Orb, a divinely inspired artifact bonding his empire to his bloodline. He is assassinated shortly afterward. Arcane backlash from the sudden death of its creator fractures the orb, sending shockwaves down the eldritch bonds between the device and the land.

The ground shatters, and the Uttermost Sea rushes in, covering the majority of the empire. Tanserhall alone survives the cataclysm intact. Other shattered dwarven holds not at the bottom of the sea are mostly abandoned.
The surviving dwarves experience several decades of hunger, hardship, and isolation leading to the near collapse of their society and culture.
Wolfheim Founded. Jarl Ragnr gathers the survivors of Glymshall and forms a new kingdom thanks to a divinely blessed alliance with local packs of winter wolves and worgs.

Wotan's Promise. {@deity Wotan|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} and {@deity Volund|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} appear in dreams to the Jarl of Tanserhall, offering an afterlife in the Hall of Valhalla to those dwarves who prove themselves to be courageous and valorous.
The surviving dwarven clans declare war on the elves, blaming them for the fall of the empire. Elves flee to southern lands, leaving behind a few hidden or isolated communities.
In the aftermath, the dwarven rebuilding efforts are sporadic. In their absence, human communities are founded along the fjords and bays of the southern coast.
History begins to be recorded, first by oral stories and epic poems and later in the form of written runes.
Age of Upheaval (3000 years ago). A great cataclysm strikes an ancient island kingdom far to the southwest, sinking it beneath the waves. Tidal waves decimate coastal villages across the North.

Short summers and long winters force some humans to seek shelter with the dwarves in exchange for service in the mines or lowland farms. Bands of dwarven warriors raid other humanoid communities for workers, earning them the nickname of "reaver dwarf," an accolade embraced by the dwarves.
Stannasgard Founded (2750 years ago). The holds of Stannasgard, Thrumagard, Aurvang, and Nordheim are founded.
In the far north, the realm of Hyperborea appears. Its perfectly circular wall proves impervious to giants and gods alike.

Arrival of the North Wind (2000 years ago). {@deity Boreas|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}, the primordial spirit of the North Wind, arrives in the Northlands after being exiled by the other three wind spirits for his hatred of mortals and their upstart gods.

Elves from the Summer Lands settle in the southern lands. Word of these new elven kingdoms gives hope to the scattered elven communities in the North, sparking new flames of tension with the dwarven holds. Several small wars are fought.

Age of Ice (1750 years ago). {@deity Boreas|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} is reborn as a god with the goal of destroying his fellow wind spirits and the gods of mortals, and to cover the world in his icy winds. Under his influence, the North begins to slowly cool.

The great glaciers begin creeping down from the far north. Accompanying the ice, jotun, thursir and other giants begin moving southward. Ahead of them, ogres and trolls take captives from struggling human villages.

Birth of the Reavers (1500 years ago). After 250 years of slowly dropping temperatures, the Northlands experiences three consecutive winters of uncommon strength and duration. Crops fail and widespread famine sweeps through the North.

Dwarven longships and raiders begin to venture to nearby regions and (later) farther south to acquire supplies to sustain their holds and communities. The raids that began as a matter of survival combined with {@deity Wotan|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}'s Promise and blossomed into the "Reaver's Way" still embraced by the North today.
Thrumagard, the Thunder Mountain hold, is lost to an infestation of trolls and other monstrous creatures.

The Vanguard Kingdoms (1250 years ago). The dwarven holds of Aurvang and Nordheim ally with Issedon, a city-state populated by warriors of what is now the Trollheim region, to guard the North from the rage of {@deity Boreas|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}. The Vanguard Kingdoms are aided by powerful wizards from the legendary polar realm of Hyperborea.

The Wall, a line of magically fortified bulwarks, is completed, sealing off the mountain passes to the north of what is now Trollheim, Huldramose, and Wolfheim. For centuries, dwarven stonemasonry and Hyperborean magic hold back the hordes of {@deity Boreas|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}'s thuellai, frost giants, and ice elementals.

Tired of defeat, {@deity Boreas|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} unleashes a new weapon: living glaciers. Unstoppable masses of ice larger than the small kingdoms, these rivers of living ice move slowly but inexorably south from the Bleak Expanse, crushing everything in their path.

entries.name: Lost Kingdom of Hyperborea
entries: Stories say that beneath the apex of the world where polar lights cavort in drifting streams, the secret realm of Hyperborea explodes with verdant life, and the natural laws bend and mingle with the unbounded energies of the Outer Planes. Far beyond the current maps, where the sun only rises and sets once per year, four massive barbicans breach an otherwise unbroken circle of ten-mile-high, rune-carved granite wall. Each barbican is sealed with a priceless gate of prismatic steel big enough to swallow two longships sailing abreast. The Hyperborean gates have not opened in a thousand years, and today they are covered by layer upon layer of ice.

Within the frosty walls, the air is as warm as the deserts of the far south, and lush vegetation erupts from swampy volcanic earth. Hot springs create an otherworldly mist that drifts between jungle trees and nurtures vines and tiny flowers found nowhere else in the world. At the center of this impossible region lie the seven silent cities of the Thulang Plateau, where basaltic crypts and ancient tombs choke with treasures and horrors of a primordial age. Few ever reach the empty streets of these cities or survive their dangers.

items: A still unknown creature emerges from the depths and destroys Nordheim from within. None escape to report the true cause.

Fall of the Wall (900 years ago). Without Nordheim, the Vanguard Kingdoms fall to primordial ice and the Wall ruptures. Aurvang and Issedon are laid to ruin by {@deity Boreas|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}'s forces.
Trollheim Founded. The survivors of Issedon and the Wall flee south and east, rallying in Noatun, a far outpost of Issedon. They rename the remainder of their land Trollheim.

The Swive (850 years ago). {@deity Boreas|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} tricks the old sea god Aegir into causing the waters of the Nieder Strait to flood the great plains between Bjornrike and Huldramose, sending a tidal wave straight toward Noatun.

{@deity Njord|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}, Noatun's archmage protector, resists a corruptor sent by {@deity Boreas|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} and magically holds the waters back while humans and dwarves toil for 81 days to build an enchanted sea wall.
Most of the Bragafjall druids perish during a ritual to lift their mountain above the rising waters, creating the island of Skaldholm through their sacrifice.

Those who survived the deluge named the new sea the Swive. Meanwhile, {@deity Wotan|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} imprisons Aegir for his foolishness. {@deity Njord|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} ascends to become the new god of the seas.
Skaldholm Founded (825 years ago). The followers of {@deity Bragi|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}, the god of song and poetry, migrate to the island of Skaldholm and found a new kingdom.

Vargrike Founded (600 years ago). A mighty werewolf warlord, Wargaz the Cruel, dominates the scattered packs of wolves and lycanthropes in the northeast corner of the lands, and crowns herself the ruler of a new kingdom for the lycan folk.

Great Retreat (500 years ago). The elves withdraw from the mortal world to the Summer Lands, abandoning their courts, settlements, and outposts in the North, including the Moon Palace in what is now Vargrike.

A quarrel over the vacant elven lands between {@deity Volund|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} and {@deity Thor|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} ends with the exodus of the dwarves faithful to {@deity Volund|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}, who travel to southern lands. Those who remain in the North refuse to abandon {@deity Thor|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}, following both of the faiths, as well as the Reaver's Way.
The Mountain Wars (450 years ago). The oni lich Dakhad Atlan invades the bearfolk communities west of the Tunturi Mountains.
Bjornrike Founded (400 years ago). Mesikammen defeats Dakhad Atlan and is made ruler of the new kingdom named Bjornrike.
Halva Wayseeker, a dwarven explorer, vanishes in the far north. A series of epic songs document her previous adventures and become widely popular.
In Trollheim, Juri Jensson, a famed shipwright, invents square rigged sails, giving Northern longships great speed and agility on the seas.

Thrumagard Founded (150 years ago). The Thunder Mountain hold is retaken by the Band of the Thunder Hammer and resettled. The newest of the dwarven holds flouts tradition by welcoming humans, halflings and ravenfolk as equals.
Dwarven warlord Ottar Harjaz takes control of portions of Trollheim and Huldramose, but his proto-kingdom is shattered when he is slain by the Bear King during his aborted invasion of Bjornrike.
The vaettir, Liv Iron-Eyes, emerges from the sea to save the giantkin settlement of Eikinstad. The grateful locals pledge to help her recover the bodies of her former warriors.
20 years ago, Yohana Honeyhair became Queen of Bjeornheim
Bloody Revna, a murderous vaettir, begins attacking settlements along the western coast of the Haamu Hills.
10 years ago, elves began to return from the Summer Lands. Reports spoke of elven scouts in their old outposts and ruined cities in the North.
9 years ago, dwarven reavers established the Wolfmark and seized the city of Johzt from the Blood Kingdom.
The abandoned fortress of Kupparsheim was cleared by a band of adventurers. For a time, it served as a trading post.
King Asvaldr of Trollheim led a large raid into the southern lands but vanished in the Nieder Strait, leaving political chaos behind.
In the wilds of Vargrike, an increasing number of fey settled in ancient ruins at the behest of the fey lord Reynard.
3 years ago, the thursir and other giants of Thursrike and the western mountains marched into the human and dwarven lands of the North. Large numbers of trollkin rose to defend against the incursion.
The jotun, Guthmundur Raggnarson, seized the reclaimed fortress of Kupparsheim from the human and dwarven adventures who cleared it of monsters. He established it as the capital of Thursrike.
Wolfmark declared itself an independent kingdom.
Valdric Hohendrak, a vampire from across the Nieder Strait, secretly replaced Fraenir the Glutton in Wolfheim and took on his identity.
2 years ago, King Mesikammen married Queen Yohana, and their son Prince Alrek was born later in the same year.
King Uffi Toothless elevated Veska Flamehair to be the first trollkin jarl of Trollheim, a move that alienated many traditionalist jarls.

Osvald Thalrik, a dwarven vampire wizard from ancient Ishamagard, was awoken from a centuries-long sleep by the elf explorer Aldric Frostbourne. He established a lair in a ruined tower near Blodtindr Pass in Vargrike from which he searched for the pieces of the shattered Dominion Orb.
1 year ago, Blovurr, the heir to Wolfheim, died.
King Asvaldr inexplicably returned to Trollheim, claiming he had escaped captivity in a southern land.

Though collapsed in many places, the stones and sorcery of the Wall (or the Falling Wall as it is now known) still holds against the onslaughts of {@deity Boreas|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} and his creatures, but every year, another section topples, allowing more of {@deity Boreas|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}'s influence into the wider world.
Trollheim teeters on the edge of conflict between traditionalist jarls led by King Asvaldr and King Uffi's progressive supporters.
A strange illness strikes the guardian bees of Bjornrike. Simultaneously, Prince Alrek's health declines. Queen Yohana sends agents across the Northlands seeking a cure.

data.name: Chapter 2: Epic Regions of the North
entries: While most campaigns revolve around brave heroes desperately confronting seemingly insurmountable dangers, in the Northlands, the kingdoms, regions, and locations where these adventures take place are as much a character as the PCs themselves. Bringing these areas to life requires details, such as size, geography, climate, and population, as well as the inhabitants who live there, their culture, viewpoints, and politics. This chapter contains guidelines, descriptions, and tables designed to be used with these Northland kingdoms or altered to fit into an ongoing campaign.

The first section, {@area Northlands Settlements|051|x}, describes five kingdoms in the North. It offers an overview of each area, important settlements, influential NPCs and factions, and other notable features, including a regional map that can be dropped into any fantasy setting.
Following that, {@area Giant Jarldoms|08e|x} describes five regions occupied by the giants, trolls, and ogres so common in Norse mythology.

The final section of this chapter, {@area Adventure Locations|0bd|x}, presents a host of thrilling sites containing dangers, treasures, and mysteries. All of the locations and sites in this chapter can be adapted into a campaign or used for inspiration.

entries.name: Northlands Settlements
entries: The Northern kingdoms are small and numerous. It seems every jarl with a long hall and a few ships is a king. Indeed, many small settlements brag about their glorious land, abundant timber, and fine fishing. With so many fjords and valleys, and so few willing to brave the winters, possession of land is a matter of the boldest claiming a place and the titles to go with it. Over time, many of these small kingdoms have grown in power, helped along by dwarven mining and magic, human resourcefulness and persistence, and the wise words of the huginn and the shield-maidens. The kingdoms of the Northlands might be small, but each is a treasure to its people unlike any other.
This section details five kingdoms inhabited by familiar lineages like humans and dwarves, as well as nations ruled by more fantastic lineages such as bearfolk, lycanthropes, and ratatosk.

entries.name: Bjornrike, Kingdom of the Bear
entries: The rolling hills and coastal plains south of the Reaching Mountains are claimed by the Kingdom of the Bear. The bearfolk that reside here range widely, but the sparse population doesn't mind trespassers, as long as they respect the King and Queen of Bears and defer to their people when challenged. In recent years, the lands of the bear have hosted celebrations and suffered tragedies, but now the drums of conflict call the mighty bearfolk to arms.

Bjornrike stretches westward from the Tunturi mountains to the sea, and southward from the Hrygangur Peaks to the Vidbrun River. This massive 60,000-square-mile area hosts only a few scattered communities. It consists of mostly unsettled swaths of deep forest, hills, valleys and mountains. Though their home is blessed with abundance, the inhabitants of Bjornrike must constantly be on guard against fell threats lurking among the trees, descending from the snow-covered mountains, or from across the border. Beyond the settlement walls, vaettir and malmgoltr lurk in the forests, and the nearby mountains regularly spawn ogres and trolls. When the snows recede in the spring, nomadic raiders cross the southern border to hunt for beasts or bears alike. To the north, skirmishes between the bearfolk and the lupines of Vargrike threaten to descend into a larger conflict. Yet, the most obvious threat comes from the vaguely defined eastern border. Beyond the peaks of the Tunturi Range, oni warlords head armies of ogre, trolls, and tundra gnolls (see {@book Chapter 8|NorthlandsWorldbook|8}) and look with covetous eyes upon the Kingdom of the Bear.

According to legend, {@deity Bengta|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook|Bengta, the Bear Maiden}, created the first of the bearfolk, altering the great Northern bears into humanoid forms. The recorded history of Bjornrike begins with the fey lord Mesikammen, called "Old Honey Paws" for his fondness for sweets.

About 450 years ago, after the dwarven followers of {@deity Volund|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} abandoned many of their ancient holdings to travel to southern lands, the ogre hordes of the lich-oni Dakhad Atlan rampaged over the eastern mountains. In those early days, the bearfolk were mostly nomadic family communities. To repel this threat, Mesikammen united the scattered bearfolk beneath his beehive and bear paw banner. The Mountain Wars lasted for fifty years, until the massed army led by Old Honey Paws defeated Dakhad Atlan and his warriors at the Battle of the Broken Peaks. The victorious bearfolk declared the birth of Bjornrike as a country and established Mesikammen as their first (and thus far, only) king. The borders established by the Mountain Wars endure to this day, despite occasional skirmishes with the lycanthropes to the north or dwarven holds to the south. Yet, the bearfolk keep a watchful eye on their eastern border lest the ogres catch them unawares.

As much as the Bear King holds the people's loyalty, Queen Yohana holds the people's heart. A druid with deep spiritual ties to the Bear Maiden, she arose to her first throne some 20 years ago, appointed as the ruler of the port city of Bjeornheim. As part of an ancient agreement with the fey lord, the city boasts a semi-autonomous monarch chosen from among the foremost noble families. Yohana has proven to be a sharp and canny ruler, guiding her city to become the cosmopolitan trading hub it is today. Thanks to Yohana and {@deity Bengta|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}'s blessing, hives of giant bees act as the city's guardians. Over the years, Yohana's fame has grown and so has the Bear King's admiration and love for her. Two years ago, Old Honey Paws finally married Yohana after decades of wooing. The new Queen of Bears gave the people a thoughtful and empathetic counterpart to the Bear King's rougher nature. Despite her age, the queen soon gave birth to Prince Alrek, heir to Bjeornheim. The arrival of the Bear King's heir coincided with a hundred-fold flourishing of the guardian hives, which spread across the land to act as protectors to the realm as a whole. Many saw this as proof of a divine link between the young prince and the sacred bees of {@deity Bengta|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}, a fact that would prove tragically true.

Recently, a devastating illness struck the guardian bees, causing them to slowly sicken and die. Simultaneously, the young prince fell ill, and his condition worsens with each passing day. The druids of the land have been unable to cure the bees or the prince. While the frantic queen sends agents far and wide in search of a cure, Mesikammen looks to punish the ones responsible. Enraged beyond measure, Old Honey Paws arms and trains his bearfolk so he might show the guilty culprit what it means to goad the bears into war.
