The Illegitimate Scion thread might shift then to that of the Impoverished Noble thread. The player and GM should agree when circumstances are correct for a new thread, but the GM has the final say.

When adding new threads, the character retains all milestone benefits of previous threads. When abandoning a thread (that is, relinquishing it before achieving its stated goal), the character loses all of the thread's milestone benefits already gained. Thoses were temporary benefits that didn't become permanent because the character's focus changed, leaving the source of thoses unresolved.

entries.name: Thread Descriptions
entries: This section describes seven sample threads from which to choose. Though these threads presume a long arc of milestones, reaching from 1st level all the way to 20th level, they can be adjusted for shorter arcs by reducing the number of milestones or by reducing their spacing.
If a more personalized approach is preferred, simply use the structure of the provided threads as inspiration for creating new threads.

entries.name: Feats
entries: This section presents feats unique to the Northlands but available to characters of any setting. The feats below are organized by category—Origin, General, and Fighting Style—and alphabetized in each category. Unless noted otherwise in its description, a feat can only be taken once.

entries.name: Origin Feats
entries: These feats are in the Origin category.

entries.name: General Feats
entries: These feats are in the General category.

items.name: Greater Blessing of Freyr and Freyja

entries.name: Fighting Style Feats
entries: These feats are in the Fighting Style category.

data.name: Chapter 5: Magic and Miscellany
entries: In the Northlands, surviving the harsh world of ice and snow requires bravery and strength but also proper preparation. The right gear can mean the difference between life and death on the glaciers or when facing one of the fell monsters of the North. Indeed, equipment and treasure are a vital part of every heroic adventure. Just as important are the spells and magic items that are a hero's stock and trade.

This chapter lists the equipment available to PCs. It also contains magic items PCs might find during their adventures. Finally, it contains a selection of spells commonly seen throughout the Northlands.

entries.name: Equipment
entries: Equipment is a vital part of every heroic adventure. This section lists the equipment, such as armor, weapons, and gear, available to PCs and explains the rules for using it.

entries.name: Weapons
entries: This section lists new weapons found in the Northlands. The Weapons table lists the cost, damage dice and type, weight, weapon options, and special properties for weapons. Each weapon has a mastery property. To use a mastery property, you must have a class feature that lets you use it. The table is also split by the proficiencies required (Simple or Martial) to wield the various weapons most effectively.

entries.name: Masterwork Weapons
entries: A masterwork weapon is an exceptionally well-made version of a weapon of the finest materials available, typically crafted by an expert. While wielding a masterwork weapon you're proficient with, you have +1 bonus to attack rolls and damage rolls with that weapon (with the bonus damage matching the weapon's damage type). Note that magic weapons are already considered to be masterwork quality, so masterwork bonuses don't stack with bonuses already built into magic weapons. You can't simply make an existing weapon masterwork though. It must be crafted as a masterwork weapon from the start. A masterwork weapon can be purchased for an amount equal to the weapon's base cost + 300 gp. A single masterwork piece of ammunition costs a flat 5 GP (ignore ammunition base cost).

entries.name: Atgeir
entries: A polearm with a large, single-edged blade attached along the side of the haft. Atgeirs are thrusting weapons often used to lever enemies out of position after they have been struck.

entries.name: Bearded Axe
entries: The hook-shaped "beard" at the lower edge of the head of a bearded axe gives it its characteristic silhouette and provides a larger cutting edge than standard battle axes without excessively increasing its weight.

entries.name: Breidox
entries: Essentially a greataxe with a longer haft, the breidox was developed to deliver a powerful slash to opponents behind a protective shield wall.

entries.name: Bryntroll
entries: A massive chopping blade mounted at the end of a long pole, the bryntroll is designed to pierce the tough hides of giants.

entries.name: Seax
entries: These fighting knives are too heavy to be thrown, but they boast long blades that can punch through leather and mail.

entries.name: Snaerispear
entries: These short, javelin-like spears can be hurled great distances by means of a "throwing string," a leather strap affixed to the mid-point of the spear shaft. This allows the snaerispear to deal more damage when thrown than in melee.

entries.name: Mastery Property
entries: Mastery properties are usable only by a character who has a feature, such as Weapon Mastery, that unlocks the property for the character. A new mastery property unique to weapons of the Northlands is defined below.

entries.name: Armor
entries: This section lists new types of armor found in the Northlands that are available to PCs, and it covers special rules regarding their use. The Armor table lists the cost, AC bonus, weight, and proficiency required for each kind of armor.

entries.name: Beinagrind
entries: This armor is formed by carving disks or short shingles out of whale or giant bones and lacing them to a backing of flexible leather.

entries.name: Double Mail
entries: Also called tvifold brynja, the rings of this chain mail are doubled, so each pair is passed through by four pairs of other rings. It is very heavy and bulky.

entries.name: Hardened Mail Shirt
entries: This chain shirt has rings of adamantine or mithral woven into key areas to provide more protection than normal mail.

entries.name: Walrus Hide
entries: These thick, treated walrus hide suits are flexible but quite heavy. In addition to its defensive benefits, walrus hide counts as winter clothing when determining the effects of extreme cold.

rows.entry: {@b Medium Armor (5 minutes to Don or Doff)}
{@b Heavy Armor (10 minutes to Don or Doff)}

entries.name: Adventuring Gear
entries: This section covers standard nonmagical equipment and the rules for using it.

entries.name: Jotunskull Helm
entries: Favored by those who wish to project a fearsome aspect, these helms are fashioned from the cleaned bones of a sufficiently large giant. When you wear one, you have {@variantrule Advantage|XPHB} on Charisma ({@skill Intimidation|XPHB}) checks against Giants (at the GM's discretion).

entries.name: Skis
entries: While wearing skis, you ignore {@variantrule Difficult Terrain|XPHB} from deep snow and move at double your normal Speed while going downhill in snow. You have {@variantrule Disadvantage|XPHB} on Dexterity saves and checks while wearing skis, except those related to moving through snow.

entries.name: Skates
entries: While wearing skates, you ignore {@variantrule Difficult Terrain|XPHB} from slippery ice and automatically pass Dexterity ({@skill Acrobatics|XPHB}) checks to avoid have the {@condition Prone|XPHB} condition on ice. You move at double your normal Speed while on ice, but you have a Speed of 5 feet off the ice.

entries.name: Snow Goggles
entries: These thick glasses are set with lenses of smoky glass, preventing snow blindness.

entries.name: Snow Visor
entries: These thick bone or wood visors are bound to the head and are constructed with a narrow slit for the wearer's eyes. Creatures wearing snow visors have Immunity to snow blindness but have {@variantrule Disadvantage|XPHB} on Wisdom ({@skill Perception|XPHB}) checks relating to sight.

entries.name: Snowshoes
entries: While wearing snowshoes, you can ignore {@variantrule Difficult Terrain|XPHB} from deep snow. You have {@variantrule Disadvantage|XPHB} on Dexterity saves and checks while wearing snowshoes.

entries.name: Talharpa
entries: A musical instrument with two to four strings similar to a lyre and played with a bow.

entries.name: Mounts and Land Vehicles
entries: Travel across the Northlands can be its own adventure. From howling blizzards to roaring giants, just moving from settlement to settlement pits the adventurer against nature and monsters alike. This section details various mounts and land vehicles the intrepid Northlanders use to travel.

entries.name: Mounts
entries: A mount can help you move more quickly through the wilderness, but it can also carry gear that would otherwise slow you down. The Mounts table shows each animal's carrying capacity. See {@area Chapter 8|551|x} for new mount stat blocks.

entries.name: Mounts and Cargo
entries: An animal pulling a carriage, cart, chariot, sled, or wagon can move weight up to five times its base carrying capacity, including the weight of the vehicle. If multiple animals pull the same vehicle, add their carrying capacities together.

entries.name: Barding
entries: Barding is armor designed for a mount. Any type of armor can be purchased as barding. The cost is four times the normal cost, and it weighs twice as much.

entries.name: Land Vehicles
entries: Land vehicles can travel on solid surfaces and across physical terrain. Much like the longships presented later, the land vehicles in this section have the following statistics.

entries.name: Speed
entries: The speeds in the table include movement during a combat round, miles per hour, and miles per day.

entries.name: Crew
entries: A vehicle typically has one driver, but other crew positions may be available. The minimum number of skilled hirelings needed to operate a vehicle depends on the type of vehicle, as shown in the table.

entries.name: Passengers
entries: The table lists the number of Small and Medium passengers the vehicle can accommodate.

entries.name: Vehicle Repair
entries: If a vehicle has taken damage and has fewer than half its hit points (rounded down), a creature can spend 1 hour or more and the necessary gp worth of spare parts to repair the damage. At the end of each hour, the vehicle regains Hit Points equal to its AC (up to the vehicle's {@variantrule Hit Points|XPHB|Hit Point} Maximum). One hour of repairs requires spare parts worth a gp amount equal to 10 percent of the vehicle's base cost, as shown on the Vehicle table.

entries.caption: Land Vehicles
rows: {@vehicle Ogre War Sled (pulled by two Worgs)|NorthlandsWorldbook}

entries.name: Dog Sled
entries: Dog sleds are long, narrow frames set on metal ski-like runners and pulled by teams of trained dogs. Ideal for rossing frozen terrain, dog sleds are commonly used in arctic regions for travel, trade, and transport.

A dog sled is a Large vehicle, weighs 150 pounds, has room on the back for one driver, and can hold 3 passengers or about 800 pounds of cargo. Sleds can be swift, but much depends on the terrain, snow conditions, and other obstacles.

Dog sleds typically have teams of dogs numbering between 6 and 10. For ease of play, use the stats for a {@creature Wolf|XMM} for an average sled dog. After 6 hours of travel, a sled dog must take a {@variantrule Long Rest|XPHB} or suffer one level of {@condition Exhaustion|XPHB}.

entries.name: Ogre War Sled
entries: This brutal, oversized war sled is constructed from heavy timber, mammoth bones, and forged metal. The front features a shield-like prow crafted from a mammoth skull that provides {@variantrule Cover|XPHB|Half Cover} for the driver. Typically, war sleds are pulled by two {@creature Worg|XMM|Worgs}, though some are harnessed to a {@creature Mammoth|XMM} or other cold weather creatures.
Used by many of the giant and troll communities in the Northlands, the ogre war sled is a Huge vehicle. This heavy sled is large enough to hold two ogres.

entries.name: Ogre War Sled (pulled by two Worgs)
Longships
entries: The signature sea vessel of the Northlands is the iconic longship. Swift and agile in the water, longships are preferred by raiders, reavers, and Northern merchants of all sorts. Longships feature a removeable figurehead mounted on the prow, often carved to resemble a fearsome dragon or other beast, such as a raven or wolf, though some are sculpted as maidens, merfolk, and other aquatic creatures. The stern of the ship sports a carving as well, typically the tail of some fantastic monster.

All longships share a common design, with a keel, a stem at the prow and stern, and a hull. While many other ships have hulls with planks that meet edge-to-edge, a longship's design overlaps the planks of the hull. This pattern, known as lapstrake or clinker-built, makes longships durable against rough waters. Longship keel designs vary, with some being flatter and able to traverse shallow water and others deeper for carrying more cargo. Longship designs also share rowing benches and oars, as well as a mast for a square sail. Oars allow the crew to quickly move a longship in and out of position, even bringing shallow-keeled ships onto shore. A steering rudder on the starboard side of a longship allows it to be directed easily, whether the ship is moving forward or backward.

Ship Action. At the end of each round, a vehicle with the required number of crew members can move up to its Speed and use one action. The section on Naval Combat in Chapter 7 details rules for fighting ship-to-ship as well as various shipboard actions. The specialized actions listed in the ship stat blocks in this section can be used as shipboard actions.
The longships presented in this section differ from the one found in the core rules.

entries.name: Drakkar
entries: The largest of longships, a drakkar is also called a "dragon ship" for its stylized dragon figureheads. Drakkar are the flagships of their fleet, and they are commissioned by jarls, chieftains, and other prominent, wealthy leaders.

The larger cargo hold of a drakkar also makes it ideal for long journeys. It is capable of carrying enough supplies to reach destinations that smaller longships would be ill-equipped for. However, drakkar are not as agile as other longships in terms of turning speed or in lighter wind conditions.

entries.name: Karvi
entries: The smallest of the flat-keel longships, the karvi can traverse shallow waters to transport goods, fish, and even raiders. While a karvi can be used in battle, it is often used as a general-purpose river and coastal ship. Its size and shallow keel make it less ocean-worthy than other longboats. While a knarr is used for transporting livestock, it is common to find a karvi ferrying people to their destination.

entries.name: Knarr
entries: Suited for open water rather than shallow rivers, knarr are longships used to ferry goods and livestock across the ocean. Its deep hull allows for more cargo storage, compared with other longships of similar size, and allows the ship to be operated by smaller crews. When used in exploration or war, knarr are used to carry supplies for the crews and warriors on other ships in the fleet, rather than as battleships.

entries.name: Skeid
entries: Smaller than a drakkar, a skeid, or "slider," is still large enough to carry dozens of crew members, passengers, supplies and treasure. This warship is also amongst the fastest of the longboats, matched only by the smaller snekkja.

entries.name: Snekkja
entries: The most common of raiding longships, the snekkja, also known as the snake ship, is also the smallest of the warships. Simple and quick to build, navigate, and maintain, snekkja carry raiders into battle with efficiency, slipping away after being loaded with plundered goods and treasure.

entries.name: Magic Items
entries: Finding magic items can be the highlight of a game session. Indeed, of the many rewards available to adventurers, magic items are the most beloved. They are distinct, hard to find, and valuable. This section has rules for magic items found in the Northlands.

The GM decides where magic items appear, but they are often given as rewards for crawling through deadly dungeons or slaying the creatures that guard (and wield) them. Magic items might be available to buy and sell, though this is highly dependent on the setting.

entries.name: Magic Item Descriptions
entries: This section lists Northlands magic items. Each entry provides key information about the item, including its type, its rarity, whether it requires {@variantrule Attunement|XPHB}, and its properties.

entries.name: The Grave Blade
entries: The reavers of Wolfheim brought home many strange treasures as souvenirs and mementos from their campaigns abroad. A dwarven warrior named Essalla claimed a strange sword as her share of the spoils on one such raiding journey. Unusual in design and unadorned by dwarvish standards, it seemed destined to be a souvenir brought out only when tales of the campaign were to be told.
This sword has a dull, lifeless grey blade, and the hilt is carved from aged bone. The guard is made from ribs, and the pommel is sourced from the rounded end of a femur, both cast in bronze

The Grave Blade became known in different tales, for the threads of fate of each bearer seemed to be cut short soon after taking possession of it. It has changed hands many times over the next nine years, seemingly taken from a corpse as often as it was exchanged for gold or favors.

The blade is known for the song it hums in the presence of undead, and with the death of its carriers, the blade's song grows ever more insistent. Some say the song is a warning, while others theorize that it wants to be found and interred with the body of its first bearer.

The souvenir of so much death was lost among a merchant's wares that never reached their destination in Wolfheim, and the mystery of its song persists in tales told on dark nights when the fire burns low.

entries.name: Fabled Magic Items
entries: Fabled magic items are distinct as a rarity. A fabled item grows in power alongside the character who wields it. Rules for fabled items are summarized here, and a few fabled magic items can be found in this chapter.
A fabled magic item begins as a Common magic item. The item grants a minor, useful trait to its owner that doesn't require {@variantrule Attunement|XPHB} to use.

To access any higher-level trait, a PC must attune to it using standard {@variantrule Attunement|XPHB} rules. Once attuned, a PC can use the fabled item's more powerful properties as they increase in level. If a PC higher than 1st level attunes to a fabled item, its level-dependent properties, up to the character's current level, are immediately available.

At the GM's discretion, an item's more powerful properties might become available only after the character completes a particular quest or event related to the item's story rather than immediately upon reaching each property's required level.
If a PC chooses not to attune to a fabled item, it remains a common magic item, granting only its minor property, regardless of the character's level.
Unless otherwise noted, properties granted by a fabled item are in effect as long at the character is wearing, carrying, or touching the item.

entries.name: Skinchanger Arm Ring
entries: This arm ring is made from copper and is covered with a patina that cannot be removed.

There was once a sect of Northern warriors dedicated to learning from the animals in their region. Each member of the order sought to exemplify the capabilities and spirit of their chosen animal. The raven warrior was keen to observe and could travel far and fast. The follower of the wolf fought well in conjunction with others. Others had strength and endurance like bears.

These ideals were forged into an enchanted arm ring worn by the leader of the sect. Whether this magic was achieved with the aid of dwarves, druids, or sorcerers, none can say. With experience, the wearer of the arm ring could shapeshift into one of the three animals exemplified by the warriors.

Though the order won many victories on the battlefield, they couldn't be held in the employ of any one jarl. The wilds called to them, and they visited the settled lands of the North less and less as the years went by, until they were never seen again.

entries.name: Storrbani
entries: Thogar Giant-Hewer earned great renown through unwavering bravery but not intellectual brilliance. His unmatched courage often forged far ahead of his reason. As a youth, he could not prevent marauding giants and trolls from destroying his village and murdering his family. Left alone on the blood-soaked snow, a fire kindled deep in Thogar's heart. From that day, he unwaveringly sought vengeance against giantfolk, not for glory or renown but in the hope his daring might earn him friends or even a new family of his own.

The Giant-Hewer became a terror to trolls and giants alike. Though not the strongest warrior and certainly never the wisest, he braved troll dens and giant camps, throwing himself into battle where others paused to strategize. Yet time and again, the people he saved turned cold. His deeds, though brave, were rarely welcome. His plans resulted in the death of everyone but himself. His traps lured giants to their doom at the expense of entire villages. Those he rescued offered no feasts of thanks, only wary glances and closed doors. The more he gave, the more alone he became, yet still he fought on believing if he was only brave enough, he could win through to find a new family.

Thogar met his end in his own typical fashion. After running across the trail of a band of storm giants heading toward a village, he foolishly attacked them in the settlement square. His blade, Storrbani, slew many giants before the others fled, but unfortunately, the fires ignited by the battle burned down half the village. Thogar's shattered body lay in the remains of the wedding feast (to which the giants had been invited), and no one came to his aid or to witness his last breath. Skalds say he died utterly alone, but when the Valkyries came to collect him, he did not wish to enter Valhalla alone. Taking pity on the brave warrior, they cast his spirit into his blade, binding it there until the day he falls again, fighting beside a true friend, so together they might enter the Hall of Golden Shields side by side.

entries.name: Tordalfr's Rebuttal
entries: Tordalfr was a storm giantkin born to a human mother in a small village. After years of jibes and taunts from the children of local warriors, he snapped.

Brael, son of the village headman, and a pompous, aspiring warrior, called Tordalfr out in public, proclaiming to his assembled cronies that there was irrefutable evidence that Tordalfr was the unwanted child of forbidden lovers, and defying anyone present to offer proof to the contrary.

Tordalfr's fury reached such a pitch that the cloudless sky opened up and a bolt of lightning struck his outstretched hand, coalescing into the form of a throwing spear, which he hurled at his tormentor. The javelin struck Brael in the chest, hurling him backward and leaving a blackened, smoking crater where his heart had been. Tordalfr marched furiously from the village and never returned.

data.name: Chapter 6: Northlands Pantheon
entries: The gods of the North are many things simultaneously. Mysterious and familiar. Slippery and demanding. They display almost mortal concerns and desires, yet they are ultimately unknowable. The gods are much more than voices that answer pleas for healing, blessings, protection, and gentle repose.

Gods have their own goals. They have their own needs. Most of all, they play a game among their own kind, a game of power and deception, because gods, having once been made, can also be unmade. The gods are the greatest allies of mortals, as well as their greatest foes and betrayers. Above all else, they are focused inward, on rivalries and divine affairs, barely hearing mortal voices. Those who walk the path of the priest or petitioner should first understand this.

entries.name: First Gods
entries: The story begins in the First Age. Life sprang up in the center of the Void where rime met flame, melting and boiling. This was Aurgelmir, the first and greatest giant. Creatures sprang from Aurgelmir like branches on an oak, among them the titans, divine jotun, and the eldest of the gods. The First Giant created a world for his children, but the gods soon fought the giants for control. On the cusp of defeat, the giants cried out to their father, and Aurgelmir chose to fight alongside them. In response, the gods slew Aurgelmir and cut the branch of Yggdrasil from which the world hung, destroying it. All of Aurgelmir's first giant offspring perished, apart from {@deity Bergelmir|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} and {@deity Angrboda|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}. Together, they saved the lesser jotun and their other descendants. The giants have never forgotten this murder. Since that day, they've nursed a grudge, and they hope one day to see the gods' dominion ended and their forefather avenged.

The victorious gods, meanwhile, fashioned a new world from the body of Aurgelmir and hung it upon the broken branch of Yggdrasil. His bones became the earth, and his blood flowed out to fill the rivers and seas. From his teeth they fashioned mountains, and his hollow skull became the sky. With giants cowed by the cleaving of Aurgelmir, the gods explored their new-forged world, and soon they fell to strife among themselves. The gods of nature and the gods of passion and glory formed factions, and they fought for dominion over their new realm, and creation trembled with the blows they struck. Eventually, canny {@deity Wotan|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}, always wise and victorious, brokered a truce. The gods exchanged hostages, and peace descended once more. Smaller races took their place in the world, and the gods watched. As far as the giants are concerned, they are still the true inheritors of the world and its treasures.

entries.name: Masks and Mysteries
entries: Gods are not individuals but archetypes, manifestations of universal forces shaped by faith and place. Their appearance, name, gender, and domains vary from region to region. One god may have many names and forms across the world. Thus, gods in southern lands are masks of the Northern gods, and vice versa. Despite generations of inquiry, their secrets endure. The gods are a shifting family of alliances and betrayals. Each clings desperately to divinity, knowing even gods can wither and die. As such, the gods are unknowable and ever-changing. Only a few hold sway in any given place, perhaps five in a city, three in a town, and one in a village. Shrines can fade. Faith is practical, not exclusive; worshipers choose the god that best suits their moment of need.

entries.name: Shades of Gray
entries: In other lands, gods are often divided into "good" deities or "dark" deities. Not so in the North. In these frozen lands, the gods defy such categories, taking on dualistic roles. {@deity Wotan|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} seeks knowledge but also manipulates friends and foes alike. {@deity Thor|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} defends mortals yet also leaves destruction in his wake. {@deity Freyr and Freyja|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook|Freyja} brings beauty but walks hand in hand with war. Even {@deity Loki|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}, who is destined to begin Ragnarok, has saved the gods as often as he's endangered them.

Bound to fate, yet struggling against it, the gods of the North are their own worst enemies. They scheme, betray, love, and wound each other with relentless regularity. Their grudges and hatreds spill over into the mortal world, and none of the gods think twice about using mortals as pawns.

Few Northlanders devote themselves to a single deity. Most acknowledge all gods as powerful and best not angered. Although most people have a deity or two that are close to their heart, it's not uncommon for Northlanders to call upon local gods when traveling, abandoning them with equal casualness when they move on. A human wouldn't think twice about saying a hasty prayer to {@deity Angrboda|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} in the face of some monstrous foe.

Worship and faith are not questions of choosing between "good" or "evil." They are appeals to the god who speaks to an individual's moment of need. If mortals are wise, they revere the gods not for their place in some cosmic balance but because they are the storm, the hunger, the secrets beyond sight, and the power to move the heavens.

entries.name: Major Deities
entries: The stern gods of the Northlands are forbidding, bloody, grim, and dangerous—to outsiders. Northern humanoids take joy in the delights of gods that call them to excellence, that invite great boasts and greater deeds, and that laugh louder than thunder.

Piety in the Northlands is a curious thing. Although the gods have their share of true believers, most people regard the gods as unruly kings rather than divine beings: powerful and dangerous if crossed, helpful when bribed or flattered, and thankfully easy to appease with tribute.

Blood is the usual sacrifice. Goats, cattle, or horses suffice most of the time, but it's not uncommon for humans, dwarves, or trollkin to go beneath the knife when dire portents and evil occurrences demand a response. Each god prefers offerings delivered in a particular way: {@deity Wotan|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} demands sacrifices are hung and pierced by spears, while {@deity Baldur|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}'s offerings are burned, and {@deity Thor|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} prefers heads bashed in with a sacred hammer.

Druids, oracles, and even witches are all common roles for priests. Full-time clerics in the southern style are a relative rarity, treated more as favored champions than clergy. Most priests also pursue another role, from jarl or captain to soothsayer, hunter, or smith. Worship isn't something to be kept separate from everyday life; it takes place in feasting halls and forges, on battlefields and the swaying decks of longships.

entries.caption: Major Gods of the North
rows: Giantkin, giants, monsters, seers, werekin, witches
Frost giants, ice elves, ogres, trolls
Guards, jarls, scouts, travelers, and wanderers

entries.name: Minor Divinities
entries: Apart from the major gods, there are a few minor deities who are either worshiped in the Northlands or whose veneration has lapsed in the current age. It is possible to find shrines to these minor gods in some communities, but this is rare. They are typically worshiped by specific groups or species.

The exception to this is the {@deity Norns|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}. Virtually everyone in the Northlands respects the three ladies of fate and offers prayers to them at one time or another. The {@deity Norns|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} don't encourage temples raised to them, and the few that have been built quickly fell to misfortune and ruin.

entries.caption: Minor Gods of the North
rows: Only scattered followers, mostly cultists and witches

entries.name: Other Deities
entries: Aside from the major and minor gods, there are other deities and beings of power who bask in the worship of isolated communities or scattered pockets of faith.

data.name: Chapter 7: Running Northlands Campaigns
entries: This chapter contains an assortment of mechanics to help GMs run adventures in the Northlands. While the rules below aren't required to enjoy thrilling adventures in the North, they are designed to deepen the themes and concepts presented throughout the other chapters of this book.

entries.name: Reputation
entries: An individual's reputation is of paramount importance to the people of the North. As canny {@deity Wotan|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} said, "Cattle die, kin die, even the self dies, but glory never dies for the one able to achieve it." To be a hero in the Northlands, and thus earn a place in the afterlife, is to perform deeds with an eye toward how they shape your reputation. Yet, renown isn't static—it ebbs and flows. A hero might gain great honor for killing a mighty dragon, but if they act dishonorably, their reputation will tarnish and rot away.

Reputation is an optional rule that tracks your character's prestige and provides a way to leverage that renown to perform cinematic and epic actions by temporarily assuming narrative control of the game.

entries.name: Character Reputation Score
entries: Your character's reputation is measured by a score much like an ability score modifier. A novice warrior might have +1 reputation, while the greatest champion of the realm might have +10 or higher. Unlike ability scores, this modifier begins at 0 and is not adjusted due to skills or characters levels. Reputation increases when you perform gain renown for deeds and noteworthy acts of daring, and it decreases if you are caught committing dishonorable acts. Multiple characters can gain reputation by performing the same deed together. The {@table Reputation Thresholds|NorthlandsWorldbook} table shows the levels and benefits of reputation.

Note, this system specifically governs what people know about you. If no one witnesses you committing a dishonorable act, your reputation in the mortal world won't suffer. Similarly, if you slay a great wyrm, but no one believes you, your reputation won't improve. Gods, {@deity Norns|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}, and other divine beings might be aware of what you did, and it might affect your chances of going to Valhalla, but unless other people witness or learn of what you did, your reputation modifier will not change.

entries.name: Deeds and Dishonorable Acts
entries: Deeds are acts of heroism accomplished by the PC or party, like saving a village from raiders, slaying a dragon, or finding a fabled lost treasure. Acts need not be victorious combat to count as deeds. A merchant who brings back a longship laden with goods can gain renown, as can an artist who creates a masterpiece. As your character accomplishes deeds, they gain more reputation, advancing through various thresholds or stages, but they can lose reputation by getting caught acting dishonorably. You should keep track of the number of deeds you have accomplished, as they determine your reputation threshold.

entries.name: Rule of Five
entries: If you accomplish five deeds, and others learn of them, you advance to the next threshold level.

It is important to note that a deed isn't every amazing thing an adventurer does. Deeds need to be notable, worthy of saga and song. As a general guideline, a deed is something a PC or party does that dramatically alters the storyline of the game. So fighting monsters is not necessarily a deed since almost everyone in the Northlands does that frequently, but driving away the legendary ice worm might be. If you accomplish the same deed twice, the second usually doesn't count as a deed. The GM and the player should decide together what accomplishments count as a deed.

entries.name: Dishonorable Acts
entries: The antithesis of deeds are dishonorable acts. Violence isn't necessarily dishonorable nor is killing. In the North, major dishonorable acts include murdering an innocent, breaking an oath, breaking the rules of hospitality, violating the peace of the althing, and cowardice in the face of danger. The GM should determine if your actions are dishonorable acts and if enough people have found out about them to damage your reputation.

entries.name: Rule of Three
entries: If you commit three dishonorable acts that others learn about, you lose all accumulated deeds and are reduced by one threshold level.

entries.name: Thresholds
entries: Thresholds are best described as "reputation levels" measuring your character's renown. Each stage has prerequisites based on character level and provides small regional bonuses.

At each stage, you must accomplish five deeds to advance to the next threshold, however, you can't move to the next threshold until you reach the character level minimum of that threshold. For example, a level 3 character with 5 deeds can't gain more reputation or move from the Obscure to the Known reputation threshold until they reach level 5. Each time you advance to a new threshold, your deeds counter resets to 0.

Your threshold level also determines what type of reputation challenge you can attempt and a few minor benefits. You must be in an area where your reputation is known (as determined by the GM) to benefit from the regional bonuses.

entries.name: Reputation Challenges
entries: Once per character level, you can leverage your fame and renown to attempt a Reputation Challenge. If you succeed, you take narrative control of the game for a limited time, essentially becoming the GM to resolve the dramatic moment. If you fail, you lose reputation as the word of your failure spreads. This places a tremendous amount of power in your hands, and as such, the GM can always step in if things get out of hand.

entries.name: Making a Challenge
entries: As a {@variantrule Reaction|XPHB} at any time, you can announce you are making a Reputation Challenge. With GM agreement, you can even do so if you have already used a {@variantrule Reaction|XPHB} this turn.

When you make a Reputation Challenge, you must explain to the GM what your PC plans to do. Be descriptive and dramatic as this moment should be a heroic! The GM might suggest alterations but generally should work with you to agree on what happens to your character, the other PCs, and the world of the game. This is called the "narrative."

items.name: Challenge Types
items.entry: As part of the narrative, you must also decide what challenge type you are attempting: Low, Medium, High, or Epic. You must meet the reputation threshold prerequisite to attempt any challenge. The GM might rule your proposed narrative sounds like a higher type than you qualify for, so you might have to scale things back.

items.name: Low Challenge ({@dc 10})
entries: This represents a heroic action or dramatic moment that influences the immediate situation or a small group of people. It might turn the tide of a small battle, impress a local lord, or rally a frightened village.

items.name: Medium Challenge ({@dc 12})
entries: This represents a major feat that affects an entire town, settlement, or faction's immediate course of action. It can reshape relationships, affect regional politics, or change the direction of a local conflict.

items.name: High Challenge ({@dc 14})
entries: This reshapes the destiny of an entire region, kingdom, or major power. It brings about permanent shifts in the world's politics, military balances, or magical forces.

items.name: Epic Challenge ({@dc 16})
entries: This represents mythic-level events that echo across nations, planes, and generations. These deeds are worthy of legend and saga and may change the course of the world.

entries.name: Challenge Roll
entries: After you and the GM agree on the narrative and challenge type, you must roll a {@dice d20} plus your reputation bonus to determine the outcome.

entries.name: Success
entries: If you succeed, your proposed narrative happens as you described it.

entries.name: Failure
entries: If you fail the challenge roll, you lose all of your accumulated deeds and are reduced by one reputation threshold.

entries.name: Challenge Guidelines
entries: Taking control of the game is intended to give you a narrative way for your characters to overcome obstacles and be the dynamic heroes you've imagined them to be. It is NOT a method to one-shot a bad guy or to suddenly gain personal wealth. While this feature gives you control of the narrative for a moment, don't forget that your character's story is also part of the world and part of the rest of the party's story. Be polite, be respectful, include others, and have fun!
Here are some general guidelines for your narratives:

items: Your narrative can happen during combat or outside it.

The amount of time your narrative takes is enough to complete the description of the challenge you discussed with the GM. As indeterminate as it sounds, the time of this can vary. Low challenges might only be a couple of rounds, while an Epic challenge might take an hour, a day, or even more.
What you describe should be within the bounds of logic, even if it's rather unlikely.
In general, you don't need to roll for narrative actions, though the GM may add new obstacles into your narrative that require a roll.
Your narrative takes the same amount of time as your normal turn, or longer if the GM allows.

Your narrative can include multiple actions, but unless the GM allows it, you can't cast more than one spell or make more than your normal number of attacks, unless you could otherwise cast more than one in a turn or make more than your normal number of attacks in a turn, such as through a Fighter's Action Surge feature.

If you attack a foe with weapons or spells, you can choose to roll normally, or with your GM's approval, you can automatically hit and kill a number of foes equal to half your {@variantrule Proficiency|XPHB|Proficiency Bonus} if each creature's CR is equal to or less than half your character's level.
You can add or change elements of the world to fit your narrative, if the changes are logical and approved by the GM.
Don't interfere with other players' agency for their characters, and/or be sure to consult with other players if their characters have a role to play in your narrative.

entries.name: Holmganga (Dueling)
entries: Questioning someone's honor, accusing them of a crime or of cowardice, or falsely claiming credit for heroic deeds is asking for a fight. Sometimes it happens by accident—especially at drunken feasts—and Northlanders laugh off such offenses with a flyting contest or over rounds of mead once a sincere apology is given. But at other times, only bloodshed can heal wounded pride.

If the offender fails to publicly apologize for the offense within three days, a duel called a holmganga ("going to the island") results. Such duels typically occur on an island, at a crossroads, in a sacred glade, or on a cloth staked to the ground. Each warrior can take personal arms, armor, and three Holmganga shields to the dueling ground.

entries.name: Matching Equipment
entries: It is considered honorable to match your opponent in terms of arms and armor. So a PC with powerful magical gear facing a warrior with nonmagical equipment is expected to use similarly nonmagical arms and armor. This isn't a "rule" so much as expected custom, and it's possible those present are unaware one opponent has an unfair advantage. A combatant who doesn't do so might gain a dishonorable act (see Reputation above), as determined by the GM.

entries.name: Holmganga Shields
entries: The shields used for Holmganga are not the same as normal battle shields. They are thinner and break when their wielder is struck with an attack dealing 15 {@variantrule Hit Points|XPHB} or more. A {@variantrule Critical Hit|XPHB} always breaks a holmganga shield. Breaking a shield or throwing it down ends a "round" of fighting, allowing a brief respite (no more than a minute) to catch one's breath. The fight ends only when one combatant flees or cannot continue.

entries.name: The Duel
entries: It is traditional for a Holmganga duel to end when one opponent is knocked unconscious. In mechanical game terms, it means you reduce your foe to 0 {@variantrule Hit Points|XPHB} with a melee attack, but you choose to instead reduce them to 1 {@variantrule Hit Points|XPHB|Hit Point} and give them the Unconscious condition. However, deaths have been known to occur during duels over serious matters, such as deciding a jarldom or the ending of a long feud. Killing an opponent in the holmganga isn't dishonorable unless the reason for the duel is viewed as minor.

Honorable folk of all professions are expected to duel when necessary. If a duel is grossly mismatched, a champion can fight in one's place, or the defender can appeal to the local althing and petition to have the duel declared unfair. Failure to show up earns a reputation as a nithingr (coward) and outlaw for a year or two.

entries.name: Reward
entries: Victory at the Holmganga Simple upholds your side of the triggering argument or dispute. It can count as a deed, as determined by your GM.

entries.name: Flyting Rules
entries: Feasts in the Northlands tend to be rowdy affairs with much boasting, drinking, and carousing. At times, a jarl may wish to size up a visitor and test their cunning, or a quarrel may need to be defused before it becomes a duel or a murder that triggers a generational feud. This is where flyting comes in.

Flyting is a duel of insults where two participants take turns insulting one another, in more and more creative ways, until anger or embarrassment reduces one side to speechlessness. The contest can be used for entertainment, to resolve simple quarrels, or to defuse a situation. A flyting typically begins when one person challenges another publicly in a manner not egregious enough to trigger a duel—perhaps a verbal insult or a social misstep.

Facts aren't relevant in a flyting. The "truth" of the insults thrown around in a flyting is of lesser importance than the speaker's rhyming skill and humor. The winner of the contest is the one who best sways the audience with their creative insults.

entries.name: Rhythm and Rhyme
entries: The challenger gives an insult and the challenged replies with their own. Importantly, the answering insult needs to copy the rhythm of the challenger's insult, and the last word of both insults must rhyme. For example, if {@deity Loki|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} is taunted with "Foul deceiver, you are a snake with an uncouth manner!" He might reply with "Pale braggart, you wield your wit like a drooping hammer."

entries.name: How Many Rounds?
entries: This depends on the participants, but often it is 3-5 exchanges total. The GM should determine how many rounds the contest is to last before it begins.

entries.name: Flyting Steps
entries: When a flyting is called, use the following steps.

items.name: Appoint a Judge
entries: The two participants agree on a judge chosen from among the people in attendance. This individual is usually not personally connected to either participant or at least is someone who can remain neutral. The judge gauges the reaction of the audience to determine which participant has swayed the greater number of attendees. At the game table, the judge is usually the other players and the GM.

items.name: Participants Face Off
entries: They usually stand atop a long table in the longhouse or some area where they can be seen and heard by the audience.

items.name: Challenger Goes First
entries: This is typical, but if not, the two participants can roll {@variantrule Initiative|XPHB} to see who begins.

items.name: Round 1: Opening Insults
entries: Often the first round of insults is part boast, part stating the grievance against the opponent, and part insult.

items.name: Rounds Continue
entries: The rounds continue until the predetermined number is reached, one of the participants stumbles (can't respond cleverly, repeats themselves, or fails to rhyme), or when the audience declares a winner as determined by the judge.

entries.name: Rewards
entries: Often the honor of the participants is at stake or the resolution of some squabble. It is considered very dishonorable to dispute the result of a flyting or to seek revenge because of one. At a feast, rewards of mead is common. Victory at flyting can count as a deed, as determined by your GM.

entries.name: Easing Flyting Gameplay
entries: Some players may find their characters are far better at spontaneous rhyming insults than they are. To make this easier for those players, below are a series of words and their corresponding rhymes. Players can also use the Kennings in the section later in this chapter.

When using these tables, the Challenger must end their insult using a word on one of the rows. This allows the other participant to simply choose a rhyming word on the same row for their own response.
Both participants of the flyting must agree to either use the tables or perform freestyle.

entries.name: Kennings
entries: The cultures providing inspiration for the Northlands used a poetic metaphor called "kenning" in their riddles, poems, and songs. A kenning is a play on words that replaces a concept, usually a single word, with more figurative language. For example, a popular kenning for the sea was "whale's road." Often associated with skaldic poems, kennings draw on cultural and mythical knowledge. They are immensely useful and imaginative ways to add flavor and a unique cultural feeling to prophecies and games set in the Northlands.

entries.name: Using Kennings in Flyting
entries: Kennings can be amazing poetic forms for a flyting duel.

entries.name: Using Kennings in Prophecies
entries: Kennings are well-suited for creating prophecies because the wordplay inherent in their metaphors allows for a variety of interpretations. In a prophetic reading, the term "Night's Ship" could refer to the moon, a shadowy vessel, or perhaps a dream.

entries.name: How to Create Kennings
entries: The typical manner of making kennings is to combine a noun and a verb, or two nouns, in any order, to form a two-word phrase. This phrase is a descriptive phrase used in place of a more obvious or literal wording. Occasionally, three (or more) words are used to form a kenning if two words are insufficient to create the meaning.

entries.name: Prophecies and Omens
entries: The rules in this section reviews two types of prophecies (greater prophecies and prophetic blessings/warnings), gives helpful suggestions on how to construct prophecies, and introduces a way to reward players for using prophecies. This section also includes a table of omens and a few predetermined sample prophecies.

entries.name: Prophecies
entries: Prophecies at their core are predictions of events to come. They often contain cryptic language that leaves them open to a myriad of interpretations. While prophecies might hint at destiny, they are open to interpretation because, by their very nature, they are vague. Unless handed down by a deity or powerful entity, the prophecies most Northerners encounter are communicated to them by seers. As mortal beings, seers can only grasp at the complex weavings of the {@deity Norns|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}. This is why they speak in vague terms rather than in specific names, dates, and events. Prophecies given by seers are known as prophetic blessings or prophetic warnings.

entries.name: Greater Prophecies
entries: Greater prophecies are most commonly found in myths, legends, and tales, and they typically come directly from the {@deity Norns|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}, detailing information for major life or world changes. These prophecies cryptically speak of fixed and unchangeable events in the future. Fantasy literature features this sort of prophecy often. In the Northlands, greater prophecies are exceedingly rare, as the {@deity Norns|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} don't often reveal the weft and weave of their loom to mere mortals. When PCs seek out a seer to hear a prophecy, they never receive greater prophecies. These are purely in the hands of the GM to give or withhold and should have a major impact on the story or world. They also typically don't have the benefits or consequences used in prophetic readings (detailed later in this section). The effects of fulfilling a greater prophecy are much larger than bonuses enjoyed by a single person, as these are outcomes that change nations.

entries.name: Why Use Prophecies?
entries: Prophecies can serve many functions in a campaign. They can be the focal point of the entire narrative, though this should be done sparingly, as the PCs, not a cryptic omen, should be driving the story. They can be used to provide information the GM wants to release in an in-game way. They can foreshadow future events, giving players a wonderful moment of "Oh! That's what the phrase 'Void Monarch' meant!" They can function as a through-line or guidepost for the campaign. When the players feel lost or out of focus, they can turn to the mysterious prophecy given by the GM to get the momentum of the campaign back on track. Finally, prophecies can be used as the fodder of the antagonist(s) in the campaign. The evil wizard might be searching for an ancient prophecy about a powerful relic, or the hoard of fanatical cultists might be invading because they follow the prophecy of their bloodthirsty deity. Above all else, remember that a prophecy is not fate.

entries.name: Prophetic Readings (Blessings/Warnings) and Rewarding Fulfillment
entries: Prophecies are broken up into prophetic blessings and warnings. In many games or stories, prophecies are traditionally relegated to the background, perhaps foreshadowing a coming event or giving the PCs a trail to follow. But they don't have to be. Prophetic blessings and warnings are brief glimpses of the loom of fate given to PCs by seers or supernatural creatures.

entries.name: Prophetic Blessing
entries: A prophecy suggesting an action during a certain sort of circumstance.

entries.name: Prophetic Warning
entries: A prophecy warning the PC to avoid a certain action during a certain sort of circumstance.

Each blessing or warning features three parts: a trigger, an action, and an outcome. The trigger is a short, cryptic element, circumstance, or description that the PC can recognize during game play. The action is an act or activity the PC takes in response to the trigger. The outcome is the result of the PC performing the action in response to the trigger. Outcomes are seen more often in greater prophecies but can also be used to add flavor to a prophecy.

By design, the trigger, action, and outcome are vague and non-specific, allowing them to be applied to a wide variety of situations. When a PC (or GM) decides a trigger applies to something occurring in a game, they can act to fulfill the rest of the blessing or warning. Doing so gives the PC a magical benefit or lets them avoid a potential consequence.

entries.name: Overview
entries: The specifics of this system are detailed later, but in general here is how it works.

items: The PC approaches a seer and asks a specific question.
The player makes a prophecy roll to determine the power of the reading and if it is a blessing or a warning.
A blessing comes with a benefit and a warning comes with a consequence.
The benefit or consequence can be selected by the player, be the result of a roll on a random table, or be chosen by the GM.
The prophetic blessing or warning is generated using the tables shown later and contains at least one "trigger."

entries: Later, the player or GM can decide if the trigger of their blessing or warning applies to a current circumstance in the game. If it does, they can attempt to fulfill it or avoid it.

items: For a prophetic blessing, the PC can perform the action described in the prophecy. If they do so, they gain the blessing's benefit.
For a prophetic warning, if the PC chooses to act in the way prohibited in the warning, they incur the warning's consequence.

entries.name: Prophecies and Omens are Vague
entries: When the PCs receive omens or prophecies in a game, the strange sighting or cryptic words absolutely need to be open to different interpretation. They should be "signs" that can be interpreted differently depending on the person, hindsight, and circumstance. They can mean different things to different viewers, or even to the same viewer depending on how the campaign unfolds.

From a GM's perspective, the vagueness of an omen or prophecy keeps your options open in case the needs of the campaign change. It does the game no good if a specific prophecy is suddenly rendered useless when a PC dies unexpectedly. Instead of calling out the specific name of the trollkin druid PC, a good prophecy might refer to "Child of Two Worlds" or "Seeker of Balance." The new dwarven cleric PC in the game might fit those same titles. It's all a matter of interpretation. Flexibility is the power of prophecy for a GM. If the PCs hear a prophecy, but the events of the campaign end up different than the GM expected, the prophecy wasn't incorrect—the interpretation of it was.
More examples are included in this chapter, but here are a few helpful suggestions when creating omens or prophecies.

items: Couch prophecies in symbolism and mysteriously vague titles.
Make omens seem out of the ordinary but not immediately threatening.
Keep dates and locations vague or unclear.
Use kennings or allusions rather than the exact creature, site, or phenomenon you plan on using later .
Use metaphors or pseudonyms instead of specific names (especially the PCs' names).
Make sure prophecies can unfold in a few different ways.
Make sure omens can be seen in different ways.
Limit the scope of prophecies so they hint about a limited event not the entire scope of someone's life.
Use omens to foreshadow and/or enhance the mood you wish for the table.

entries.name: Creating a Prophecy
entries: The section demonstrates how to create greater prophecies and prophetic blessings or warnings. If you are creating a greater prophecy, you can skip to Step 3: Generate the Prophecy.

entries.name: Step 1: Prophecy Roll
entries: The first step in creating a prophetic blessing or warning is the prophecy roll. When a seer or other entity gives a prophetic blessing or warning to a PC, the player must roll a prophecy roll to determine the power of the reading and whether it is a prophetic blessing or a warning. This roll is a simple {@dice d20} roll plus the PC's reputation modifier (see {@variantrule Reputation|NorthlandsWorldbook}), or half of the PC's {@variantrule Proficiency|XPHB|Proficiency Bonus}, whichever is higher.

entries.name: Step 2: Determining Benefits and Consequences
entries: The next step is to determine any benefits or consequences of a prophetic reading. Players can choose a benefit with their GMs approval, they can roll a {@dice d8} and consult the appropriate table, or the GM can choose it for them. Consequences are best chosen by the GM or determined randomly.

Each blessing/warning grants a game-specific aspect to the PC when the prophetic reading is fulfilled. Benefits and consequences are divided into three levels: Least, Greater, and Legendary/Dire. The relative power of the benefit or consequence increases with each stage.

Each benefit and consequence lists its duration. If a duration seems not to fit the listed benefit or consequence due to the specific circumstances of the game, the GM can change the duration. A GM can always choose to extend or end an effect, if doing so would better support the prophecy.

entries.name: Step 3: Generating the Prophecy
entries: The third step in the process features tables allowing GMs to select (or roll randomly to determine) the triggers, actions, and, optionally, the outcomes of the prophetic readings. GMs can also use the tables to generate a greater prophecy.
Prophecies (especially prophetic blessings or warnings) almost always begin with either "When" or "If," and the trigger and action together should form a complete sentence.

entries.name: Trigger
entries: To determine the trigger, roll a {@dice d20} once for each column in the Trigger table, combining the outcome into a vague description. GMs can use a bit of poetic license to make the trigger sound better. For example, if the rolls determined the words "Dry/Wet," "Guardian," "Bellows," and "Holy Place," the resulting trigger might be "When the arid guardian bellows in the holy temple."

entries.name: Action
entries: To create the action, roll a {@dice d20} for each column in Action table and combine the outcome into a vague description. Due to the number of possible results, GMs should rearrange the results and/or add words as necessary so the action makes sense. For example, if the rolls determined the words "Run," "Relic," "Behind," and "Concealment," the resulting trigger might be rephrased as "Run from behind the concealed relic," with the word "from" added for clarity.

If the prediction is a prophetic warning, the action element must be described as something to avoid. Remember, the GM will be the one identifying a trigger as being active, but they might not share that information with the players. For example, if your rolls determined a different set of words, such as "Hold," "Relic," "Inside," and "Light," the prophetic warning might be "Don't hold the relic inside the light."

entries.name: Outcomes
entries: An outcome is a change to the world, for good or for ill. The Outcome tables below offer suggestions for changes, both large and small, that could occur when a greater prophecy is fulfilled. Prophetic blessings and warnings don't usually have an outcome because the benefit or consequence serves that role. If GMs wish to use an outcome with a prophetic reading, they should begin each outcome with the word "to," such as "To derive new knowledge..." Outcomes should be matched with the nature of the benefit or consequence. For example, the "gods bestowing a blessing" could be used for attacks having {@variantrule Disadvantage|XPHB} against you.

To create an outcome, choose a column in the table (or roll a {@dice d4} to determine it randomly) and then roll a {@dice d20} for that column. Reword the outcomes as needed to fit the prophecy's trigger and action and to form a complete sentence. Typically, prophecies only have one outcome, but GMs can certainly add a second for particularly momentous predications. Greater prophecies always have an outcome attached to them.

When presenting an outcome in a prophecy, the outcome should be phrased as an event that has not happened, yet also in a manner to fit with the "When" or "If" that began the prediction. Use words like "will," "shall," and "lest" to indicate a future tense.

For example, rolling a {@dice d4} and a {@dice d20} to choose a random outcome results in "Sleeping god awakens" (a societal change), giving us a prophecy that, if triggered, will cause a sleeping god to wake up.

entries.name: Final Prophecy
entries: After going through these steps, the trigger, action, and benefit/consequence (or outcome) should form a complete sentence. Using the samples we've seen so far, a prophetic reading with a greater blessing would be: "When the arid destroyer bellows in the holy temple, run from behind the concealed relic to gain {@deity Volund|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}'s protection." (Resistance to fire damage) Using the samples, a greater prophecy would be: "When the arid destroyer bellows in the holy temple, run from behind the concealed relic, and the sleeping god will awaken."

entries.name: Sample Prophetic Blessings and Warnings
entries: Presented here are several prophetic blessings and warnings along with possible interpretations to show how players can identify the triggers in different ways. Some elements of these samples are not found in the tables in Step 3, to demonstrate how GMs can invent their own.

entries.name: Least Prophetic Blessing
entries: {@i When the storm casts its shadow, seek shelter within the ancient to sip from Mimir's well.}

entries.name: Benefit:
entries: If you do so, you gain {@variantrule Advantage|XPHB} on Intelligence- and Wisdom-based ability checks for 1 hour.

items: Shadow of the storm could be a literal storm overhead. But it could also be a creature or situation. The fury of a giant could be described as a "storm," so then the giant's shadow might be identified as the trigger.

A player could "seek shelter within the ancient" by moving into an old structure. But "ancient" could also be a term for a mountain, so stepping into a cave would fulfill the action portion of the blessing. Similarly, moving beneath the branches of a mighty tree could be viewed as seeking shelter within the ancient.

entries.name: Legendary Prophetic Blessing
entries: {@i When the stars hide their faces, quench the wound-brand to strike like Sleipnir.}

entries.name: Benefit:
entries: If you do so, once in the next 24 hours, you can use an action to move up to twice your speed and make a melee attack. You don't provoke {@action Opportunity Attack|XPHB|Opportunity Attacks} when moving in this way. If you successfully hit a creature, the target is pushed 10 feet away from you and has the prone condition.

items: Stars hiding their faces could be a kenning for darkness. It could also be interpreted more literally as people looking away from a situation.

The most obvious meaning for "quenching the wound-brand" would be to take something on fire and extinguish it. But wound-brand could be a kenning for a sword or weapon, and quenching is a smithing term for plunging hot metal into water. So instead, a player might take that to mean they merely have to stick their weapon into water.

entries.name: Greater Prophetic Warning
entries: {@i When the light speaks in screams, don't answer the call with wyrd-craft, or suffer Thor's fate.}

entries.name: Consequence:
entries: If you cast a spell before the end of your next turn, you have the {@condition Poisoned} condition for {@dice 1d4} rounds. While you have the {@condition Poisoned} condition from this effect, your thoughts are muddled, so you can only cast cantrips.

items: The light speaking in screams could be something like a {@spell Fireball|XPHB}, which is bright and causes screams of pain. It could also be a glowing foe who is yelling.

The warning against answering the call with wyrd-craft is pretty straightforward as it is referring to spellcasting. That said, a player could instead decide wyrd-craft refers to an enchanted weapon, thus the warning would say not to attack the "screaming light."

entries.name: Dire Prophetic Warning
entries: {@i When an ancient roar fractures the land, don't spill the dew of slaughter, or your hand will betray your allies.}

entries.name: Consequence:
entries: The first time you deal damage with an attack at any point in the next 8 hours, you become cursed for 1 minute. While cursed, at the start of each of your turns, roll a {@dice d6}. On a result of 1 or 2, you must move and make a melee attack against a random creature. If you can't reach a creature with your movement, you can instead take the Dash action to move toward a random creature.

items: An ancient roar fracturing the land could be an earthquake, but it could just as easily be a yelling giant striking the ground with her club, or an erupting volcano.

The warning not to spill the dew could be viewed as meaning "don't spill a container or vessel nearby." The phrase "dew of slaughter" is a kenning for blood, so it could also be a warning not to spill blood, either your own or (more likely in this case) the blood of a foe.

entries.name: Sample Greater Prophecies
entries: Here is a complex Greater Prophecy crafted using the various tables described in this section. As shown here, GMs can roll several times on the various tables to make longer prophecies if they wish.

entries.name: Sample Greater Prophecy
entries: "When a great king withholds secrets, and the statue of the brave awakens in the village square, bind well the rune-carved blade with blessed steel, or the forbidden rite shall unearth the sleeping god. Should this come to pass, hope can yet be restored if the fractured binding is cast anew with bloody stone."

entries.name: Construction
entries: This complicated greater prophecy follows this format, with some additional words thrown in for clarity:

items: Trigger (great king withholds secrets)
Trigger (statue awakes in village)
Action (bind blade with steel)
Outcome (forbidden rite awakens a god)
Outcome (hope is restored)
Trigger (fractured binding cast anew)
Action (with bloody stone)

entries.name: Omens
entries: Small signs, portents, and sightings work hand-in-hand with prophecies to foreshadow future events. While not as informative as a prophecy, omens provide flavor and can increase the mystery and tension in a game. GMs can use them as much or as little as they wish, but a good balance is different for every game, campaign, and table. Include too many omens and the GM risks blunting their impact. Provide too few omens and the table won't have the tone or vibe the GM is striving for.

The tables in this section provide examples of three different types of omens to add into a game: hopeful, foreboding, and mysterious. Some are portents of good things, others are warnings of dire events, and some are just mysterious. GMs can use these suggestions as a base and invent their own omens.

In most cases, the GM should choose the type of omen they wish, altering the omen as needed to fit the circumstances of the campaign, but if a more random generation method is preferred, roll a {@dice d4} and consult the Omen Types table.

entries.name: Ships and Sea Combat
entries: The naval combat rules presented here are intended to make the ship a dynamic and exciting part of any conflict.

entries.name: Ship Siege Weapons
entries: In the real-world cultures that inspired the Northlands, longships typically didn't utilize ship-mounted siege weapons. Instead, the warriors aboard them made use of melee and ranged weapons they could carry, not relying on weaponized machinery to do their battles. Depending on your setting of choice, weapons such as ballistae or mangonels may be loaded onto a longship if it suits your style of play. For such times, siege weapons are included in longship entries in Chapter 5, which can be removed if they do not make sense for your particular game.

Ship-mounted weapon attack rolls are equal to the Strength or Dexterity modifier of the ship (whichever is higher). The damage bonus is also equal to the higher of the ships Strength or Dexterity modifier. A PC firing a ship-mounted weapon can choose to use their own ranged weapon attack bonus and damage bonus instead of the ship's if they wish, using the higher of their Strength or Dexterity.

items.name: Ballista
items.entry: A massive crossbow that fires weighted bolts. A ship-mounted ballista can be loaded and aimed by the crew using the Operate Ship Weapon action.

items.name: Naval Ram
items.entry: This metal and wood ram is mounted to the front of the ship at or below the water level. It can be used to smash a hole in the side of another vessel. If the ship moves more than 30 feet first, a ram deals an additional {@damage 1d10} Piercing damage.

items.name: Ship Catapult
items.entry: A small ship-mounted catapult used to throw stones at enemy vessels. Loading and aiming a ship catapult requires a {@action Utilize|XPHB} action, and firing it uses another. Multiple crew can operate the same siege weapon to perform these actions in the same round.

entries: Some of the possible siege weapons are described here.

entries.name: Movement (Sail and Rowing)
entries: Use the {@variantrule Speed|XPHB} statistic provided with the vehicle. If you draw from another source, and the only {@variantrule Speed|XPHB} provided for a vehicle is in miles per hour, a handy approximation of the number of feet the ship moves per round is to take the value given for the vessel's miles per hour and multiply it by 10. This assumes the ship is being piloted. For example, a galley moves at 4 mph with average winds, or 40 ft. per round. If you are playing on a grid, round to the nearest multiple of 5 when counting squares. The {@variantrule Speed|XPHB} listed for longships includes its sail speed and its Rowing {@variantrule Speed|XPHB}.

entries.name: Changing Direction
entries: Sailing vessels don't quickly turn. A ship changing direction without completing a shipboard action moves the first half of its {@variantrule Speed|XPHB} in the direction it is facing and rotates 45° before moving the second half of its movement. For example, a turning galley would move 20 ft. in the direction it began the round and then another 20 feet at a 45° diagonal to its previous course.

entries.name: Direction of Wind and Drifting
entries: The direction of the wind is of critical importance to sailing a ship, determining if it can easily move in a straight line or is forced to tack back and forth. These rules simplify the importance of wind direction, assuming that the crew is tacking and making other appropriate adjustments to the sails. If a ship is not controlled, it drifts in the direction of the wind at the start of each of its turns: 5 feet for light wind, 10 feet for average wind, and 15 feet for strong wind. If the ship is being rowed, it generally ignores the effects of wind and drift, unless in storm conditions.

entries.name: Turning Into the wind
entries: The one direction ships never want to go is directly into the wind. A vessel that turns into the wind and tries to move in that direction has its {@variantrule Speed|XPHB} halved. If the ship's speed is greater than 0 feet while moving into the wind, the crew member at the helm must succeed on a {@dc 12} Strength ({@skill Athletics|XPHB}) or Wisdom ({@skill Survival|XPHB}) check to turn the ship. If the crew member fails to turn the ship, or the ship's {@variantrule Speed|XPHB} was reduced to 0 feet., it drifts in the direction of the wind and is stuck until the wind changes.

entries.name: Wind Speed
entries: Distance traveled assumes average wind speeds. Over the course of days, this is likely to be the case. During a combat round however, that doesn't have to be the case. If there is no wind, sailing ships don't move. If there are light winds, halve the ship's {@variantrule Speed|XPHB}, and if there are strong winds, double it. Longships also make use of rowers.

entries.name: Sea Weather
entries: Traveling by sea in a fantasy world means encountering strange weather in addition to the normal variations of wind and visibility. Use the Wind and Precipitation tables to determine weather conditions. Effects on movement assume the ship is powered by sails. If it is rowed or derives its power from some other source, an effect might not be relevant.

entries.name: Naval Combat
entries: A ship-to-ship battle can be a thrilling addition to your adventure. Without using the rules in this section, GMs can run ship encounters like any other combat. At the end of each round, all ships involved in the encounter can maneuver as the players or GM wishes. This is certainly the quickest method of handling naval combat.
For GMs and players who want more involved ship encounters, here is an optional set of rules to help create electrifying ship combats.

entries.name: Crew Member Stat Blocks
entries: The average sailor has the statistics of a {@creature Bandit|XMM} or {@creature Pirate|XMM}. A quick stat block for an officer could be a {@creature Pirate|XMM} or a {@creature Viking|NorthlandsWorldbook} (see {@book Chapter 8|NorthlandsWorldbook|8|Trollkin}), while the captain might use a {@creature Wolf Reaver Dwarf|ToB1-2023} or {@creature Pirate Captain|XMM} stat block.

entries.name: Initiative
entries: Ships move and act last in {@variantrule Initiative|XPHB}, and their crews are assumed to be the ones performing the chosen action. Player characters and unique foes not concerned with running a ship roll {@variantrule Initiative|XPHB} as normal. However, determine {@variantrule Initiative|XPHB} between competing vessels each round.

To decide which ship acts first, determine which ship has the advantage of position by having the person at the helm of each ship make a Strength ({@skill Athletics|XPHB}) or Wisdom ({@skill Survival|XPHB}) check. The winner chooses whether to act first or delay. If the helm has no one assigned, that ship automatically fails the check.

entries.name: Using Ship-Mounted Weapons
entries: Unlike a standard siege weapon, large shipboard weapons require separate {@action Utilize|XPHB} actions to load, aim, and fire. In a raiding party, it's assumed that sufficient crew members have been hired to operate all ship-mounted weapons. The {@action Operate Ship Weapon|NorthlandsWorldbook} action allows the crew to reload and aim the weapon, but it still requires another action to fire it. If an enemy is in the firing arc of a weapon, generally 90° from the direction it is mounted, the gunnery crew can attempt to fire on it.

entries.name: Ship Damage
entries: A ship taking damage in combat can suffer various effects. This damage can come as the result of weapon fire, spells, or impacts with physical objects. Consult the {@table Damage to the Ship|NorthlandsWorldbook} table for the effects of damage to the hull.

entries.name: Targeting Crew and Casualties
entries: Ship weapons typically aren't used against enemy sailors. The opposing vessel is a much easier target. However, sailors might be injured as collateral damage from an attack. When an attack scores a {@variantrule Critical Hit|XPHB}, in addition to rolling the damage dice twice, determine the location of the ship that was hit using the {@action Disable Station|NorthlandsWorldbook} shipboard action.

Roll a {@dice d6} to determine how many crew members in that area are {@condition Unconscious|XPHB} and dying. If a PC or NPC with medical skill or magical healing does not take action to save them, 75 percent of them die in {@dice 1d4} rounds. If a PC is in the area hit, they take half the damage dealt by the attack from flying shrapnel. If the PC succeeds on a Dexterity save with a DC equal to the enemy gunner's attack roll, they instead take no damage from shrapnel.

entries.name: Actions during Ship Combat
entries: During a naval engagement, the PCs can act independently from the ship with its crew, or they can work with them as determined by the players.

entries.name: PCs During Combat
entries: PCs can choose to act as they would in any other combat. Throwing {@spell Fireball|XPHB|Fireballs} and raining down a volley of arrows remain effective tactics. Note however, that most engagements begin at {@dice (2d6 + 2) * 100|(2d6 + 2) x 100} feet, so PC attacks are not generally in range when engagements commence. PCs can also use their turn to perform a shipboard action. A PC doing so must use the {@action Ready|XPHB} action on their turn. Then, once the ship has moved at the end of the round, they can use their {@variantrule Reaction|XPHB} to do their readied shipboard action.

entries.name: Ship and Crew During Combat
entries: Ships and crew act at the end of the {@variantrule Initiative|XPHB} round. On its turn, a vehicle can move up to its {@variantrule Speed|XPHB} and use a shipboard action. The players should decide together what this ship action is going to be. PCs who delayed their actions on their turns can make additional shipboard actions. Unless noted otherwise, the same shipboard action can only be performed once per turn.

entries.name: Shipboard actions
entries: There are a number of actions the crew of the ship (and potentially the PCs) can take in ship-to-ship combat.

entries.name: Raiding
entries: In the culture of the Northlands, raiding other communities dates back to the Reaving. These expeditions served a variety of purposes depending on who conducted them. For some, they were a method of earning glory, training young warriors, punishing foes, or (more typically) securing badly needed resources. Historically, raids involved securing a ship, gathering a crew, sailing often great distances to a location, attacking it, and returning with treasure. Played out fully, a raid could be a campaign all by itself, and GMs are certainly free to run them that way.
