These optional rules, however, allow various portions of the raiding journey, or even the entire raid, to occur "off-stage" by abstracting them. This keeps raids feeling fast and thrilling.

entries.name: A Word About Theft and Raiding
entries: For a Northlander, raiding is not the same as thievery. To steal something from someone is not honorable and violates the various rules of hospitality. Raiding, however, is not "theft" because you are fighting someone for their treasures. Even if the "battle" consists of sneaking up on a location, setting it on fire, and cutting down the inhabitants as they flee the blaze, it's considered a fight and thus an honorable means to seize the rewards. The general guideline for a reaver is anything goes, as long as it doesn't stain their honor.

The typical goal of a raid isn't to take territory or inflict the most damage. Instead, it is to gather the most resources or treasure without losing too many warriors or your own supplies in the process. Thus, raids tended to be lightning-fast assaults rather than sieges.

entries.name: Using Raiding Rules
entries: These rules break raids down into abstract phases—preparation, journey, raid, and return—with each phase determined by rolling dice and consulting tables. Successes or failures from each phase affect the next subsequent phase. A few other aspects are also abstracted for ease of play.

entries.name: Cost
entries: To participate in the raid, a PC must spend coins, as determined by the target of the raid (see the {@table Raiding Target|NorthlandsWorldbook} tables). This is an abstracted cost reflecting a share of the cost of outfitting the expedition, but in return, the PC gets a greater share of plunder taken.

entries.name: Time
entries: Raiding activities are typically measured in weeks, each of which is roughly assumed to be at least 5 days, where 8 hours per day are spent pursuing the current activity. Each phase of the raid indicates the amount of time in "weeks" that occurred.

entries.name: Distance
entries: While it is important for the GM to know how far the target of the raid is, the exact distance is somewhat meaningless for the purposes of these rules. More distant targets chosen during the preparation phase may require GMs to adjust the tables in other phases to account for the particulars of various climates, hazards, flora, and fauna found in those locations.

entries.name: Raiding Roll and Spoils Dice
entries: Just as the time and distance of the raid are handled abstractly, the actual raid and the amount of plunder taken is abstracted in a mechanic similar to rolling attack and weapon damage in combat. While raiding, PCs make a raiding roll against a DC determined by the size of the target (plus any additional modifiers). If successful, the PCs then roll a spoils die to determine how much plunder is gained.

In general, 1 spoil is worth 500 GP, regardless of it being a bag of grain, bars of steel, a pouch of gems, or a crate of chickens. This isn't a replacement for standard treasure; instead, it serves as a shorthand for the "wealth" taken during the raid. The spoils gained in a raid reflect what goes directly to the PCs. This assumes NPCs already received a separate share of the proceeds of the successful raid.

The abstractions presented by this system provide a way for PCs to track the costs and rewards of a raid without getting bogged down in the minutia of weights and cargo lists. However, any phase can be replaced with actual in-game play according to the needs of the GM. For example, the preparation, journey, and return phases could be handled abstractly, but the raid itself could be a full combat encounter.

entries.name: Raiding Phases
entries: The four phases of a raid are preparation, journey, raid, and return, and they are detailed here.

entries.name: Preparation
entries: In the first phase, the PCs determine the following aspects.

items.name: The Target
entries: Choose the place to be raided.

items.name: Ship Upgrades
entries: Pay for additional upgrades for the ship.

items.name: Additional Raiders
entries: Recruit a crew of hearty warriors.

items.name: Special Resources
entries: Gather provisions, ship repair materials, and deal with other details for the journey.

items.name: The Cost
entries: After calculating the total based on their choices, PCs each pay a share to fund the raid.
Making wise choices during the preparation phase can mean the difference between a successful raid and an abject failure.

entries.name: Journey
entries: In the second phase, the PCs must contend with the voyage to the raiding target, overcoming hazards and obstacles. Success or failure when doing so can grant bonuses (or penalties) during the next phase.

entries.name: Raid
entries: In the third phase, the raiders reach their destination and conduct a fast assault on the target before additional defenders can be mobilized to oppose them. The PCs make a raiding roll and roll the spoils die to determine the level of the raid's success and the amount of plunder taken. How things go here can directly impact the ease (or difficulty) of their trip home.

entries.name: Return
entries: In the fourth phase, the PCs return home, hopefully with their ship laden with spoils. Much like the journey phase, the return features hazards and obstacles. This phase can be more difficult if the raid went poorly.

entries.name: Outcome
entries: Once all of the phases are complete, the GM tallies up the positive and negative results of the entire voyage to determine the final spoils of the raid.

entries.name: Preparation Phase
entries: The preparation phase involves recruiting warriors, upgrading a ship, and gathering supplies for the raid. But the first decision to be made is to choose a target.

entries.name: The Target
entries: Raids can be carried out on various targets, from small hamlets, to forts, to major cities. The dangers the reavers might face, including armed defenders, increase with the scale of the target, but so do the possible rewards.
The PCs can use the Raiding Targets table to choose the target of their raid, as well as the types of loot typically found in the listed communities.

If the GM plans to run the raid phase as an encounter, a table of different settlement sizes has been provided to show the average number of defenders. The number of reavers needed to raid various settlements detailed in the abstracted table is the same here.

entries.name: Ship Upgrades
entries: The choice of ship, number of warriors, supplies, and so forth are abstracted in this system. The funds paid by the PCs to participate in the raid include an appropriately sized ship crewed by enough warriors to attempt the raid against the chosen target settlement.

If the players and GM wish to explore ship options in more detail, consult the Naval Combat section earlier in this chapter. Additionally, Chapter 5 contains specific information about the most common vessels used in the North. As a reminder, all crew members are expected to operate the vessel as well as participate in the raid itself.

As part of the preparation phase, the PCs can choose to enhance their ship with a variety of options. Each of these enhancements gives the PCs a bonus to their raiding roll, spoil dice, or other mechanics, but using them also increases the cost each PC must pay to participate in the raid. Each upgrade is only usable once during this raid to give a bonus in one phase. If an upgrade is not used, it is wasted. These upgrades don't have any mechanical function in naval combat.

entries.name: Additional Raiders
entries: A contingent of warriors large enough to tackle the chosen target comes with the funds paid by the PCs. However, some parties might wish to bring more warriors along to ensure victory. The PCs are not going to be able to empty a village of warriors to crew their longship. At best, they'll convince half of a community's able-bodied reavers to sign on. Raiding is a risk not only for those participating but also for the communities they leave behind. Every raider lost during a raid means one fewer warrior to defend the village against monsters or raids, as well as one fewer worker to do the vital tasks to keep the settlement going.
In general, the size of community hosting the raid (or the place where the raid leaves from) directly relates to the number of extra warriors available to be recruited.

Additional warriors can be hired in bands, ranging from 5 to 100. Each group gives a bonus to the raiding roll during the raid phase, but it also comes with an associated cost added to the sum the PCs pay to fund the raid (see the Extra Warriors table). Only one group of extra warriors can be added to each raid.

entries.name: Special Resources
entries: The base level funds provided by the PCs provide a decent amount of provisions, repair materials, and other supplies for the raid. Aside from that, there are special resources PCs can purchase (see the Special Resources table). Similar to ship upgrades, these resources give bonuses to raiding rolls, spoils dice, and other game elements. Each special resource is only usable once during a raid to give a bonus in one phase. If a special resource is not used, it is wasted.

entries.name: The Journey
entries: In the second phase, the PCs must contend with the voyage to the raiding target while overcoming hazards and obstacles. Success or failure can grant bonuses (or penalties) during the next phase. The PCs make a group roll on the Sea/Land Journey table for each week of travel (see Abstracted Time/Distance in this section). GMs can choose to add additional rolls on the Sea/Land Journey table as they wish. To emphasize the epic themes of the raid, the GM should be as descriptive as possible.

entries.name: Abstracted Time/Distance
entries: Rather than delve into the minutia of travel speeds and distance, those aspects are abstracted in the journey phase to 1 week of time for most destinations. The GM can always add time to the voyage to account for things such as setting elements or for more distant destinations.

entries.name: Land Raiding
entries: Not all raids need to be conducted via the sea. The communities of giants to the North offer tantalizing targets for metal, rare resources, hides, and relics. Due to the geography of the Northlands, most reavers utilize ships for direct assaults on raiding targets or to travel to a landing site near the target for an overland attack. Raiding PCs aren't required to use ships if their target is reachable by marching, though most groups of warriors won't want to trek hundreds of miles across frozen mountains when they could just sail there.

entries.name: The Raid
entries: In the third phase, the PCs reach their destination and conduct a fast assault on the target before additional defenders can be mobilized to oppose them.

entries.name: Raiding Roll
entries: The moment has come! Screaming their battle cries, the reavers leap from their longboats or charge through the snow-covered field toward the (hopefully) unsuspecting settlement. Determining the result of a raid requires the players to make a group raiding roll against the DC of the target settlement.

The raiding roll is equal to {@dice 1d20}, modified by any bonuses or penalties gained during the previous phases. If the result of this roll meets or exceeds the DC, the raid succeeds and grants a bonus to the spoils die, as well as additional benefits. However, a result lower than the DC indicates the raiders were driven off but still managed to grab some plunder on the way out. Rolling below the DC gives a penalty to the spoils die and may result in other complications. The Raiding Roll table displays all of these results.

entries.name: Important NPC Captives
entries: If the raid captures an important NPC, that individual can be ransomed back to their family or community. The negotiations and exchange can take some time, but many Northlands jarls are more than pleased to take such captives off the PCs hands in exchange for favors, like gaining renown or learning hidden lore, or for a lump sum of gold, a magic item, or another reward determined by the GM.

entries.name: Spoils Die
entries: Once the raiding roll is resolved, the PCs can roll the spoils die for the target settlement, adding any adjustments incurred during the current and previous phases. As a reminder, the result of this roll is the share of plunder going directly to the PCs. The raiding rules assume NPC warriors receive a separate share from the total among of loot taken.

entries.name: The Return
entries: In the fourth phase, the PCs travel home (hopefully) laden with spoils from a successful raid. Repeat the journey phase, adjusting rolls as necessary. This phase can be more difficult if the raid went poorly, and failures here can cost the PCs a portion of their spoils.

entries.name: Outcome
entries: Once all of the phases are complete, the GM and the players tally up the positive and negative results of the entire voyage to determine the final spoils of the raid.
The total spoils handed to the PCs can be immediately exchanged for gold pieces or standard equipment of equal value. One spoil is worth 500 GP.

With GM approval, PCs can instead exchange their spoils for magic items. The availability of items depends on the size of the settlement the PCs return to after their raid is complete. Typically, this is the same location they left from, but that isn't a requirement. The Spoils Exchange table shows the number of spoils that can be exchanged for magic items of different rarities, as well as the minimum size of the settlement likely to have such an item.

The exact nature of an item gained by the PCs should be a discussion between the players and the GM. Since magic item rarity offers a wide range of value for items, not every item will be available just because they have enough spoils to exchange for it. Settlements might also charge more for certain items than is shown on the table, due to campaign circumstances. The GM makes the final determination on all magic item availability and cost.

entries.name: Who Leads the Raid?
entries: Are the PCs leading the raid themselves? Or are they joining a raid led by an NPC? Either way, the players are the ones making decisions for the raid and will exert a degree of narrative control over all of the NPCs involved in it. If the PCs join a raid led by an NPC, the cost they pay up front is a bit like investing in the expedition. If it is successful, the PCs get a larger share of the plunder than the average warrior. GMs can, of course, have NPC leaders push for larger shares, perhaps setting up some fun roleplaying confrontations.

entries.name: Raids as Downtime Activities
entries: The raiding rules presented in this chapter can be used as downtime activities. Typically, this works best if all of the PCs choose to embark on the raid together, especially since most raids take at least two weeks to conduct. GMs can shorten this time by giving the raid expedition a few of the ship upgrades or special resources that reduce the sailing time. This might be advisable if some of the PCs go raiding and others stay behind. That way, everyone is on the same time frame.

entries.name: Northlands Weather
entries: As mentioned in {@book Chapter 1|NorthlandsWorldbook|1}, the North is generally a cold environment, with most areas experiencing extreme cold during winter. The following rules feature optional game elements for environmental obstacles in the Northlands.

data.name: Chapter 8: Northlands Bestiary
entries: This chapter includes an assortment of new monsters to incorporate in your adventures. In addition to dangerous creatures, you will also find listings for various NPCs and mounts found in the Northlands.

entries.name: Creatures
entries: This section contains statistics for an assortment of creatures found in the Northlands.

entries.name: Brunnmigi
entries: {@i Poison-Spitting Plague Fox}
{@color A large bear or foxlike beast with mottled, patchy fur, and a distended belly scuttles about. It is covered in boils and pustules.|006abe}

items.name: Habitat:
items.entry: Arctic, Coastal

items.name: Treasure:
items.entry: None

entries: A brunnmigi is a monstrous creature that spreads disease and pollutes sources of fresh water. Brunnmigi delight in the suffering of others, typically by befouling wells and streams with their plague-bearing spittle. Settlements in the Northlands rely on painstakingly dug wells, and having their source of water rendered unusable often leads to the entire village scattering, lest they succumb to thirst.

entries.name: Dragon, Fafnir
entries: {@i Dwarf Cursed into Dragon Form}

{@color This bat-winged monster has a sinuous body covered in scales the color of weathered iron. Its limbs are powerful, but warped, bending in impossible ways. The monster's head is like that of a dragon, but it has too many eyes, and whiplike tentacles circle its skull like a crest. Its maw is lined with rows of long fangs, and its underside is speckled with golden coins, jewelry, and gemstones embedded between its scales.|006abe}

items.name: Habitat:
items.entry: Arctic, Grasslands

items.name: Treasure:
items.entry: Gold, Arcana

entries: Fafnir was once a dwarf, one of the four sons of the famed smith Hreidmarr. When their brother was mistakenly slain by {@deity Loki|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}, the clever god gave their father a magical ring as wergild. This item, called Andvaranaut, was supposed to bring untold wealth, but the ring bore a horrible curse. Inflamed by greed, Fafnir killed his father to possess the ring and drove his brothers into exile. The curse and his own avarice warped and changed the dwarf until Fafnir transformed into a serpentine dragon with gold coins and gems embedded in his belly. It also destroyed Andvaranaut.

Fafnir makes his lairs in isolated caves often carved into the base of a hills or into the side of high cliffs. He changes lairs frequently, paranoid that his hoard will be stolen from him. The area within 1 mile of Fafnir's current lair is warped, causing creatures to become greedy and possessive of their belongings.

entries.name: Drake, Nidhogg-Blooded
entries: {@i Twisted Burrowing Serpent}
{@color This wolf-sized dragon has spindly legs and a wide jaw filled with numerous rows of small, sharp teeth.|006abe}

items.name: Habitat:
items.entry: Arctic, Underground

items.name: Treasure:
items.entry: Any

entries: Nidhogg-blooded drakes are blessed, or some suggest, corrupted, by the dread wyrm {@deity Nidhogg|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}, who lies imprisoned beneath the World Tree, constantly gnawing on the roots. {@deity Nidhogg|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}'s foul influence spreads from Yggdrasil infrequently, but drakes attracted to his lair are imbued with his darkness before they venture into the wider world.

entries.name: Eikthyrnir
entries: {@i Thorny Stag Horror}

{@color The creature's pelt resembles that of a deer, but denser and shaggy, like that of a bear. Its antlers are disproportionately large and curved into long, wickedly sharp points above eyes that burn with uncanny fire. Thorny brambles have pushed through the beast's skin from within, wrapping around its body and antlers like climbing ivy.|006abe}

items.name: Habitat:
items.entry: Planar (World Tree)

items.name: Treasure:
items.entry: None

entries: Eikthyrnir are enormous stag-like horrors formed when stags consume World Tree acorns that have been corrupted by evil energies. They stalk the branches of the World Trees, occasionally reaching mortal planes, where they spread horror and carnage.

entries.name: Fenrikyn
entries: {@i Howling Fangs and Chains}
{@color This massive, warped canine has frothing jaws and chains that wrap around its body, obeying its every whim.|006abe}

items.name: Habitat:
items.entry: Arctic, Forest, Hill

items.name: Treasure:
items.entry: Any

entries: Fenrikyn are warped worgs and winter wolves, altered by the influence of {@deity Fenris|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}, the Great Wolf. Fenrikyn roam the cold forests and the hills of the Northlands, devouring all that they encounter. Generally solitary, fenrikyn have been known to gather into small packs or to take over a pack of wolves or worgs. Though they despise most living things, they reserve their greatest enmity for good-aligned canines and followers of the god {@deity Tyr|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}.

entries.name: Fleshcrawler
entries: {@i Crawling Flesh that Wears a Face}

{@color This creature resembles a humanoid-shaped collection of partially formed body parts, including muscles, bones, organs, ligaments, and facial features. Countless small pseudopods squirm from every part of its body, occasionally falling off and writhing as if still alive.|006abe}

items.name: Habitat:
items.entry: Any

items.name: Treasure:
items.entry: Any

entries: Horrific nightmares that somehow escaped from the sealed land of Hyperborea, fleshcrawlers seek to reproduce and spread their infestation across the world while causing as much pain and destruction as possible.

Their attacks temporarily warp the physical form of the target, twisting flesh and bone painfully. These attacks also renders the victim potentially vulnerable to infestation by the flesh-like webs that they spawn.

Once a host is infected, the fleshcrawler controls that creature's actions like a puppeteer. Over the course of a few days, the host grows weaker as it is consumed from within, until nothing remains of the original form but its skin. This becomes a cocoon for a new fleshcrawler, which emerges in its fully grown form.

Fleshcrawlers are typically encountered alone or in small groups, though some keep a clutch of newly infected humanoids nearby. Thanks to its limited telepathy, the fleshcrawler can sense the presence of others of its kind and rarely competes for prey or new hosts.

entries.name: Fossegrim
entries: {@i Cavorting Fey Musicians}

{@color This small being is attired in a fur-lined vest and pointed cap. It has greenish skin, a long nose, and twinkling black eyes. It smiles mischievously and pulls a fiddle from behind its back.|006abe}

items.name: Habitat:
items.entry: Forest, Hill, Mountain, Underwater

items.name: Treasure:
items.entry: Arcana, Individual

entries: Mysterious water fey that are mystically linked to waterfalls and streams, fossegrim resemble gnome-sized creatures with vaguely troll-like features, including pale green skin and bulbous noses. Fossegrim can also disguise themselves as attractive humanoids of the species most prevalent in the region to lure humanoids into heedless revelry.

Every fossegrim owns a musical instrument, such as a fiddle, lyre, or shawm, which it can play to weave powerful, enchanted melodies. While a fossegrim's musical instrument doesn't display any magical properties in the hands of others, some fossegrim have been known to teach talented humans and elves some of their tricks in exchange for companionship or food.

entries.name: Garmr
entries: {@i Roaring Maw of the Underworld}

{@color This large, foul-looking hound possesses a coat of worm-eaten fur in shades of black and gray, an oversized mouth, and glowing eyes. It snarls menacingly, the ground trembling beneath it.|006abe}

items.name: Habitat:
items.entry: Forest, Planar (Lower Planes), Underground

items.name: Treasure:
items.entry: None

entries: The garmr is a horse-sized canine fiend with mangy black fur dripping with maggots, and a massive mouth filled with razor-sharp fangs that rot anything it bites. Garmrs are said to be born from a mythical hound that serves the goddess {@deity Hel|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}, or somehow related to {@deity Fenris|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}. They are vicious and cruel creatures that bully fiends and spirits and sometimes lead groups of devils and lesser undead into battle.

Garmrs can create earth tremors with their howls, and several garmrs working together can cause powerful shockwaves similar to those produced by an earthquake. Their howls are particularly effective in subterranean tunnels and passages, and can be used to block off entrances or bury intruders.
Despite their similarities to hell hounds, garmrs are distinct creatures. Meetings between the two types of creatures almost always end in battle unless a more powerful fiend controls both groups.

entries.name: Giant, Jotun
entries: {@i World-shaking Primordial Giants}
{@color Tall enough to look a titan in the eye and strong enough to wrestle a dragon, jotun are the lords of giantkind and the immortal enemies of the gods.|006abe}

The enormous halls of the jotun are carved in mountains and glaciers throughout the North. As foes of the Northern gods, jotun plot to regain their former status as lords of creation. Many know ancient secrets and snippets of antediluvian arcane lore, and the most powerful among them straddle the line between mortal and demigod.

Like many giants, jotun enjoy a challenge. Only the mightiest heroes can challenge a jotun's might in physical combat, and most resort to cunning or trickery to defeat a jotun. However, jotun are no fools and catch on to trickery quickly.

entries.name: Giant, Lightning
entries: {@i Wayward Children of Storms}

{@color Standing more than twice as tall as a human, this gray-skinned giant has pure white eyes and hands that crackle with tendrils of electricity. A bolt of lightning coalesces in the giant's hands into a staff of glowing blue-white energy that it wields with fearsome intent.|006abe}

items.name: Habitat:
items.entry: Hill, Mountain

items.name: Treasure:
items.entry: Armaments

entries: Lightning giants dwell in large, windy caves and storm-struck keeps in mountainous terrain, raising giant goats and keeping dire wolves as pets. They are muscular and humanlike in appearance, with hair constantly blown as if by a gale, and eyes and skin crackling with electricity.

Northlanders sometimes refer to these giants as the children of {@deity Thor|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}, a fact the Thunder God is quick to refute. They believe that the first lightning giant resulted from a union between {@deity Thor|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} and a particularly attractive hill giant maiden. These tales do not amuse lightning giants, and they take umbrage with anyone who spouts them. The shield-maidens of {@deity Sif|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} hold particular hatred for these giants, viewing their mere existence as a slight upon their patron goddess.

While they don't share the same habitat as storm giants, lightning giants revere them for their greater prowess and size, and defer to them whenever they meet. Storm giants don't view lightning giants quite as favorably, viewing them as overly clingy.

entries.name: Giant, Thrudgelmir
entries: {@i Multiheaded Giant of Malice}

{@color Six distinct heads rise from the massive shoulders of this giant, which towers above its surroundings. Blue, runic tattoos adorn its exposed flesh, and it holds a black iron maul in each hand. It smashes the mauls together, releasing sparks of elemental energy as it prepares to attack.|006abe}

items.name: Habitat:
items.entry: Hill, Mountain, Swamp, Underground

items.name: Treasure:
items.entry: Armaments

entries: Millennia ago, a clan of giants in the far north discovered something alien in their endless realm of ice and snow. The exact nature of this object is not known, though some speculate it was a Hyperborean relic or perhaps a device from beyond the mortal plane. Whatever its origin, the strange item warped their minds and bodies, causing them to sprout additional heads and increasing their malevolence sixfold.

Thrudgelmir are intelligent and remorseless hunters that require substantial amounts of food to sustain their grotesque frames. Seldom do thrudgelmir giants gather in numbers, but when they do, the folk of the Northlands fear what may come of it.

entries.name: Giant, Thursir
entries: {@i Canny Gluttonous Crafters}
{@color The giant's hair and beard are plaited with rings and other bits of decorative stone and metal, and it carries a large, rune-inscribed hammer.|006abe}

Greedy and aggressively competitive, thursir are smaller than most types of giants. They dwell in vast caverns under frozen mountains, where they labor to forge chains, armor, and massive engines of war. Items forged by a thursir are of the highest quality, and other giants often seek thursir smiths to outfit their people in times of strife.
When not toiling at the forge, these giants entertain themselves with gluttonous feasts and boisterous wrestling competitions, or they raid human settlements for food and valuables.

entries.name: Gnoll, Tundra
entries: {@i Hunters of the Frigid Wastes}

{@color A lean hyena-headed hunter with dirty white fur leaps up through the cover of the snow, its hand clasped around a twisted metal blade. The creature emits a low rumble from the back of its throat as it fixes glowing blue eyes on the nearest threat.|006abe}

items.name: Habitat:
items.entry: Arctic, Desert, Grassland, Hill

items.name: Treasure:
items.entry: Armaments, Individual

entries: Tundra gnolls dwell in the blizzard-ravaged deserts and plains of the Northlands. They are fierce hunters that prey on nearly all other denizens of the lands they inhabit. A tundra gnoll's fur is a light, ice-white color, allowing it to blend seamlessly into the snowy background, though older hunters sometimes have a blue tinge to their fur.

Tundra gnolls are more cunning and patient than their brethren in other lands and can spend hours waiting for potential prey to pass by. This is often necessary, considering the bleak and inhospitable terrain in which they live. They typically dwell in small tribes in tundra regions but can also be found in pine barrens and snow-covered hills.
Giants and hags sometimes employ tundra gnolls in their forces, though they can only be adequately managed through the use of force, intimidation, or substantial bribes of food and treasure.

entries.name: Grendelkyn
entries: {@i Lurking Shadow of Terror}
{@color Appearing out of the shadows, this creature is a hideous patchwork of fur and scales, with ungainly arms and an elongated mouth filled with wicked teeth.|006abe}

items.name: Habitat:
items.entry: Forest, Hill, Underwater, Urban

items.name: Treasure:
items.entry: Any

entries: A Grendelkyn is a monstrous fey clad in writhing shadows, with overly long arms, bloody talons, and a misshapen head. They despise humanoids and regularly creep into longhouses and other locations under the cover of night to snatch up unwary prey, focusing their attacks on the most vulnerable members of the household.

Grendelkyn can breathe and operate normally underwater, and their lairs are often located in deep lakes or ponds on the edge of civilization. Despite their appearance, they are not related to trolls and are thought to be tied to an ancient story surrounding a festive mead hall and the hero who frequented it.

entries.name: Hafgufa
entries: {@i Lurking Ship Destroyers}
{@color A massive predatory fish the size of an island just finishes gobbling the last of a whale when it turns its eyes on your ship.|006abe}

items.name: Habitat:
items.entry: Coastal, Underwater

items.name: Treasure:
items.entry: Any

entries: The hafgufa is a titanic sea monster that preys on whales and ships. A hafgufa often lurks near the surface along trade routes, its mouth open so wide that its teeth jut above the waterline and appear as rocks that must be navigated between.

When attacking, the hafgufa typically uses its terrible breath to incapacitate prey before plucking them up with its tentacles to feed into its open mouth. Alternatively, it simply attacks the ship, ripping it to shreds and then grabbing sailors from the water.

The hafgufa's gullet often contains valuable or interesting objects. Since the creature lives for centuries, the item could have been lost for generations. Roll on or choose a result from the Swallowed Treasure table (or any item of your choice) to determine what a swallowed creature finds.

Every 20 to 30 years, a hafgufa spawns thousands of worm-sized wriggling offspring. These spawn feed on one another, growing rapidly as they consume their kin. The few remaining spawn separate to find their own hunting grounds, often a fjord or bay where they can prey on fish, or the people who fish those waters.

This predation can last for weeks or months, until the hafgufa spawn has sated its hunger and swims to a deep, dark place in the ocean to sleep and grow into its full size over the course of the next few years.

entries.name: Hamingja
entries: {@i Friendly Guiding Spirit}
{@color There is a stirring in the air, and then a creature materializes out of the emptiness. The being is small and vaguely foxlike, with luminous fur and eyes that radiate a warm kindness.|006abe}

items.name: Habitat:
items.entry: Planar, Urban

items.name: Treasure:
items.entry: None

entries: Hamingjas are beneficial celestial spirits that attach themselves to worthy individuals of good heart or heroic destiny. They are naturally invisible and only show themselves when their hosts are in mortal danger. When a hamingja is visible, it typically appears as a domestic animal, such as a cat or dog, or more rarely an attractive humanoid. No matter its shape, the hamingja's form is outlined with a shimmering radiance. Its natural form is that of a canine or feline creature with radiant eyes and iridescent fur.

Hamingjas provide their hosts with a shot of luck when needed, transferring some of their spiritual essence to the host. A hamingja only leaves its host when the host is killed, the hamingja is destroyed, or the host becomes evil in alignment.
Rarely, a hamingja stays with the same family or clan for decades or even centuries, jumping from one family member or clan member to the next.

entries.name: Jorumungkyn
entries: {@i Horrid Serpent of the Depths}

{@color This titanic monster is a chimera of fish and serpent parts, all covered in greenish-white scales and black spines. Its body leaks a foul greenish-black oozes. It roars, a wheezing shriek, its luminous green eyes the size of shields.|006abe}

items.name: Habitat:
items.entry: Arctic, Coastal, Underwater

items.name: Treasure:
items.entry: None

entries: Considered the lesser offspring of the famed World Serpent, jorumungkyn are gigantic sea serpents displaying a mix of a deep-sea fish and dragon features. Their ghostly coils rise from the frigid chasms of the world's oceans to encircle ships and drag them down to a watery grave. Jorumungkyn are infamous for the lethality of the poison that bubbles from their mouths and pores. This poison acts like oil in water, forming a deadly layer on the surface of any ground or liquid it touches.

Jorumungkyn stalk the seas and attack anything that gets in their way. They are a blight upon the oceans and are hated by most intelligent underwater species. Occasionally, aboleths attempt to enslave jorumungkyn to do their bidding. While this typically results in the aboleth being killed or severely injured, sometimes the aberration wins out, and it gains a powerful servant in the process.

entries.name: Lindwurm, Sea
entries: {@i Seal Snake of the Bitter Waves}

{@color At first, this creature resembles a normal, if gigantic seal with a disturbingly large mouth. But when it gets closer, you realize that the beast is anything but normal. Its skin is covered in fine scales, and short spiny ridges sprout from its back. It opens its mouth to reveal shark-like teeth.|006abe}

items.name: Habitat:
items.entry: Arctic, Coastal, Underwater

items.name: Treasure:
items.entry: None

entries: Unwary or ignorant hunters and sailors often mistake sea lindwurms for enormous seals. However, while their heads are vaguely seal-like, their bodies are more serpentine in appearance, with smooth, blackish-purple scales and large flippers that allow them to drag themselves up onto ice floes and beaches on the rare occasions when they leave the water's safety.

Sea lindwurms use their seal-like appearance to sneak up on unwary boats, but this is not their only means of capturing prey. Their bite carries a potent toxin that causes a spreading paralysis in their victims, and they can slap their flippers on the water's surface to stun enemies.
Sea lindwurms and common lindwurms sometimes meet out on the pack ice or in fjords. Typically, these meetings end in a furious struggle between the two monsters.

entries.name: Malrgotr
entries: {@i Iron Bristles, Golden Tusks}

{@color A boar the size of a small cart, this monster has a mane of golden bristles covering its head and upper body, and large tusks and teeth that also seem to be composed of golden metal. The creature strikes the ground with sharp hooves, raising clods of dirt, and growls threateningly.|006abe}

items.name: Habitat:
items.entry: Forest, Grassland, Swamp

items.name: Treasure:
items.entry: None

entries: The malrgotr is a monstrous boar-like creature inhabiting dark, misty forests and peatlands. Its body is covered in long metallic bristles, and its tusks shine gold in what little sunlight filters through the clouds and mist. While the malrgotr is a living creature, much of its body is composed of inorganic metal, almost as if it were the work of a divine crafter like Volund.

The malrgotr is not an evil creature and behaves much like an ordinary boar in the wilds. However, it appears to be infuriated by engineered structures, such as walls or farmsteads. It attempts to destroy any such structure it encounters, even if doing so would put it in danger.

Some have postulated a connection between the malrgotr and the legendary gullinbursti, a massive boar with golden features created by the dwarves for the goddess {@deity Freyr and Freyja|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook|Freyja}.
A malrgotr's dead body can be harvested for gold and iron. Its corpse provides 50 pounds of iron and 20 pounds of gold.

entries.name: Ogre, Great
entries: {@i Hulk of Chaos and Ruin}

{@color This giant wears a mishmash of furs and leather and carries a massive ship's anchor in its hands. Its arms and chest bulge with rippling muscles, and its face radiates a brutish malevolence.|006abe}

items.name: Habitat:
items.entry: Arctic, Forest, Hill, Mountain, Swamp, Underground

items.name: Treasure:
items.entry: Armaments

entries: Ogres are one of the more prolific giant species of the Northlands. Large groups of ogres frequently rampage across the forests and hills, attacking communities of dwarves, humans, and trollkin. At the head of many of these groups stands an ogre that towers over the rest, an abomination of bulging muscle and fearsome tusks.

{@deity Angrboda|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} and {@deity Bergelmir|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} created the first great ogre after a contest ensued between the two deities to see who could improve upon the ordinary ogre, often viewed as the weakest of all the giants. In the end, neither god won, resulting in a failed behemoth of enormous size that still retained the common ogre's avarice, selfishness, and lust for destruction.

Great ogres take enormous pleasure in smashing beautiful things and reducing humanoids to gory paste. They often wield tree trunks and anchors as mauls, and the vilest among them wear mummified humanoid limbs as jewelry.

entries.name: Runewright
entries: {@i Greedy Undead Wizard}
{@color A skeletally thin, robed figure saunters toward you, writhing runes on its gray skin glowing with putrid light.|006abe}

items.name: Habitat:
items.entry: Any

items.name: Treasure:
items.entry: Arcana, Relics

entries: A runewright is a rune using wizard whose obsession with gathering magical knowledge and power continues beyond its death. Runewrights seek magic of all kinds, hoping that amassing it will give them insight into the nature of the runes, and indeed the fundamental nature of magic itself. It is a hunger that will never be sated and only ends with the runewright's destruction.

A runewright bears some resemblance to the person it was in life, especially with regard to its clothing and adornments. However, beneath its clothes, its skin takes on a stony hue, with glowing, almost writhing runes carved into it. When the runewright uses the power of a particular rune, that rune glows with a putrid light. The only rune not inscribed on the skin of a runewright is Dagaz, which symbolizes laying the dead to rest.

entries.name: Selkie
entries: {@i Seal-Skin Shapechanger}

{@color A young man dances on the shore, graceful upon the sand. When he notices you, he stops and reaches for a nearby cloak. As it swirls around his shoulders, he disappears. In his place, a seal slips beneath the ocean waves.|006abe}

items.name: Habitat:
items.entry: Coastal, Underwater

items.name: Treasure:
items.entry: Any

entries: Selkies are fey creatures that transform into seals using magical sealskins. Their humanoid forms are beautiful, with webbed hands and feet. If deprived of its sealskin, a selkie can't change its shape and will do all it can to retrieve the skin. Selkies vary in temperament; some are kind, while others are malicious tricksters.

Selkies live on secluded islands but travel to coastlands in summer to trade with coastal enclaves, sometimes even wooing or marrying fisherfolk. Selkies rarely remain, for the sea and its freedom call to them each high tide.

Selkies believe that long ago, an archfey of seals gave them their magical sealskins. Stealing a selkie's sealskin is considered the gravest of crimes, and they will band together to retrieve a stolen sealskin, often with violent consequences. Some selkies have learned to disguise their skins as items of clothing, especially disheveled or mundane clothing, such as belts, hats, vests, or cloaks, to avoid attracting the attention of thieves. An individual selkie's skin works only for them, becoming nonmagical when it dies, and can't be used by anyone else, even other selkies.

Legends tell of selkie tribes that use the skins of other sea animals to change shape. Such selkies use the skins of sharks, giant sea horses, or even orcas, and can assume those forms instead of a seal form.

entries.name: Skein Witch
entries: {@i Fell Fateweaver}
{@color The shambling figure is draped in writhing, diamond thread. Its skin is translucent, and dozens of quivering hourglasses are suspended inside its body in place of organs.|006abe}

items.name: Habitat:
items.entry: Any

items.name: Treasure:
items.entry: Any

entries: Skein witches are curators of destiny and enforcers of what must be. They voyage across the planes, weaving the strands of fate at the behest of their goddess creator. Although they carry out their charge without regard to petty mortal concerns, they can be persuaded to bend fate for powerful petitioners whose interests align with those of their goddess.

Despite their supernatural abilities, a skein witch's physical body is frail. Because of that, they tend to surround themselves with undead, constructs, or other brutish, soulless guardians cut free from the thread of fate.
Legends say that if a {@item Deck of Many Things|XDMG} is brought close to a skein witch, the witch emits a psychic wail and disintegrates.

entries.name: Skeljaskra
entries: {@i Scaled Rolling Doom}
{@color A hippo-sized beast with blue-white, pangolin-like armor, spits burning poison at a nearby villager.|006abe}

items.name: Habitat:
items.entry: Arctic, Hill, Mountain

items.name: Treasure:
items.entry: Any

entries: The voracious skeljaskra is known for indiscriminately devouring creatures, vegetation, and structures over the course of several days of constant movement and destruction. A single skeljaskra can consume hundreds of pounds of food in a single day, whether that takes the form of an elk, a field of crops, or an entire small house. Once it has sated its legendary appetite, the skeljaskra finds a cave to slumber in for weeks while it digests its massive meal.

Fortunately, the skeljaskra is typically encountered alone. However, in ill-fated years, an entire pack can emerge from the wilderness, descending on a village and devouring everything in its path. Such an event sends all living creatures fleeing from the utter destruction and leaves almost nothing behind.
Although skeljaskra can consume virtually anything, they don't digest minerals. Their droppings often contain metal or stone remnants of past meals, from iron nails to coins to small gemstones.
Once every few generations, a skeljaskra hibernates in a place suffused by magic. Over many years, it grows into a threat to entire settlements. Such horrors are known as dread skeljaskra.

entries.name: Skogsra
entries: {@i Bloodthirsty Spirit of the Woods}
{@color A bewildered traveler wanders through the forest ahead of you, clearly lost.|006abe}

items.name: Habitat:
items.entry: Forest

items.name: Treasure:
items.entry: Any

entries: The skogsra is a malign forest creature that feeds on mortal blood. It often presents itself as a beautiful person of friendly temperament, seeking the help of a traveler or hunter. It entices its victims into the forest, where it tears them to shreds as it reveals its true form: a hollow, bark-skinned monster with long, twisted limbs tipped with venomous claws. The skogsra can extend fleshy vines out of its hollow form to grasp and tangle its prey. It uses these natural weapons to overcome and paralyze its target, pulling the helpless victim into its hollow body, where it can consume the poor soul later at its leisure.
When outnumbered or facing a potent enemy, the skogsra channels the power of the storm, calling forth mighty winds, hail, and lightning.

entries.name: Trolls
entries: As a land full of giants, it's not surprising that the Northlands is home to a variety of trolls, some of which are rarely seen elsewhere.

entries.name: Troll, Fjord
entries: {@i Canny, Regenerating Fisherfolk}
{@color What looks like a troll with slimy skin and webbed fingers is pulling up a net full of fish onto a boat. It spots you and grins maliciously.|006abe}

items.name: Habitat:
items.entry: Arctic, Coastal, Swamp

items.name: Treasure:
items.entry: None

entries: Fjord trolls dwell on the coastlines of the Northern fjords and fish for sustenance in boats of their own making. They are at home in water and possess a fatty layer beneath their skin that helps protect them from the near-freezing temperatures. Webbing between their fingers and toes aid them in swimming. Despite their ease in the water, fjord trolls often fish from canoes constructed of wood and hide, which they row using their long arms and webbed hands instead of oars or paddles. Those same hands end in hooked and barbed claws that secrete a paralytic poison. This makes them effective at capturing fish and other creatures of the coast. They also have a special craw that they can fill with ice cold water and spit at their enemies.

entries.name: Troll, Gilitrutt
entries: {@i Loyal, shapeshifting guardian troll}
{@color A small troll lopes along the forest floor, muttering to itself. When it spots you, it shifts into a massive hound and charges.|006abe}

items.name: Habitat:
items.entry: Arctic, Coastal, Swamp

items.name: Treasure:
items.entry: None

entries: Gilitrutt trolls are among the smallest of troll-kind but make up for their diminutive stature by being able to shapeshift into the form of a giant hound. They mostly dwell with other trolls, acting in supporting roles, such as companions, guards, and hunting partners. Gilitrutt trolls have been known to abduct people from other settlements, and they sometimes do so after toying with the individual, making some kind of bargain the abductee typically finds difficult to fulfill.

Gilitrutt trolls are fiercely loyal, and if their companions or settlements are under threat, they defend them savagely, even giving their own lives in that defense. In addition to speaking Giant, gilitrutt trolls can communicate with one another through a series of grunts, growls, clicks, and whistles.

entries.name: Troll, Glacial
entries: {@i Grotesque Glacial Terror}

{@color A layer of jagged blue ice covers the back, arms, and claws of this pale green troll. Its eyes glow with demonic cerulean radiance, and black veins pulse underneath its translucent flesh.|006abe}

items.name: Habitat:
items.entry: Arctic, Mountain, Underground

items.name: Treasure:
items.entry: Individual

entries: Trolls have adapted to almost every environment in the world, from sweltering jungles to magically tainted sewers, yet few environments are as harsh as the glaciers and tundra deserts of the Northlands, places most trolls fear to tread.

Dwelling among these glaciers is the glacial troll, a giant that feeds on the frozen bodies of unlucky creatures. What makes the glacial troll even more repulsive is that many of the creatures trapped in ice are still vaguely aware of their surroundings when the troll begins to feed.
Glacial trolls sometimes work as guards for frost giants, though the frost giants are careful to provide the trolls with sufficient food to keep them satisfied.

entries.name: Troll, Wind
entries: {@i Capricious Storm-chasing Prankster}
{@color A small troll with blue-green skin stands at the prow of the enemy ship, its blue hair whipping about, despite the absence of wind.|006abe}

items.name: Habitat:
items.entry: Arctic, Desert, Grassland, Hill, Mountain

items.name: Treasure:
items.entry: Any

entries: Wind trolls delight in storms of all kinds and will seek them out to perform intricate dances in their gales. The true nature of their connection to storms is unknown. Some believe that a wind troll absorbs a storm's power to sustain it, drawing energy and even life from such powerful occurrences. Others believe that wind trolls worship storm gods, such as {@deity Thor|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}, or might have connections to them, and so communing with storms is a kind of religious experience for them. Whatever the reason, they are often found in the midst of storms—the larger and more chaotic, the better.

Legends have it that the first wind trolls were created by {@deity Thor|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} and {@deity Loki|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}, who wished to turn some giantkin against {@deity Boreas|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} and his minions. {@deity Thor|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} soon lost interest, so instead of teaching the wind trolls to excel in battle, {@deity Loki|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook} taught them to be tricksters and stoked their interest in interfering with others.

entries.name: Vaettir
entries: Servants of the land, vættir haunt those who disrespect the wild or ancient laws and traditions.

entries.name: Vaettir, Buried Lord
entries: {@i Restless Wrathful Undead}
{@color An armored undead warrior rises from the casket, its eyes glowing with righteous indignation.|006abe}

Buried lord vaettir are undead jarls and chieftains who arise from ancient barrows. The power and presence they possessed in life remains with them after death, allowing them to command other vaettir, who instinctively recognize their authority. They are almost always accompanied by a retinue of other vaettir who served them, or others like them, while alive.
A buried lord's status can be seen in the quality of the armor and scraps of clothing that still cover it, and in its poise, which retains its lordly quality.
While all vaettir fiercely guard their burial sites, possessions, and honor, buried lord vaettir do so with a ferocity greater than their brethren.

entries.name: Vaettir, Drowned Raider
entries: {@i Rotting Waterlogged Warrior}
{@color Brown liquid drips off the corpse of a waterlogged warrior and with it, the stench of decay and mold.|006abe}

items.name: Habitat:
items.entry: Arctic, Coastal, Swamp

items.name: Treasure:
items.entry: Armaments, Implements

entries: Drowned raider vaettir are like others of their kind—restless undead warriors who defend their belongings and burial places. They are called drowned raiders, however, because their burial sites have been flooded or otherwise contaminated with sea water, which alters their forms over time. A drowned raider vaettir has rotten, corrupted flesh that is falling off its skeleton, and it drips liquid constantly. It can regurgitate a stream of rotten, flesh-stripping seawater from its mouth.

While vaettir often defend their burial sites and possessions with a persistent fury, drowned raider vaettir tend to be more chaotic and unpredictable due to the disruption of their lairs and their bodies.

Sometimes, the flooding of a burial site pulls the vaettir's belongings out of their resting place and deposits them in distant places, drawn by the sea's currents. The drowned raider is drawn to these far-flung objects and will hunt them down in an attempt to restore itself to rest.

entries.name: Vedaja
entries: {@i Small Murderous Homunculus}
{@color A curious wooden statue, about the size of a child, stands alone, facing a forlorn corner of the desolate room.|006abe}

items.name: Habitat:
items.entry: Arctic, Coastal, Urban

items.name: Treasure:
items.entry: None

entries: Vedaja are little constructs, usually made of wood or horn, and animated by rune magic. The runes are carved into the vedaja's body along with some of its creator's blood. Vedaja were once used for a variety of purposes, but in recent years, they have mostly been animated with violence in mind. Vedaja hands are malleable and can strike in the form of a fist or narrow to a sharp, piercing point.

The appearance of each vedaja varies, though they are usually created in humanoid form. The magical energy that animates a vedaja burns inside of it and is visible through its hollow eye holes, burning with baleful light. If the vedaja doesn't move, it appears to be an inanimate wooden statuette.
Given its size, a vedaja stalks its prey from the shadows, using its inanimate appearance at times to hide in plain sight. At times, only the blood from its previous prey betrays its nature.

entries.name: Mounts
entries: This section contains statistics for creatures that serve as mounts for PCs. Some are commonly found in the Northlands, while others are rarer.

entries.name: Andahestur
entries: {@i Wingless flying steeds}
{@color A majestic silvery grey steed soars through the air without the aid of wings, its silver hooves and eyes glinting in the waning afternoon sun.|006abe}

items.name: Habitat:
items.entry: Arctic, Planar (Valhalla)

items.name: Treasure:
items.entry: None

entries: Andahestur are the mounts granted by Odin to the Valkyries to convey them in battle. They appear as white or gray steeds with silver hooves and eyes. They cannot be purchased, but they are sometimes gifted to mortals by the gods for heroic deeds or stolen from the shield-maidens by those with truly blackened hearts.

entries.name: Moose
entries: {@i Crown-Antlered Beast}
{@color The majestic beast stands nearly 7 feet tall at the shoulder, its head crowned with wide, palmed antlers.|006abe}

items.name: Habitat:
items.entry: Arctic

items.name: Treasure:
items.entry: None

entries: The temperamental moose (also called Elg) is respected for its size and majesty by the people of the Northlands.

entries.name: Reindeer
entries: {@i Snow-Treading Wanderer}
{@color Most of the brown in this large deer's coast has shed, revealing white underneath. It appears ready for the winter as it bounds through the first flurries of the year.|006abe}

items.name: Habitat:
items.entry: Arctic

items.name: Treasure:
items.entry: None

entries: Wild reindeer can be found in vast herds in the coldest parts of the Northlands. They are acclimated to cold weather. Wild reindeer are skittish, but domesticated ones have been bred for centuries for their meat, to pull sleds, and for milk.

entries.name: Sea Serpent
entries: {@i Swift Wave Snakes}
{@color Blue-green on top with white underbellies, these enormous eel-like creatures have prominent bony ridges on their heads and wide mouths with only four sharp fangs.|006abe}

items.name: Habitat:
items.entry: Coastal, Underwater

items.name: Treasure:
items.entry: None

entries: Sea serpents are most often identified while approaching by the row of sail-like fins protruding from their backs. Wild serpents are dangerous predators, but those raised from an egg imprint on their owner and make formidable mounts or guards for raiding ships.

entries.name: Sleipnirspringr
entries: {@i Eight-Legged Divine Horse}
{@color The eight-legged horse stomps its hooves in frustration, as if the entire world moves too slow for it.|006abe}

items.name: Habitat:
items.entry: Arctic

items.name: Treasure:
items.entry: None

entries: Descended from {@deity Wotan|Norse|NorthlandsWorldbook}'s horse Sleipnir, this breed of eight-legged horse tends toward dark pelts with elaborate and unusual markings. Larger, more intelligent, and far more willful than any breed of mortal horse, sleipnirspringr rarely allow themselves to be sold and are more likely to bond to kindred spirits that they encounter in the wilds, doing great deeds, or sowing chaos. They are exceedingly rare in the Northlands, and those who are honored with a sleipnirspringr's company are said to be heroes of great renown.

entries.name: NPCs
entries: This section contains statistics for various humanoids. From faithful huskarls to mysterious witches, these NPCs can be found across the Northlands and beyond, breathing life into any place the PCs wander. The stat blocks are presented alphabetically and most assume no specific species.

entries.name: Merchant
entries: Merchants focus on trading in goods produced by others. Some are simple shopkeepers, while others sail to distant ports to buy and sell their goods.

entries.name: Trollkin
entries: {@i Fierce Raiders and Reavers}
{@color A lanky berserker with greenish skin charges toward you, bloody spittle frothing from her mouth.|006abe}

items.name: Habitat:
items.entry: Any

items.name: Treasure:
items.entry: Implements, Individual

entries: In the North, the masses huddle in fear at night, dreading the horns and howls of reavers come to slaughter and pillage. Trollkin have a well-deserved reputation for their prowess on the battlefield and longship deck. Raiding is a staple industry among the settlements in the North, and the trollkin are in high demand by recruiting captains and warlords.

In a trollkin village, warriors who prove themselves to be especially violent undergo special rituals to imbue them with the primal power of the North. Trollkin Berserkers push to fight in the front lines, eager to bring their power to bear against their foes.

Trollkin raiders might crew pillaging longships, hunt alongside a troop of other reavers, or be found among mercenary companies. They are trained equally in ranged and melee combat, depending on their regenerative nature to keep them in the battleline.

entries.name: Witch
entries: Witches seek knowledge, power, and connection in their communion with nature and the forces beyond mortal perception. They cultivate their bonds to eldritch forces, some becoming the guardians at the gate, attendants of deep knowledge, while others hold darker desires.

data.name: Appendix: Northlands Encounters
entries: In the Northlands, the chance for a random Encounter depends greatly on the type of game you are running and the danger inherent in the areas the PCs traverse. The Encounter tables below are divided into general geographical regions—Coast, Forest, Glacier/Tundra, Hill/Mountain, Ocean, Road, and Town.

The monsters indicated in the tables can be found in the {@book Northlands Worldbook|NorthlandsWorldbook|8}, {@book Tome of Beasts 1|ToB1-2023}, or the {@link core rules|https://www.dndbeyond.com/sources/dnd/br-2024}. If your roll results in such an Encounter and you don't have the appropriate book, you can roll again, substitute your own monster, or simply choose a different Encounter in that table.
